topics.title: Math and classical ML
topics.about: Linear algebra, probability, optimization, and the classical models that still win on tabular data.

questions.title: A decision tree with no depth limit scores 99% on training data and 71% on validation. What do you try first?
questions.answer: A 28-point gap between training and validation is the textbook sign of high variance: the tree has memorised the training set. Constrain it (max_depth, min_samples_leaf, pruning), or average many trees (a random forest). More data also helps, if you can get it.
options: Limit the tree: a maximum depth, or a minimum number of samples per leaf.
Train for more epochs.
Add more features so the tree has more to work with.
Switch to a deeper model, such as a neural network.

questions.title: A 10-class image classifier gets 64% on training data and 63% on validation. People score 95% on the same task. What's the problem?
questions.answer: Both numbers are low and close together: high bias (underfitting). Add capacity (a bigger model, better features), reduce regularisation, or train longer. Collecting more data is the classic wrong move here.
options: The validation set is too small.
Not enough training data.
High bias: the model is too simple to fit even the training data.
High variance: it's overfitting.

questions.title: You run 5-fold cross-validation on 10,000 rows. How many rows does each of the five models train on?
questions.answer: Each fold holds out one fifth for validation and trains on the other four fifths: 10,000 × 4/5 = 8,000 rows. Every row is used for validation exactly once across the five runs.

questions.title: A demand forecast scores 0.92 R² with random 5-fold cross-validation and 0.55 in its first month in production. What's the most likely cause?
questions.answer: Validation has to mimic deployment. A forecaster always predicts the future from the past, so validate the same way: train on everything before a cut-off date and test on what follows (a rolling or expanding window). Random folds let neighbouring days, which are highly correlated, sit on both sides of the split.
options: Five folds is too few.
The model needs more regularisation.
Production data is always noisier.
Random folds let the model train on days after the ones it's tested on.

questions.title: In a churn model, the most important feature by far is `account_closure_reason`. Validation AUC is 0.99. What do you conclude?
questions.answer: For every feature, ask: would I know this value at prediction time? A closure reason is written when the account closes, which is the event being predicted. Remove it and anything derived from it, then expect validation AUC to fall to something believable.
options: The model is overfitting, so add regularisation.
Target leakage: that field only gets filled in once a customer has churned.
Drop the feature, because one feature shouldn't dominate.
It's a strong feature. Ship the model.

questions.title: A colleague oversamples the minority class with SMOTE, then splits the data into train and test. Test recall is excellent. What's wrong?
questions.answer: SMOTE creates new minority points by interpolating between real ones. Done before splitting, a test example's near-copies land in training, and the model gets credit for recognising them. Split first, then resample only the training portion, ideally inside a pipeline so cross-validation does it per fold.
options: The test set is too small.
Nothing. SMOTE is the standard fix for imbalance.
Synthetic points built from test examples' neighbours end up in training, so the test set is contaminated.
SMOTE should be applied to the test set too.

questions.title: Out of 1,000 transactions, 20 are fraud. Your model flags 50 transactions, and 15 of those are fraud. What is its precision?
questions.answer: Precision = true positives ÷ everything flagged = 15 ÷ 50 = 0.3. Of the transactions the model flags, 30% are fraud.

questions.title: Same model: 20 frauds in the data, 15 of them flagged. What is its recall?
questions.answer: Recall = true positives ÷ all actual positives = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75. The model catches three quarters of the fraud.

questions.title: Same model, precision 0.3 and recall 0.75. What is its F1 score? (Three decimals is fine.)
questions.answer: F1 is the harmonic mean: 2 × 0.3 × 0.75 ÷ (0.3 + 0.75) = 0.45 ÷ 1.05 = 0.429. The harmonic mean is pulled towards the lower of the two, so a model can't score a high F1 by being good at only one of them.

questions.title: 1% of users are fraudulent and your model has 99% accuracy. What should you report instead?
questions.answer: With heavy imbalance, accuracy mostly measures the majority class. Report precision and recall at your operating threshold, and use PR-AUC to compare models, because it's dominated by performance on the rare class. ROC-AUC counts true negatives in its false-positive rate, and with 99 negatives per positive that rate stays small even when most flags are wrong.
options: Accuracy is fine, because 99% is high.
Precision and recall at the threshold you'll use, plus PR-AUC.
ROC-AUC alone.
Mean squared error.

questions.title: A test catches 99% of a rare condition and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. The condition affects 1 in 1,000. If someone tests positive, what's the probability they have it? (As a decimal.)
questions.answer: Out of 100,000 people, 100 have the condition and 99 of them test positive. Of the 99,900 healthy people, 1% (999) also test positive. So 99 ÷ (99 + 999) = 0.090, about 9%. Even a very accurate test has low precision when the condition is rare. Bayes' rule is the formal version of this count.

questions.title: The fraud team can review 200 cases a day. How do you choose the model's threshold?
questions.answer: When a person acts on each flag, the operational constraint sets the threshold. Rank by score and take the top k, then evaluate with precision@k. If the cost of missed fraud is known, compare it with the cost of a review to decide whether the team needs more capacity.
options: Pick the threshold that maximises F1.
Use 0.5, the default.
Pick the threshold that maximises accuracy.
Rank each day's transactions by score and send the top 200: the threshold follows from capacity.

questions.title: Your model has a ROC-AUC of 0.95, and its predicted probabilities will be used to set insurance prices. What else do you check?
questions.answer: AUC is about ranking, calibration is about the probabilities. Check a reliability diagram (bucket the predictions, compare the average prediction with the observed rate in each bucket) or the Brier score. If the curve is off, fit Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data. Boosted trees and naive Bayes are often poorly calibrated out of the box.
options: Nothing. 0.95 AUC is excellent.
Calibration: whether a predicted 20% risk really happens about 20% of the time.
Accuracy at a 0.5 threshold.
Feature importance.

questions.title: A model predicts 0.9 for an example that turns out positive. What is the log loss for that one prediction? (Natural log.)
questions.answer: Log loss for a positive is −ln(p) = −ln(0.9) = 0.105. Compare with a confident miss: predicting 0.1 for the same positive costs −ln(0.1) = 2.30, more than twenty times as much. Log loss punishes confident wrong answers hard.

questions.title: You have 500 features and suspect only about 20 matter. You want a linear model that uses few of them. Which regularisation?
questions.answer: The L1 penalty's corners sit on the axes, so the optimum often lands where many weights are exactly zero. Use elastic net (L1 + L2) when the important features are correlated with each other: plain lasso tends to pick one of a correlated group arbitrarily.
options: Dropout.
L1 (lasso): it pushes many weights to exactly zero.
L2 (ridge): it shrinks every weight.
No regularisation, then drop features with small weights.

questions.title: Your features range from 0–1 (a ratio) to 0–1,000,000 (income). Which of these models doesn't care about the difference in scale?
questions.answer: Anything based on distances, dot products or penalties on weights needs standardised features: kNN, SVMs, regularised linear models, neural networks. Tree-based models don't, because each split only compares values within one feature.
options: Logistic regression with L2 regularisation.
Gradient-boosted trees.
An SVM with an RBF kernel.
k-nearest neighbours.

questions.title: A random forest's built-in feature importance ranks `zip_code` (30,000 distinct values) at the top. Should you believe it?
questions.answer: Mean decrease in impurity is computed on training data and is biased towards high-cardinality and continuous features. Permutation importance on held-out data asks a cleaner question: how much worse does validation get when this feature is shuffled? If zip code still matters, consider target encoding (computed within folds) or grouping to region.
options: Not yet. Impurity-based importance favours features with many distinct values. Check with permutation importance on validation data.
Yes, if the forest has many trees.
No. Zip codes are never useful.
Yes. The forest found it most useful.

questions.title: k-nearest neighbours works well on 5 features but poorly once you add 195 more mostly-irrelevant ones. Why?
questions.answer: With many dimensions, the nearest and farthest neighbours end up at nearly the same distance, so "nearest" stops meaning much. Each irrelevant feature adds noise to every distance. Select features, reduce dimensions (PCA), or learn a metric. Or use a model that weights features, such as boosted trees.
options: k is too small.
kNN needs more training epochs.
The features need one-hot encoding.
In high dimensions, distances become similar for all points, and the irrelevant features drown out the useful ones.

questions.title: Two features in a linear regression have a correlation of 0.98. Their coefficients flip sign between training runs on resampled data. What's happening?
questions.answer: When two features carry nearly the same information, many combinations of their weights fit equally well, so small changes in the data swing them around. If you need interpretable coefficients, drop or combine one of them, or use ridge regression, which spreads the weight stably. The variance inflation factor (VIF) measures the problem directly.
options: The model is underfitting.
One of the features must be leaking the label.
Multicollinearity: the model can trade weight between the two almost freely, so individual coefficients are unstable.
The learning rate is too high.

questions.title: Income is missing for 30% of loan applicants, and applicants with missing income default twice as often. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: Here data is not missing at random. Not reporting income tells you something. Impute (the median, or a model-based estimate) so the model has a number, and add an indicator so it can learn that missingness matters. Gradient-boosted trees such as XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values natively by learning which branch they go down.
options: Fill with the mean and say nothing else.
Drop the rows with missing income.
Drop the income feature.
Impute a value, and add a binary "income was missing" feature.

questions.title: You have a tabular dataset and two candidate base learners: deep decision trees that fit the training rows almost perfectly, and decision stumps that barely beat a constant. You can afford one ensemble method for each. Which one gets bagging and which one gets boosting, and why?
questions.answer: Bag the deep trees and boost the stumps. Deep trees have low bias and high variance, and averaging many of them trained on bootstrap samples cancels the variance without adding bias. Stumps have high bias and low variance, and boosting builds them in sequence so each new one corrects the errors of the ensemble so far, which drives the bias down.

questions.title: Your training stack can run in float16 or in bfloat16. A teammate picks float16 because it keeps more digits. Which format do you pick for training, which for inference, and what extra mechanism does one of them need?
questions.answer: Pick bfloat16 for training. It has the same 8-bit exponent as float32, so it covers the same range up to about 3.4e38, and activations, logits and gradients that spike past 65,504 do not overflow. float16 has 10 mantissa bits and more precision, but its 5-bit exponent caps at 65,504 and underflows gradients below about 6e-8, so it needs loss scaling to train. For inference, where values are bounded and precision matters more, float16 is the usual choice.

questions.title: Two variants of a classifier differ by one hyperparameter. On one held-out split, variant B beats variant A by a small margin, and the team wants to ship B. Design the evaluation that decides whether B is better, and say what you would report.
questions.answer: One split gives one noisy number, so the gap could be chance. Run k-fold cross-validation with the same folds for both variants, keep the per-fold differences, and test whether their mean is far from zero with a paired t-statistic. Report the mean and spread of each variant's fold scores, the mean difference and the statistic, and keep the test set out of the comparison.

questions.title: Your classifier trains on a cross-entropy loss. A reviewer asks why you do not train on the KL divergence between the labels and the predictions instead. Explain how the two quantities relate and what would change, if anything, in training.
questions.answer: Cross-entropy of P and Q equals the entropy of P plus the KL divergence from P to Q. The labels fix P, so their entropy is a constant during training, and the two objectives have the same gradient. With one-hot labels the entropy is zero and the two numbers are equal: minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class.

questions.title: A colleague builds a dense layer that takes 784 inputs and gives 128 outputs. The first forward pass stops with a shape error. Which dimensions does the weight matrix need, and how do you read an error like this one?
questions.answer: The matrix is 128 by 784: one row for each output and one column for each input. A matrix product needs the inner sizes to agree, so a 128 by 784 matrix times a 784 by 1 input gives a 128 by 1 output. An error means the inner sizes differ, and the fix starts with the shapes of every operand written on paper.

questions.title: A node in a classification tree holds 6 cats and 4 dogs. Give its Gini impurity and its entropy in bits, and explain how a tree uses either number to choose a split.
questions.answer: The class shares are 0.6 and 0.4. Gini is 1 minus the sum of squared shares, so 1 minus 0.36 minus 0.16, which is 0.48. Entropy is minus the sum of share times log base 2 of share, which comes to 0.971 bits. The tree tries every feature and threshold and keeps the split with the largest drop from the parent's impurity to the weighted impurity of the two children.

questions.title: You add a new layer to a from-scratch network and run a gradient check. The relative error between the analytical and the numerical gradient is about 1e-3 for one weight. A teammate says the backward pass has a bug. Before you agree, how do you decide whether the fault is in the backward pass or in the check itself?
questions.answer: A relative error near 1e-3 is in the warning band, so first make the check trustworthy. Use the two-sided difference, set the step to the range from 1e-5 to 1e-7, run the check in float64, and compute the relative error with the max of both magnitudes in the denominator. If the error stays near 1e-3 or grows under those conditions, the backward pass is wrong; if it drops below 1e-5, the check was at fault.

questions.title: A language model scores a sentence as the product of the probability of each word. For long sentences the score is exactly zero, and two long sentences can no longer be compared. What went wrong, and what do you compute instead?
questions.answer: The product of many small probabilities underflows to zero in floating point. Add the log probabilities instead, and the sum stays a finite negative number. A more negative sum means a less likely sentence, and the order of the sentences is unchanged.

questions.title: You fit a logistic regression with gradient descent on a small dataset where one line separates the two classes with no errors. The loss falls at every epoch, the weights grow at every epoch, and the run never settles. A colleague proposes a squared error loss instead, because it has a clear bottom. What is happening, and what do you do?
questions.answer: On separable data the log loss has no finite minimum: scaling the weights up pushes every probability closer to its label and the loss closer to zero, so descent walks forever. Squared error through a sigmoid is a worse trade, because that cost surface is not convex and has flat regions where the gradient dies. Keep the log loss and add an L2 penalty, which gives one finite, unique minimum.

questions.title: A random forest's feature importance puts a user id column near the top of the list. The column is an integer with a different value in almost every row. The team wants to build a product rule around it. What do you tell them, and how do you check?
questions.answer: The default importance is the mean decrease in impurity, summed over every split that used the feature. A column that is distinct on nearly every row offers a huge number of candidate thresholds, so trees split on it to carve out small pure groups by chance, and those impurity drops add up on the training data. Run a permutation importance check instead: shuffle the column on held-out data, measure the drop in accuracy, and expect close to zero for an id.

questions.title: You minimize the Rosenbrock function from the point (-1, 1). Plain gradient descent creeps along the curved valley and needs thousands of steps. The same run with momentum arrives much sooner. Explain what the valley does to plain descent and what momentum changes.
questions.answer: In a narrow valley the gradient points across the valley, not along it, so each plain step jumps from one wall to the other and makes little progress toward the minimum. Momentum keeps a velocity that sums past gradients. The across components flip sign and cancel, the along component keeps its sign and builds up, so the path is smooth and fast.

questions.title: A regression report shows a negative R-squared on the test set. A teammate says the metric code must be broken, because R-squared lives between 0 and 1. How do you answer?
questions.answer: R-squared is one minus the ratio of the residual sum of squares to the total sum of squares around the mean. It is 1 for a perfect fit, 0 for a model that only predicts the mean, and below zero when the model does worse than that constant. A negative value is a real result, and it says the fitted model hurts on this data.

questions.title: A team keeps growing a model. Test error falls, then spikes as the parameter count approaches the number of training rows, then falls again as they keep going. The classical U-shaped curve predicts the spike but not the second fall. Explain what the curve shows, and give the team a rule about model size.
questions.answer: The spike sits at the interpolation threshold, where the model has just enough capacity to fit every training row and is forced into one specific, noise-sensitive solution, so variance peaks. Past it, many solutions fit the training data and gradient descent's implicit regularization picks a simple one, so error falls again. That is double descent. The rule: stay well below the threshold with explicit regularization, or go well past it; the worst place to sit is on it.

questions.title: A language model has a vocabulary of V tokens. On a held-out text, its mean cross-entropy per token, measured in nats, equals the natural log of V. Estimate the perplexity and say what the number tells you about the model.
questions.answer: Perplexity is the exponential of the mean cross-entropy, so here it equals V. On average the model is as uncertain as a uniform pick over the whole vocabulary. A trained model should sit far below V. The mean alone does not prove that the model learned nothing, because other per-token predictions can give the same average, so check per-token predictions and the data.

questions.title: Automatic differentiation can push derivatives forward from the inputs or pull them backward from the output. Training frameworks pick the backward direction. Why, and in which situation would the forward direction be the better choice?
questions.answer: A network has millions of parameters and one scalar loss. Reverse mode seeds the output with a gradient of 1 and gets the gradient of every parameter in one backward sweep. Forward mode needs one sweep for each input variable, so it wins only when the inputs are few and the outputs are many.

questions.title: A teammate standardizes the whole table with a scaler, then splits it into training, validation and test rows, and reports a test score. In production the score is well below that number. Name the fault in the pipeline and describe a setup where the test number predicts production.
questions.answer: The scaler saw the test rows, so the mean and standard deviation carried information from the test set into training. That is data leakage, and it makes the reported score optimistic. Split first, fit every preprocessing step on the training rows only, and apply the fitted transform to the other two sets.

questions.title: A from-scratch cross-entropy passes its unit tests on small logits. On real batches the loss comes back as inf. You print the batch and one logit vector is [100, 101, 102]. Walk me through the cause and the fix, and say why the fix is not an approximation.
questions.answer: The exponential of 100 is about 2.69 times 10 to the 43, far past the float32 maximum of about 3.4 times 10 to the 38, so each term of the softmax denominator overflows and the ratio is inf or nan. Subtract the largest logit from every logit before the exponential. The probabilities are identical in exact arithmetic, and the largest term is now exp(0), which is 1.

questions.title: Take-home. Build a stacking ensemble on a tabular classification dataset with three base models from different families and a logistic regression meta-learner. Deliver the training code, a comparison with each base model alone, and a written argument that the meta-learner was never trained on a prediction made for a row the base model had already seen. Describe how you structure the work and what you check before you submit.
questions.answer: Generate the meta-features with k-fold cross-validation: for each fold, fit the base models on the other folds and predict the held-out fold, so every training row gets base predictions from models that did not train on it. Fit the meta-learner on those out-of-fold predictions, then refit the base models on all training rows for test time. Compare on a test set that neither level touched, and report the base models and the stack side by side with fold spreads.

questions.title: A binary classifier reports 95 percent accuracy on a dataset where 95 percent of the rows are negative. The product owner is happy. You are not. Which numbers do you ask for, and how do you choose the decision threshold for this product?
questions.answer: A model that always says negative also gets that accuracy, so the number proves nothing. Ask for the confusion matrix, then precision, recall and F1 at the current threshold, and the AUC-ROC for the ranking. Move the threshold from the default of 0.5 toward the error that costs the product more: raise it when a false positive is expensive, lower it when a missed positive is expensive.

questions.title: A feature pipeline computes the variance of a column with the formula mean of x squared minus the square of the mean, in float32. On a column with values near one million the result is far from the true value and sometimes negative. Explain the cause and propose a formula that holds.
questions.answer: The two terms are each about 10 to the 12 and almost equal, and their difference is the small true variance. In float32 the spacing between neighboring numbers at that size is far larger than the variance, so the subtraction returns rounding noise, which can be negative. Compute the variance from centered values instead: subtract the mean first, or use the running update that the lesson calls the Welford algorithm.

topics.title: Deep learning
topics.about: Backpropagation, losses, optimizers, initialization and how to debug a network that does not learn.

questions.title: A freshly initialised 10-class classifier should predict roughly uniform probabilities. What cross-entropy loss should you see on the very first batch? (Natural log.)
questions.answer: Uniform predictions give each class probability 1/10, so the loss is −ln(1/10) = ln 10 = 2.303. It's a free sanity check. A language model with a 50,000-token vocabulary should start near ln 50,000 ≈ 10.8. A first loss far above that means the initialisation is too large (confident wrong predictions). A first loss far below it means the labels are leaking into the inputs.

questions.title: Training loss sits at 2.30 for a 10-class problem and doesn't move for 1,000 steps. What's your first debugging step?
questions.answer: Loss stuck at ln(classes) means the outputs are still uniform: gradients aren't reaching the weights, or they don't change anything. The classic causes are a learning rate of 0 or tiny, the optimiser not given the model's parameters, a forgotten optimizer.step() or zero_grad(), frozen layers, or inputs and labels that don't line up. Overfitting one batch separates "the code is broken" from "the problem is hard" in a couple of minutes.
options: Add more layers.
Try to overfit a single batch of 32 examples. If it can't, the bug is in the code, not the data.
Collect more data.
Train for 10,000 more steps.

questions.title: Training loss keeps falling. Validation loss falls until epoch 5, then rises every epoch. What's happening, and what do you do?
questions.answer: Training loss falling while validation loss rises means the model is fitting noise specific to the training set. Stop at the best validation epoch, then reduce the gap: weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, a smaller model, or more data.
options: Train longer and validation will come back down.
Overfitting from epoch 5: keep the epoch-5 checkpoint (early stopping), then add regularisation or augmentation.
The learning rate is too low.
Validation data has a bug.

questions.title: Loss jumps up and down by a lot from step to step and doesn't trend down. What do you change first?
questions.answer: Wild oscillation with no downward trend is the classic sign of a learning rate that's too high. Lower it, add warmup if you haven't, and check the batch isn't tiny (very noisy gradients look similar). A learning-rate range test, increasing the rate gradually over a few hundred steps and watching where the loss starts to blow up, finds a sensible value quickly.
options: Lower the learning rate, by 3–10×.
Use a bigger model.
Raise the learning rate to escape a bad region.
Remove the learning-rate warmup.

questions.title: Training in fp16, the loss suddenly becomes NaN after 200 steps. What's the most likely cause?
questions.answer: fp16's range is narrow, so a spike in activations or gradients overflows to inf, and the next operation produces NaN. Fixes, roughly in order: use bf16 if the hardware supports it (fp32's exponent range), use dynamic loss scaling with fp16, clip gradients, lower the learning rate, and look for an unstable operation such as a softmax or log on unclamped values.
options: The model is too small.
Too much weight decay.
The dataset contains NaN labels.
Values overflowing fp16's range, which tops out around 65,504: exploding activations or gradients.

questions.title: Evaluating the same checkpoint twice on the same validation set gives 81.2% and then 79.6%. What did you forget?
questions.answer: In training mode, dropout randomly zeroes activations and batch norm uses the current batch's statistics, so outputs change from run to run. Call model.eval() before evaluation (and wrap it in torch.no_grad() to save memory), then model.train() before training resumes.
options: Turning off gradient calculation.
Setting a random seed for the validation loader.
Switching the model to evaluation mode, so dropout is still active.
Shuffling the validation set.

questions.title: The learning rate warms up linearly from 0 to 3e-4 over the first 2,000 steps. What is it at step 500?
questions.answer: Linear warmup: lr = 3e-4 × 500 ÷ 2,000 = 7.5e-05. Warmup avoids huge, badly-directed updates in the first steps, before Adam's moment estimates have settled. It matters most for transformers trained with large learning rates.

questions.title: After warmup, the learning rate follows a cosine decay from 3e-4 down to 0 over the remaining steps. What is it exactly halfway through the decay?
questions.answer: Cosine schedule: lr = min + ½ (max − min)(1 + cos(π t ÷ T)). At t = T/2, cos(π/2) = 0, so lr = ½ × 3e-4 = 1.5e-04. The rate falls slowly at first, fastest in the middle, and slowly again at the end.

questions.title: Why do most transformer fine-tuning recipes use AdamW rather than Adam with an L2 penalty added to the loss?
questions.answer: In plain Adam, an L2 term becomes part of the gradient, then gets rescaled by the per-parameter adaptive denominator, so the effective regularisation varies by parameter in ways nobody intended. AdamW subtracts lr × weight_decay × w separately from the adaptive update, so decay behaves like true weight decay. In practice it generalises better and its settings transfer more reliably between models.
options: AdamW is faster per step.
AdamW doesn't need a learning rate.
With Adam, an L2 penalty gets divided by the adaptive denominator, so weights with large gradients are barely regularised. AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights.
Adam can't train transformers.

questions.title: You raise the batch size from 256 to 1,024 on the same SGD setup. What's a common starting point for the learning rate?
questions.answer: For SGD, the linear scaling rule (multiply the learning rate by the batch-size ratio, with warmup) is a good starting point up to fairly large batches. For Adam-style optimisers, square-root scaling is a common heuristic. Either way, treat it as a starting point and check with a short sweep.
options: Divide it by 4.
Keep it the same.
Multiply it by 4 (linear scaling), with a warmup.
Learning rate doesn't depend on batch size.

questions.title: A transformer trains well but the loss spikes sharply every few thousand steps, then slowly recovers. What's a standard fix?
questions.answer: Occasional loss spikes usually come from a rare batch producing a huge gradient. Gradient-norm clipping rescales the whole gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold, so the direction is kept but the step is bounded. If spikes continue, lower the learning rate, check for bad data in those batches, and look at the Adam epsilon and beta2 settings.
options: Remove the warmup.
Raise the learning rate.
Switch from AdamW to plain SGD.
Clip the global gradient norm, often to 1.0.

questions.title: With He initialisation for a ReLU layer that has 512 inputs, what is the standard deviation of the initial weights? (Three decimals.)
questions.answer: He initialisation draws weights with variance 2 ÷ fan_in, so std = √(2 ÷ 512) = 0.0625. The factor of 2 makes up for ReLU zeroing half its inputs, which keeps the variance of activations roughly constant from layer to layer. Xavier (Glorot) uses 1 ÷ fan_in, or 2 ÷ (fan_in + fan_out), which suits tanh.

questions.title: You train a segmentation model with batch norm, and memory limits you to 2 images per GPU. Results are poor and noisy. Why, and what do you do?
questions.answer: Batch norm normalises with the mean and variance of the current batch. With 2 examples those estimates are mostly noise, and the running statistics used at evaluation time don't match what training saw. GroupNorm and LayerNorm normalise within each example, so they don't depend on batch size. SyncBatchNorm computes statistics across all GPUs.
options: Remove all normalisation.
Use a larger learning rate.
Batch statistics computed from 2 examples are very noisy. Use group or layer normalisation, or synchronised batch norm across GPUs.
Batch norm doesn't work with images.

questions.title: A plain 50-layer network trains worse than an 18-layer one, even on the training set. What's the usual fix?
questions.answer: Worse *training* accuracy with more layers is the degradation problem, not overfitting. Residual connections (x + f(x)) make the identity function easy to represent and give gradients a direct path back through the network. Normalisation and careful initialisation help too. This is the ResNet result, and it's why every transformer block has two residual connections.
options: More dropout.
More training data.
A larger learning rate.
Residual (skip) connections, so each block learns a change to its input.

questions.title: Adam keeps a running average of the gradient and a running average of its square, and divides each by one minus beta to the power t before the update. A teammate deletes those two divisions to simplify the code. What changes in the first steps of training, and when does the change stop mattering?
questions.answer: Both averages start at zero, so at step one the first moment is only (1 - beta1) times the gradient, a tenth of it with beta1 at 0.9, and the second moment is a thousandth of the squared gradient with beta2 at 0.999. The divisions rescale both to unbiased estimates. Without them the square root of the second moment is shrunk more than the first moment, so the ratio and the step come out too large while the averages warm up. The first moment's factor is close to 1 after about 50 steps, but the second moment's factor, 1 - 0.999 to the t, stays well below 1 for thousands of steps, so without the division the step stays too large for that long.

questions.title: You want weight decay on a transformer trained with Adam. One engineer adds an L2 penalty on the weights to the loss. Another uses an AdamW optimizer with a weight decay argument. They say the two are the same thing. Are they, and which do you choose?
questions.answer: They are the same only under plain SGD. In Adam, a penalty inside the loss becomes part of the gradient and is divided by the running gradient size like every other term, so weights with large gradient variance get less decay and weights with small variance get more. AdamW subtracts lr times lambda times w after the adaptive update, so every weight shrinks by the same fraction. Choose AdamW; the lesson makes it the default for transformers for this reason.

questions.title: Take-home. Implement a learning rate schedule as one function of the step: a linear ramp from zero to a peak, a cosine decay from the peak to a floor, and a fixed floor after the last step. Deliver tests that pin the value at every boundary, prove the curve has no jumps, and show that a resumed run lands on the right value. Describe your design and your tests.
questions.answer: Write one function with three branches: up to the warmup step, the peak times the step over the warmup length; between the warmup step and the total, the floor plus half the gap times one plus the cosine of pi times the progress since warmup ended; past the total, the floor. Test the fixed points: zero at step zero, the peak at the end of warmup from both branches, the floor at the last step and the floor one step later. Add a continuity test that bounds each one step change, and a resume test that computes the schedule from a saved global step.

questions.title: After a few hundred steps at a high learning rate, a ReLU network's loss stops falling. You log the activations after each ReLU, and in two layers more than half of them are exactly zero on every batch. Explain what happened to those units, why they cannot come back on their own, and what you change.
questions.answer: First confirm that the units are dead and not only sparse: over a large sample, a dead unit is zero on every input. A ReLU unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input outputs zero and has a derivative of zero, so it receives no gradient and its weights never move again. A large update, driven by the high learning rate, pushed those units' weights and biases far enough negative that no input brings them back. Lower the learning rate, re-initialize the dead units or the dead layers, and move to an activation with a gradient on the negative side, such as a leaky variant or GELU.

questions.title: Xavier initialization sets the weight variance to 2 over the sum of fan in and fan out. Kaiming initialization sets it to 2 over fan in. Both are called variance preserving. Explain what each one preserves, where the 2 in Kaiming comes from, and what happens to a 50 layer ReLU network that starts from a plain standard normal.
questions.answer: A layer's pre-activation variance is fan in times the weight variance times the input variance, so a weight variance of 1 over fan in keeps the signal size constant through a linear layer. Xavier balances that condition between the forward and the backward pass, which gives 2 divided by the total of the two fan counts, and it suits sigmoid and tanh, which are near linear around zero. ReLU zeroes half of its inputs and halves the variance at each layer, so Kaiming doubles the variance of each weight to 2 over fan in to compensate. A standard normal with a fan in of 512 multiplies the variance by 512 at every layer, and the signal explodes within a few layers.

questions.title: A team ports a vision training recipe to a transformer and keeps batch normalization. Training is unstable, and text generation with one sequence at a time produces garbage. Explain why transformers use layer normalization instead, and when you would go a step further to RMSNorm.
questions.answer: Batch normalization normalizes each feature across the batch, so its statistics depend on the batch size and on which sequences share the batch; with small batches they are noisy, with a batch of one they are meaningless, and training and inference run different code paths. Layer normalization normalizes across the features of one sample, so it does not depend on the batch and is identical in both modes, which is what variable length sequences and single sequence generation need. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the shift parameter, keeps the accuracy, and saves about 10 percent of the normalization cost, which is why most recent large language models use it.

questions.title: A run trains for hours with a smooth loss. Then, within three logging intervals, the loss jumps, becomes inf, and every value after that is NaN. The same recipe worked on a smaller model. Give your ranked list of causes, the evidence that separates them, and the changes that keep it from happening again.
questions.answer: A clean run that dies late is almost always an oversized update: the peak learning rate is too high for the larger model, a rare batch produced a huge gradient, or the schedule reached its peak at a point where the model was already sensitive. The logs separate the cases: for an explosion the gradient norm spikes before the loss does, while a forward pass overflow, such as a softmax without the max shift or a normalization over a zero variance, shows a normal norm and a loss that goes to inf in one step. Fix with gradient clipping by norm at 1.0, a lower peak with warmup, and a loss computed from logits, then resume from the last good checkpoint.

questions.title: A ten class classifier trains for many epochs, and the cross-entropy loss sits at about 2.3 the whole time, on training data and on validation data. Nothing crashes. What does that number tell you, and in which order do you debug?
questions.answer: Minus the natural log of one tenth is about 2.3, the loss of a model that gives every class the same probability, and the lesson's table reads a loss stuck there as a uniform prediction with no usable signal. The mean alone does not say why. Run the one batch overfit test first: a failure points at the loss, the backward pass, the optimizer hookup or misaligned labels, and a pass sends you to the data path to check that labels line up with inputs. Only then look at the learning rate, the gradients and the architecture.

questions.title: A binary classifier trained with mean squared error on a balanced dataset settles on an output near 0.5 for every input. The loss is low and stable, and the optimizer reports no problem. Explain why the optimizer is content and which loss you switch to.
questions.answer: With two classes split evenly, a constant output of 0.5 gives a squared error of 0.25 on every row, which the lesson calls the minimum MSE a model can reach without learning anything, and the sigmoid's flat regions give MSE almost no gradient near a confident wrong answer. Cross-entropy charges minus the log of the predicted probability of the true class: 0.693 for 0.5, 0.01 for 0.99 and 4.6 for 0.01, so it pushes each prediction toward its label. Switch to binary cross-entropy.

questions.title: You are about to launch a multi-day training run on a new architecture with a new data pipeline. Design a check that runs in about 30 seconds and must pass before the run starts. List the classes of bugs it catches and the ones it does not.
questions.answer: Take one small batch of 8 to 32 samples and train on it alone for a few hundred steps. The loss must fall to near zero and the training accuracy must reach 100 percent. A pass shows that the loss function, the backward pass and the optimizer hookup work, and that the model can fit this batch, but not that each input has its correct label, because a model can memorize a wrong but consistent pairing as well. It says nothing about generalization, leakage or the full data loader, so it is the first gate and not the last.

questions.title: You inherit a model with no known good learning rate and a compute budget of a few hours. Design the procedure that picks the peak learning rate and the schedule for the run, and say what you log to defend the choice.
questions.answer: Run a learning rate range test first: train for about a hundred steps while the rate grows exponentially from 1e-7 toward 10 and record the loss at each rate. Take the rate where the loss falls fastest and set the peak about 10 times lower. Then run a linear warmup over 1 to 5 percent of the steps into a cosine decay with a floor near a tenth of the peak, or the 1cycle policy when the budget is short and the total step count is fixed. Log the range test curve, the schedule curve and the gradient norm beside the learning rate at every step.

questions.title: A transformer with Kaiming-initialized weights trains without trouble at 20 layers and diverges at 126 layers with the same recipe. Nothing else changed. Explain why depth breaks it even with a variance preserving initialization, and what the GPT-2 style fix does.
questions.answer: Kaiming keeps the variance constant through each sub-layer, but a residual block adds the sub-layer's output back onto its input, and the variance of a sum of independent terms adds. With N residual additions the stream's variance grows in proportion to N, so a deeper stack carries a larger residual signal, and the attention logits and feed-forward activations built from it grow with it. The GPT-2 fix scales the weights of the layers that write into the residual stream by 1 over the square root of 2N, so the accumulated variance stays the same at any depth.

questions.title: A network has ten hidden layers, each with a sigmoid activation. Estimate the largest factor that the sigmoid derivatives alone let a gradient keep on the way from the loss to the first layer, and say what that number means for training.
questions.answer: The sigmoid derivative is s times (1 - s), which peaks at 0.25 when the output is 0.5. Backpropagation multiplies by that derivative once per layer, so after ten layers the activation factors multiply to at most 0.25 to the tenth power, about one millionth. Each layer also multiplies by its transposed weight matrix, and weights with a norm above 1 can enlarge the gradient, so the figure bounds only the activation part. With the small initial weights of the lesson, the first layers receive almost no signal and stay near their initialization while the last layers learn, which is the vanishing gradient problem.

questions.title: A junior engineer removes every activation function from a 10 layer network to make it faster and reports that training still runs and the loss still falls. What did they build, and why will it fail on XOR or on a spiral dataset?
questions.answer: Two linear layers compose into one: W2 (W1 x + b1) + b2 equals (W2 W1) x + (W2 b1 + b2), which is a single matrix and a single bias. Ten linear layers are one linear layer with extra parameters and the same decision boundary, a hyperplane. XOR and a spiral need a curved boundary, so the network cannot fit them at any width or depth.

questions.title: A saved model gives a different test accuracy each time you evaluate it on the same test set with the same weights. The data loader does not shuffle. What is the most likely cause, and which two layer types are involved?
questions.answer: The model is still in training mode at test time. Dropout keeps zeroing random units, so each forward pass runs a different subnetwork, and batch normalization keeps using the mean and variance of the current batch instead of its running averages. Switch to evaluation mode before inference and turn gradient tracking off.

questions.title: A transformer recipe starts the learning rate at zero and ramps it linearly up to the peak during the first steps, then decays it with a cosine. A teammate wants to start at the peak to save those steps. Explain what the ramp protects, how long it should be, and how to write it down so the recipe scales to a longer run.
questions.answer: The first updates are the fragile ones: the weights sit near their initialization, Adam's running estimates of the gradient mean and variance are built from a handful of samples, and the gradient norm is large and noisy. A full size step on that footing diverges or drops the model into a plateau it never leaves. Warmup keeps the effective step small until the statistics settle, over about 1 to 5 percent of the total steps, and the schedule should express that length as a fraction of the run rather than as a fixed step count.

questions.title: A single perceptron learns the AND and OR gates in a few epochs. On the XOR gate it never converges, even after 1000 epochs. Why not, and what is the smallest change to the model that makes XOR learnable?
questions.answer: A perceptron takes a weighted sum, adds a bias and applies a threshold, so its decision boundary is one straight line. AND and OR put their ones on one side of a line. XOR puts the ones at (0, 1) and (1, 0) and the zeros at (0, 0) and (1, 1), and no single line separates those two pairs. Add a hidden layer: two neurons that compute OR and NAND, and an output neuron that ANDs them, give XOR exactly.

questions.title: A network with a hidden layer of 512 units is initialized with every weight and every bias at zero. Training runs for thousands of epochs and the loss barely moves. Learning rate and data both check out. What is wrong, and why does a small random perturbation of each weight fix it?
questions.answer: Every neuron in the layer starts identical, so each computes the same output, receives the same gradient and takes the same update. They stay identical for the whole run: the layer holds the parameters of 512 neurons and the function of one. Random initialization gives each neuron its own starting point, so the gradients differ and the neurons learn different features. The scale of that randomness then decides whether the signal survives the depth.

topics.title: Transformers
topics.about: Attention, positions, the transformer block, the KV cache and the cost of long context.

questions.title: What is a foundation model, and how is it different from a regular ML model?
questions.answer: A foundation model is pretrained at very large scale on broad data, so it learns general representations instead of solving one narrow task. That makes it a shared base you can adapt to many tasks through prompting or fine-tuning, without training from scratch. A traditional model is trained on data for one specific task. Classical models such as XGBoost are still the better choice for structured tabular data, tight latency budgets, low cost, or when you need explainable decisions.

questions.title: What is a foundation model, and how is it different from a regular ML model?
questions.answer: A single large model pretrained on broad data at massive scale, general-purpose enough to be adapted (via prompting or fine-tuning) to many downstream tasks — instead of one model trained from scratch per task.

questions.title: What is a Large Language Model, and what is it actually trained to do?
questions.answer: A neural network (almost always a decoder-only Transformer) trained to predict the next token given everything before it. Nothing more exotic than that at the objective level — the wide range of downstream behavior (chat, code, reasoning) emerges from scale plus post-training on top of that one pretraining objective.

questions.title: What is tokenization, and why can't LLMs just read raw text?
questions.answer: Splitting text into a fixed vocabulary of subword units (tokens) the model actually operates on — characters are too fine-grained (long sequences, no semantic unit), whole words are too coarse (unbounded vocabulary, can't handle unseen words).

questions.title: A BPE tokenizer meets the rare word "unfathomability". What does it do?
questions.answer: The algorithm most LLM tokenizers use to build that subword vocabulary: start from individual characters/bytes, and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until you hit a target vocabulary size. Frequent words end up as one token; rare words fall back to smaller subword pieces.
options: It adds the word to the vocabulary on the fly.
It maps the word to a single unknown-word token.
It always splits the word into single characters.
It splits the word into smaller subword pieces that are in its vocabulary.

questions.title: What are embeddings?
questions.answer: Dense numeric vectors representing tokens (or whole sentences/documents) such that semantic similarity corresponds to geometric closeness — the representation everything downstream (attention, retrieval) actually operates on.

questions.title: Remove positional encoding from a bidirectional (encoder) Transformer. How does it see "dog bites man" versus "man bites dog"?
questions.answer: Self-attention on its own is permutation-invariant — it has no notion of token order. Positional encoding injects order information into the input so the model can tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog."
options: Attention weights encode word order on their own.
It still reads left to right, like an RNN.
It can't tell them apart: each token's representation is the same in both, because self-attention ignores order.
Only the first word's position is lost.

questions.title: What is self-attention?
questions.answer: The mechanism letting every token in a sequence look at every other token and weight how much each one matters for updating its own representation — computed from Query/Key/Value projections of the same input.

questions.title: What are Query, Key, and Value in attention?
questions.answer: Three learned linear projections of the same input: Query represents "what am I looking for," Key represents "what do I offer" for every other position, and the Query·Key similarity produces attention weights that combine the Values into the output.

questions.title: You drop the 1/√d_k scaling from attention in a model with d_k = 128. What goes wrong first?
questions.answer: Without scaling, dot products grow large as the key dimension grows, pushing softmax into a region with near-zero gradients (it saturates toward one-hot). Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores in a range where softmax stays well-behaved.
options: Nothing, because softmax normalises any scale.
Scores grow with the dimension, softmax saturates towards one-hot, and gradients through it nearly vanish.
Memory use grows.
Attention becomes uniform across tokens.

questions.title: What is multi-head attention, and why not just use one big attention head?
questions.answer: Running several smaller attention computations in parallel, each with its own learned projections, then concatenating the results — letting different heads specialize in different kinds of relationships (syntax, coreference, position) instead of one head averaging everything together.

questions.title: In an encoder-decoder translation model, where do the queries, keys and values in the decoder's cross-attention come from?
questions.answer: Self-attention: Query, Key, and Value all come from the same sequence. Cross-attention: Query comes from one sequence (e.g. a decoder), Key and Value come from a different one (e.g. an encoder's output) — how an encoder-decoder model lets its decoder attend to the source input.
options: Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder's output.
All three from the decoder.
Queries from the encoder, keys and values from the decoder.
All three from the encoder.

questions.title: Someone trains a decoder-only language model and forgets the causal mask. Training loss drops unusually fast. What happens at generation time?
questions.answer: Causal masking blocks a position from attending to future positions, which is what makes autoregressive next-token generation well-defined — without it, predicting token *n* could see token *n+1*, which doesn't exist at inference time.
options: It can no longer produce text of any kind.
It generates better, because it saw more context in training.
Nothing changes, because masking only matters during inference.
It fails: in training it could see the next token, so it learned to copy instead of predict.

questions.title: A model has 24 layers and 16 key-value heads of dimension 64, and stores the cache in fp16. How much KV cache does each token add? (KiB.)
questions.answer:
Keys and values, for every layer and KV head: 2 × 24 × 16 × 64 × 2 bytes = 98,304 bytes = 96 KiB per token. A 4,000-token conversation needs about 375 MiB for one user.

Storing each generated token's Key/Value projections so they don't get recomputed on every subsequent step — without it, generating token *n* would redo the attention computation for all *n-1* prior tokens from scratch. It's also the dominant consumer of GPU memory during serving, which is why techniques like GQA/MQA exist to shrink it.

questions.title: Design the attention stack of a new 70B-class decoder that must serve 128K-token contexts on a single 80 GB accelerator at batch size one. Cover the head layout, the positional scheme, the kernel, and the memory arithmetic that ties them together.
questions.answer: Start from the memory, because it decides the rest. With 8 key-value heads, 80 layers and a head size of 128 in a 16-bit type, the stored keys and values cost 4096 bytes per token per layer, about 10 GiB at 32K and 40 GiB at 128K before a single weight is loaded. So the head layout is grouped-query or latent attention, the stored type is reduced to FP8 to halve those bytes, the positional scheme is rotation with base scaling so that the model reaches 128K without a position table, and the kernel is a tiled one so that the N by N scores never touch main memory. Then count again: at 16 bits the weights of a 70B-class model alone are larger than the 80 GB card, so the weights also need a 4-bit type before the cache and the activations can fit beside them.

questions.title: An attention module between an encoder and a decoder runs without any exception, but the model's accuracy slowly falls behind the reference implementation. When you print the context tensor, its second dimension is the encoder length instead of the decoder length. Walk me through the diagnosis.
questions.answer: A module that runs and still produces the wrong shape is a broadcast bug, and a silent broadcast is the worst attention bug because it degrades accuracy instead of crashing. Write the expected shapes first: scores and weights are batch by decoder length by encoder length, and the context is batch by decoder length by the encoder state width. Then find the matmul whose operands were swapped or not transposed, fix it with one transpose or reshape, and add asserts on the shapes and on the weights summing to one.

questions.title: A paper draft shows attention heatmaps as proof that the model "reasons over the right tokens". You are the reviewer. What do you say about the heatmaps, and what would convince you that a given head does something specific?
questions.answer: Attention weights are a distribution over positions, and on their own they are not an explanation: for some tasks they can be permuted or replaced by arbitrary alternatives without changing the prediction, so a heatmap shows where mass went, not that it mattered. Ask for an ablation or a counterfactual, zero or shuffle the head and show that the prediction moves. The head roles that have survived probing are specific and testable: heads that attend to the previous token, copy heads, and induction heads that find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it.

questions.title: Count the parameters of a decoder stack with a model width of 4096, 32 layers and a SwiGLU feed-forward network at an expansion of 2.6. Then add an untied embedding and output head for a vocabulary of 128K. Where does the total land, and why is the published model of that size a little different?
questions.answer: Per block, attention takes 4 d^2 for the four projections and SwiGLU takes 3 d (r d), about 3 r d^2. At the given width and expansion that is about 67M plus 131M, about 198M per block, and 32 blocks give about 6.3B. The untied embedding and head add about 1B, so the stack lands near the published 8B. The real model uses grouped-query attention, which shrinks the key and value projections, and a wider FFN at an expansion of 3.5, which moves parameters from attention to the FFN while the total stays close.

questions.title: A decoder must not read tokens that come after the current position. A teammate proposes to run the softmax first and then set the weights of later positions to zero. Why is that wrong, and where does the usual triangle of negative infinity really come from?
questions.answer: Zeroing weights after the softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to one, and the later tokens already shaped the normalization. The mask adds minus infinity to the scores before the softmax, so the exponential gives an exact zero there and each row is a distribution over the past alone. The triangle is not a patch on attention: a causal running average is a lower-triangular row-normalized matrix, and the mask is that same zero pattern written in the input domain of the softmax.

questions.title: This is the take-home we send: train a small decoder-only transformer on a character-level text corpus of about one megabyte, on a laptop, and return the code, the loss curves and a few samples. Tell me how you would approach it, what a reviewer checks in your submission, and which results prove that the model works.
questions.answer: Build the small reference shape: a character tokenizer over the 65 symbols of the corpus, a token embedding plus a learned positional embedding, a stack of pre-norm blocks with RMSNorm, causal multi-head attention and a SwiGLU network, a final norm and a head tied to the embedding, trained with a shift-by-one cross-entropy on random 256-character windows. Use AdamW, a cosine schedule with warmup and gradient clipping at 1.0, and hold out the last 10 percent of the text for validation. The bar from the lesson: a 4-layer, 4-head model of width 128, about 800K parameters, goes from about 4.2 to about 1.5 training loss in 2,000 steps, about 6 minutes on a laptop, with validation loss under 2.0 that tracks the training loss and samples that look like the corpus.

questions.title: You lead a pretraining run with a fixed compute budget. One plan trains a 175B-parameter model on 300B tokens. Another trains a much smaller model on far more tokens. Which do you pick, how do you defend it to leadership, and when would you deliberately train past the point that the scaling law calls optimal?
questions.answer: Compute is about 6 times the parameter count times the training tokens, so the budget fixes the product and leaves the split open. The compute-optimal split is about 20 tokens per parameter; the first plan has about 1.7 tokens per parameter, which the lesson calls ten times undertrained, and a 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens beat that 175B model on every benchmark at 2.5 times less inference cost. If the model will serve a large volume, go past the optimum on purpose: train smaller and longer, because training is paid once and inference is paid forever.

questions.title: A decoder generates 100 tokens one at a time from an empty prompt. Count the token states each loop computes for the prefix: a naive loop, and a loop that caches the key and value vectors of earlier tokens. Then count the query-key comparisons that remain with the store, and name what the store deliberately leaves out.
questions.answer: The naive loop runs every prefix token through the layer again at every step, so it computes 1 plus 2 plus 3 and so on up to 100 token states, which is 5050 and grows with the square of the length. With the stored keys and values, each step computes the state of the new token only, 100 in total. The new query still meets every stored key, so the cached loop still makes 5050 query-key comparisons: the store removes the recomputed key and value vectors, not the comparisons. The store holds no queries, because a past token never asks a question again; only the newest token does.

questions.title: Between two model sizes a benchmark accuracy goes from near zero to high. The team calls it an emergent ability and asks for a larger budget to find the next jump. How do you evaluate the claim before you sign?
questions.answer: Ask what the scorer is. Exact match and thresholded accuracy are discontinuous: a model that gets most digits right scores zero until it gets all of them right, so a smooth gain in the underlying probabilities shows up as a cliff. Re-score the same checkpoints with a continuous metric such as the cross-entropy of the target answers; if that curve is smooth, the jump belongs to the scorer and not to the model. Plan the budget against the continuous curve, which the scaling law predicts reliably.

questions.title: A model was trained with a context of 8K tokens. The product now needs 128K. You have a modest fine-tuning budget and no budget to pretrain again. Lay out the options by the way the model encodes position, and give me the plan you would run.
questions.answer: The answer depends on the positional scheme, so read the config first. A learned absolute table has no row past the trained length and cannot be extended without new parameters. With rotary embeddings you scale the base or interpolate the positions, with NTK-aware scaling, YaRN or LongRoPE, and fine-tune on long sequences; the lesson's reference is a model family that went from 8K to 128K this way. Linear-bias attention extrapolates by construction, but you cannot switch a trained model to it for free.

questions.title: A colleague refuses to enable Flash Attention on a quality-sensitive model because "approximate attention changes the outputs". Is it an approximation? Explain what the kernel changes and what it keeps, with the memory argument that motivated it.
questions.answer: It is exact. The kernel tiles the computation so the full N by N score matrix never lands in the GPU's main memory; each tile is scored, exponentiated and accumulated in on-chip memory with a running maximum and a running sum, and the final normalization matches the single-pass softmax up to floating-point reordering. What changes is the memory traffic: three round trips to main memory become one write per output tile, and the footprint drops from N squared to N. The numbers that leave the kernel are the same as standard attention.

questions.title: You are choosing the attention variant for a new 70B-class decoder: full multi-head, multi-query, grouped-query, or MLA with its compressed latent. What does each one do to the memory that decoding holds per token, and what do you give up with each?
questions.answer: All four keep the same number of query heads; they differ in how many key and value heads exist, and only the keys and values are stored during decoding. Multi-query shares one key-value head across every query head, the smallest cache and some quality loss. Grouped-query uses a group of key-value heads, cuts the cache by n_heads / n_kv_heads and keeps nearly full quality, which is why it is the default. Latent attention compresses keys and values to a low-rank vector and decompresses at attention time, so it saves even more memory and pays extra FLOPs.

questions.title: You change an attention layer from one head to eight heads and keep the model width fixed. What happens to the parameter count, to the compute, and to what the layer can represent? And why do practitioners refuse to make heads narrower than about 32?
questions.answer: The parameters do not change: the four projections are still d_model by d_model, and the heads are only a reshape of the same matrices into slices of width d_model / n_heads. The compute stays about the same because the per-head attention runs as one batched matmul over the head axis. Each head can specialize on its own relation, and the output projection is where the heads mix. The lesson's rule of thumb keeps a head at a width of 32 or more, because a narrower head sees too few dimensions, and above 256 you lose the benefit of many small specialists, while the sqrt scaling itself keeps the score variance constant at any width.

questions.title: A new decoder-only language model on a vocabulary of 64 tokens reaches a training loss near zero after only some hundreds of steps, and the sampled text is nonsense. Name the two most likely causes and the check that tells them apart.
questions.answer: On real text, a loss far below the logarithm of the vocabulary size this early, with nonsense samples, most likely means the model can see its own target. Either the causal mask is missing, so position i reads the token at i plus one through attention, or the targets were never shifted, so the input and the target are the same sequence. Check the attention weights: if any mass sits above the diagonal the mask is gone; if the weights are triangular, print one batch and compare the input and target columns.

questions.title: You inherit a decoder block written in the 2017 style: layer normalization after the residual add, a ReLU feed-forward network at four times the width, sinusoidal absolute positions summed into the input, bias terms on every linear layer, and full multi-head attention. Review it against what production decoders ship today and justify each change you ask for.
questions.answer: Move the normalization in front of each sublayer and switch it to RMSNorm; replace the ReLU network with SwiGLU at about 2.6 times the width so that its three matrices match the old parameter count; replace the sinusoid with rotation of the queries and keys; drop the biases; and use grouped-query attention to shrink the decode-time cache. Every change is one function substitution and the tensor shapes do not move. The evidence: pre-norm trains deep without warmup tricks, SwiGLU gains about half a point of perplexity in the published model papers, rotation gives relative position and a knob for long context, and grouped-query cuts cache memory by the ratio of query heads to key-value heads.

questions.title: Take a sentence and shuffle its words. Feed both versions through a self-attention layer that has no positional signal. How do the two outputs relate, and what are the three families of fixes you would name?
questions.answer: The output rows come back shuffled in the same way and nothing else changes, because attention only computes pairwise similarities between tokens. Order carries meaning in language and code, so the model needs a second signal. The three fixes are a position vector added to the embedding, a learned table or a fixed sinusoid, a rotation of the queries and keys by an angle that grows with position, and a distance penalty added to the scores.

questions.title: Three products land on your desk: a search ranking model over documents, a coding assistant that writes code, and a speech-to-text system. Which transformer shape do you pick for each, and what does the pretraining loss have to do with the choice?
questions.answer: Encoder-only for ranking and embeddings, decoder-only for generation, and encoder-decoder when the input is a clear source sequence such as audio to transcribe. An encoder reads both sides of every position and trains on masked prediction, which gives strong representations and no way to generate. A decoder trains on next-token prediction behind a causal mask, so it can generate, and it scales cleanest, which is why it won language. The loss decides whether the model can produce text at all.

questions.title: The 2017 paper placed the layer normalization after the residual add. Almost every model since about 2019 places it before the sublayer. What changed, how would you demonstrate the difference in one afternoon, and what does RMSNorm change on top of that?
questions.answer: Post-norm sends the gradient of the skip path through a normalization at every layer, so at depth the gradient shrinks and the run needs a warmup schedule to survive. Pre-norm keeps the skip path unnormalized, so the gradient reaches the embeddings cleanly and a deep stack trains without warmup tricks. Demonstrate it by stacking twelve layers of each variant with the same initialization and printing the gradient norm at the embedding after one backward pass. RMSNorm then drops the mean subtraction, one fewer operation, with the same stability in practice.

questions.title: A new teammate has read the word "attention" a hundred times and still cannot say what a query, a key or a value is. Explain the three to them in one minute. Then tell me what changed between the 2014 encoder-decoder version and the version inside a transformer.
questions.answer: Attention is a soft lookup. Each token produces a query that asks for information, a key that says what the token holds, and a value that the token hands over when it is picked. The query is scored against every key, the scores go through a softmax, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. In the 2014 version the query was the decoder state and the keys and the values were the same encoder states; a transformer takes all three from one sequence through three learned projections.

questions.title: A transformer block has two skip paths, one around attention and one around the feed-forward network. What do they do for training, which of the two sublayers moves information between tokens, and why does a dropout layer placed on the skip path itself break something?
questions.answer: The skip path makes the gradient additive across depth, so its norm stays in scale through a twelve-layer stack instead of shrinking at every layer, and it lets each block learn a small update to a running representation instead of a full replacement. Only attention mixes tokens; the MLP applies the same two layers to every position on its own. Dropout belongs after the attention softmax, on the attention output before the residual add, and after the second linear of the MLP; on the skip path it breaks the identity that carries the gradient, and early stacks that did this trained brittly.

questions.title: The rotary scheme rotates every query and every key by an angle that is proportional to the token's absolute position. Yet everyone says it encodes relative position. Resolve the apparent contradiction, and tell me the one unit test you would write to prove the property.
questions.answer: The rotation acts on pairs of coordinates with the angle pos * theta_i. When a query from position m meets a key from position n, the dot product on each pair picks up cos((m - n) * theta_i), so only the gap survives and the two absolute positions cancel. The test: rotate two random vectors at positions (a, b) and again at (a + k, b + k), then assert that the two dot products agree within floating-point error.

questions.title: In the attention formula the raw scores go through a division before the softmax. A new engineer calls the division a convention and removes it to save one multiply. What happens to training, and how would you show the effect in ten minutes?
questions.answer: A dot product of two vectors grows with their length, so without the division the scores grow with the key dimension. Large scores push the softmax into a region where one key takes almost all of the weight and the gradient to every other key is close to zero, so learning stalls. The division by sqrt(d_k) keeps the variance of the scores about constant for any head size. Show it with random Q and K at d_k = 64: print the score range and the softmax weights with and without the division.

topics.title: Tokenization, sampling and decoding
topics.about: How text becomes tokens, how a model picks the next token, and how speculation makes decoding faster.

questions.title: Two changes shipped in one week: the target model moved to its next version, and a new customer whose traffic is mostly code was routed onto the same cluster. Speculative decoding has been on for months. Since then the mean inter-token latency fell 25 percent, the P99 rose 15 percent, and throughput at the usual concurrency is down. Diagnose it.
questions.answer: Both changes attack acceptance. The draft head was trained against the previous target version, so its distribution drifted and more drafts reject; the code traffic shifts the input distribution away from the general chat data the head was trained on, where acceptance falls into the 0.4 to 0.6 band. A rejected draft costs a verify and a re-roll, two passes that serialize under a full batch, which is exactly a tail that worsens while the mean still improves. Read acceptance per traffic slice and per target version from the engine's speculative metrics, retrain or roll back to a head aligned with the new target, and gate speculation per request class.

questions.title: Walk me through one training step of byte-pair encoding on a small corpus, and tell me what the trained artifact actually is.
questions.answer: Start with every word split into base symbols, bytes or characters. Count every adjacent pair across the corpus, weighted by how often each word appears, merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol with the next free id, rewrite every occurrence, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. The artifact is the ordered list of merges; the vocabulary follows from it, and the same list applied in the same order is what encoding uses later.

questions.title: Three subword algorithms dominate: byte-pair encoding, WordPiece and Unigram. Contrast how each builds its vocabulary, tell me which one can give two different segmentations of the same word on purpose, and name the libraries you would reach for.
questions.answer: Byte-pair encoding merges the most frequent adjacent pair, bottom up. WordPiece also merges bottom up but scores a pair by the count of the merged piece over the product of the counts of its parts, so it prefers pairs that co-occur more than chance, and it marks continuation pieces with a double-hash prefix. Unigram works top down: it starts from a large candidate set, assigns each piece a probability, and prunes the pieces whose removal hurts the corpus likelihood least, which is why it can also sample alternative segmentations for regularization.

questions.title: A fine-tuned chat model answers well in the training notebook. The deployed service, with identical weights, returns rambling text that runs until the token limit. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find?
questions.answer: At the flat token sequence the model actually receives, not at the list of messages. A chat model was trained on one exact layout of role markers, special tokens and newlines; a missing newline, a swapped marker or an extra space puts the input outside the training distribution, and the end-of-turn token stops being predicted. Print the token ids of the same request from both paths and diff them, and check that the special tokens arrived as their reserved ids and not as the bytes that spell them.

questions.title: You are about to pretrain a model that will later serve a large volume using speculative decoding. Three ways to get a draft are on the table: bake sequential multi-token modules into pretraining, train a hidden-state draft head after pretraining, or reuse a small model of the same family. Give the decision with its costs, and name the gate you measure before you ship the flag.
questions.answer: If I control pretraining and the hidden size is at least 4096, I bake in the sequential modules: about 10 percent slower training buys a denser supervision signal and a draft that accepts 80 percent or more at depth one. If the weights already exist, I train a post-hoc head on the verifier's features with about 60 to 200B tokens; it is backward compatible and reaches 0.88 to 0.92 acceptance on general chat. A same-family small model needs no training and sits around 0.55 to 0.70. Whatever I pick, the gate is measured acceptance on my own traffic mix at production concurrency, with the flag off below about 0.55 and the tail latency watched, not the mean.

questions.title: A classifier prompt asks for one of three labels and the model answers with a paragraph, so the parser crashes. Three layers of fix exist. Explain how the strongest one works at the level of the logits, and why it is often faster than free generation, not slower.
questions.answer: Prompting asks nicely, a vendor's structured-output API does it on the server, and constrained decoding does it locally by editing the logits. At each step a logit processor computes which vocabulary tokens can advance the target grammar, a JSON schema, a regex or a context-free grammar compiled to a state machine, and sets every other logit to minus infinity, so the softmax puts probability only on valid continuations and an invalid output is unreachable. It can be faster because the search space shrinks and because tokens that the grammar forces, such as a fixed key name, are emitted without a model step.

questions.title: You are starting a 7B model that must serve many languages and also be strong at code. Design its tokenizer: the algorithm, the library, the vocabulary size, the coverage settings, and the validation plan you would gate the training run on.
