questions.answer: Train a byte-fallback subword vocabulary on a corpus that mirrors the target mix of languages and code, with a pre-tokenizer that keeps leading spaces and separates digits and punctuation so that code tokenizes cleanly. For a model in the 1 to 10B range the heuristic is 50 to 100k tokens, and the multilingual requirement pushes to the top of that range or beyond it; set the character coverage near 0.9995 so that rare scripts are kept rather than mapped to unknown. Gate on tokens per word per language, the unknown rate, the compression ratio against a reference encoder and a byte-exact round trip, and freeze the tokenizer file hash in CI before the first training step.

questions.title: Walk the line from a separate small draft model to the current generation of hidden-state drafts. What limitation did each step remove, and why does feeding the draft the verifier's internal features help so much?
questions.answer: A separate small model from the same family accepts around 0.6 of its tokens, because its distribution drifts from the verifier's. The first hidden-state draft replaces it with a one or two layer network that reads the verifier's last-layer features, so the draft starts from the verifier's own representation and acceptance rises to 0.7 to 0.8. The second generation proposes a tree of candidates and verifies every branch in one pass with a tree-shaped attention mask, lifting acceptance per accepted-path token above 0.85. The third drops the feature-matching loss, trains on direct token prediction, and feeds the draft its own previous outputs during training, which removes exposure bias and reaches 0.88 to 0.92.

questions.title: At encode time a BPE tokenizer holds the complete merge table. Why does it have to replay the merges in the order they were learned, and what goes wrong when two merges could fire at the same spot?
questions.answer: Encoding must reproduce what training did to the same text, and training saw the merges one at a time in that order. If merge one created "th" and merge five created "the" from "th" plus "e", then "the" can only form after "th" exists. When two merges could apply at one position, the one with the lower rank, learned earlier, wins; change that rule and the same text yields different ids, so the model sees a distribution of ids it was never trained on.

questions.title: A pretraining team wants to supervise each position on more than the next token. One design puts several independent output heads on the backbone. Another chains small modules, one per extra depth. Which design gives you a usable speculative draft at inference, and what does it cost during training?
questions.answer: The chained design. Module k takes the previous depth's hidden state and the embedding of the actual next token, runs its own small transformer block, and reuses the shared embedding and the shared output head, so its prediction of the token at t plus k plus 1 is conditioned on the token at t plus k, which is the same causal chain a decoder follows and lets the module draft tokens at inference with acceptance at depth one of 80 percent or more for about 1.8 times throughput. Independent heads all read the same hidden state and cannot condition on each other. The training cost is about 10 percent slower pretraining and about 14 h squared parameters per module, with a loss weight of 0.3 early and 0.1 later.

questions.title: A customer in Korea reports that the same prompt uses up far more of the context window than the English version, and the bill is higher too. Why does this happen, and what does a model builder do about it?
questions.answer: The vocabulary was trained on English-heavy text, so its merges cover English and other scripts fall back to short pieces or raw bytes. Korean averages 2 to 3 tokens per word on an older vocabulary, and non-Latin text can cost 5 to 10 times more tokens than English for the same meaning; a Chinese character is 3 bytes in UTF-8, so without merges each character is several tokens. The builder's fix is a larger vocabulary trained on multilingual data, which is why one model family grew its vocabulary from 32K to 128K.

questions.title: Before any merge runs, a production tokenizer cuts the text into chunks with a regular expression. Show me what the classic pattern does to Hello, world! Don't stop. and explain why the cut exists at all, given that the merges could run on the raw stream.
questions.answer: The pattern cuts the sentence into eight chunks, Hello, ,,  world, !,  Don, 't,  stop and .: each word after the first keeps the space in front of it, contractions split at the apostrophe, and punctuation stands alone. The merges then run inside each chunk and can never join symbols across a chunk boundary. Without the cut, training learns merges that span words, the vocabulary fills with whole phrases, and the pieces generalize worse to new text.

questions.title: You review the schema of an extraction service. It is {"answer": ..., "reasoning": ..., "date": <a strict year-month-day regex>}, enforced by constrained decoding. Compliance is perfect, yet accuracy is poor and some dates are invented. What is wrong with the design, and how do you change it?
questions.answer: Two faults that no validator can catch. The answer field comes before the reasoning field, so the model commits to an answer before it has reasoned, and the strict date pattern leaves no legal way to say unknown, so the model complies by inventing a date. Put reasoning first and the answer last, and allow a null or a sentinel for a missing date; field order is logic, not formatting, and a grammar that is too strict forces a confident wrong value.

questions.title: A draft is accepted 80 percent of the time per token and proposes four tokens per step. How many tokens does one pass of the big model produce on average, how does the draft's own cost enter, and when does a longer draft stop paying?
questions.answer: The expected tokens per verifier pass are (1 - alpha^(K + 1)) / (1 - alpha); at an acceptance of 0.8 and K of 4 that is 3.36, so about 3.36 times fewer big-model calls. The wall time per token is (K c + 1) over that expectation, where c is the draft's cost relative to the verifier, so a longer draft adds cost linearly while the geometric series saturates; at 0.8 acceptance and c of 0.05 the optimum sits around 5 to 7 drafts for about 3.2 times. The lever that matters is the acceptance rate: at a fixed K, a rise from 0.6 to 0.9 about doubles the expected tokens per pass.

questions.title: This is a take-home we send: implement a byte-level byte-pair tokenizer with training, encoding and decoding, two reserved special tokens, and a test suite. Describe the design you would submit, the tests you would ship, and the one figure you would include in the write-up.
questions.answer: Reserve ids 0 to 255 for the raw bytes and a small block above them for the end-of-text and pad markers, split the corpus on whitespace and punctuation, train by counting frequency-weighted adjacent pairs and merging the top pair with a deterministic tie-break, encode by applying the lowest-ranked merge that fits until none fits, and decode by joining the byte expansions and decoding UTF-8 once. The tests pin the byte-exact round trip on an unseen sentence, on an emoji and on a literal special-token string with the allow flag on and off, plus the merge-order property and the reserved ids. The figure is the compression curve: the encoded length of a held-out sentence as the target vocabulary grows from 300 to 600.

questions.title: Your creative-writing product samples at a high temperature and speculative decoding gives it no speedup at all, while the same setup flies on code completion. Explain the difference, and describe what the acceptance test becomes at temperature zero.
questions.answer: Acceptance depends on how often the verifier agrees with what the draft sampled. At a high temperature the target distribution is flat, the draft's samples spread across many tokens, and the acceptance ratio of verifier to draft probability falls toward one over the vocabulary size, so almost every draft is rejected and the draft's cost is paid for nothing. Code and structured output are predictable, so acceptance climbs above 0.9. At temperature zero the rule becomes a comparison: accept if the drafted token equals the verifier's most likely token, otherwise emit that token and stop.

questions.title: After a routine dependency upgrade, an evaluation score for a deployed model fell sharply. No model weights changed. Give me a diagnosis plan that starts at the tokenizer, and the control you add so it cannot happen again.
questions.answer: A model trained with one vocabulary and served with another gets different ids for the same text and produces garbage, so first hash the tokenizer file in both environments and compare. If the hashes match, check the settings that change ids without changing the vocabulary: whether special tokens are added, whether a prefix space is added, and the normalization step, because a leading space or a ligature that normalizes differently moves whole tokens. Then freeze the tokenizer hash in CI and keep golden token ids for a fixed corpus so any change fails a test before it ships.

questions.title: A team wants to grow the vocabulary of a new model from 32K to 128K tokens. The embeddings have 4,096 dimensions. Put numbers on what the change costs and on what it buys.
questions.answer: The embedding matrix goes from 32,000 by 4,096, about 131 million parameters, to 128,000 by 4,096, about 524 million, so about 400M more parameters from the tokenizer alone, and an untied output head costs the same again. In return the text compresses: an English paragraph of about 100 tokens at 32K takes about 70 tokens at 128K. Generating that same paragraph then needs about 30 percent fewer forward passes, and non-English scripts gain the most. The lesson's rule of thumb is 32k under 1B parameters, 50 to 100k from 1 to 10B, and 200k and above for multilingual or frontier models.

questions.title: Why does every current language model read subword tokens instead of whole words or single characters, and why do most of them build the vocabulary on top of raw bytes?
questions.answer: A word vocabulary cannot hold every word, so each new word becomes an unknown token and the model loses the signal. Characters never fail, but they make sequences several times longer and spend attention on spelling. Subwords keep common words whole and split rare words into meaningful pieces, and starting from the 256 byte values means any input in any script encodes with zero unknown tokens.

topics.title: Post-training
topics.about: Supervised tuning, preference tuning, LoRA and reinforcement learning on a trained model.

questions.title: When should you use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) versus fine-tuning, and how do you decide between them?
questions.answer: Use RAG when the model needs knowledge, especially facts that change often, because you can update documents without retraining. RAG also gives you citations and lets you enforce access controls at retrieval time. Use fine-tuning when you need to change behaviour, such as tone, output format, or a specialised task. Fine-tuned knowledge goes stale and needs retraining. Many production systems combine both: fine-tuning for behaviour and RAG for current facts.

questions.title: How does LoRA work under the hood, and how do you serve multiple LoRA adapters efficiently in production?
questions.answer: LoRA freezes the base model weights and learns each weight update as the product of two small low-rank matrices. Because only those small matrices are trained, the optimizer needs far less memory than full fine-tuning. Adapters can be merged into the base weights so inference has no added latency. To serve many adapters, you keep one shared base model in GPU memory and load or swap adapters per request, which is much cheaper than running a full model copy for each one.

questions.title: How does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) compare to traditional RLHF with PPO?
questions.answer: Traditional RLHF requires several stages: train a reward model on preference data, then optimise the policy with reinforcement learning such as PPO. That process is complex and can be unstable. DPO uses the same preference pairs but derives a direct loss, with an implicit reward defined relative to a reference model. It needs no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop, so it is simpler, more stable, and cheaper to train. You still need high quality preference data, and results depend on the task.

questions.title: How do you engineer high-quality fine-tuning datasets and prevent catastrophic forgetting?
questions.answer: Prioritise quality over quantity: a smaller set of clean, representative, expert-checked examples usually beats a large noisy one. Deduplicate data, remove low quality or contaminated examples, and keep train and test sets strictly separate so scores stay honest. To limit catastrophic forgetting, where new training erodes earlier abilities, mix in a portion of general or previous examples during training. Then evaluate on both the new task and older capabilities to catch regressions.

questions.title: A support bot must answer from a policy manual that changes every week. Fine-tune, or use RAG?
questions.answer: Rule of thumb: RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour. Retrieval keeps facts current and lets answers cite their source. Fine-tuning is good at teaching a format, a tone, a task-specific skill, or shortening prompts, and much less reliable at teaching facts. Many production systems use both: a lightly fine-tuned model that's good at answering from retrieved documents.
options: Fine-tune once, then never update.
Fine-tune every week on the new manual.
Neither: write a longer system prompt with the whole manual.
RAG: put the current policy in the context at query time.

questions.title: What does LoRA train?
questions.answer: For a weight matrix W (d × d), LoRA learns B (d × r) and A (r × d) with r much smaller than d, and uses W + (α/r)·BA in the forward pass. Only A and B get gradients and optimiser state, so memory and checkpoint size drop sharply. The adapter can be merged into W after training, so inference costs nothing extra, or kept separate and swapped per customer.
options: All the weights, at a lower learning rate.
Only the final classification layer.
Two small low-rank matrices per adapted weight matrix. Their product is added to the frozen original weights.
A new set of embeddings for special tokens only.

questions.title: LoRA with rank 16 on one 4,096 × 4,096 projection matrix. How many trainable parameters does that add?
questions.answer: A is 16 × 4,096 and B is 4,096 × 16: 2 × 4,096 × 16 = 131,072 parameters, against 16,777,216 in the matrix itself.

questions.title: As a percentage of that matrix's 16,777,216 parameters, how many does the rank-16 adapter train? (Percent, three decimals.)
questions.answer: 131,072 ÷ 16,777,216 × 100 = 0.781%. Across a whole model, LoRA typically trains 0.1–1% of the parameters. Optimiser state shrinks by the same factor, which is what makes a single-GPU fine-tune possible.

questions.title: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?
questions.answer: QLoRA quantises the frozen base weights to 4-bit NormalFloat, dequantises them on the fly in the forward pass, and backpropagates into bf16 LoRA adapters. Paged optimisers handle memory spikes. A 7B model's base weights take about 3.5 GB instead of 14 GB, so fine-tuning fits on one consumer GPU.
options: It quantises the adapters to 4-bit.
It removes the need for a GPU.
It trains a smaller model and then distils it.
The frozen base model is stored in 4-bit, while the LoRA adapters train in higher precision.

questions.title: You fine-tune on 10,000 examples averaging 1,500 tokens each, for 3 epochs. How many training tokens is that, in millions?
questions.answer: 10,000 × 1,500 × 3 = 45,000,000 = 45 million tokens. It's the number that sets both the cost (hosted fine-tuning is usually priced per training token) and the time (divide by your tokens per second).

questions.title: After fine-tuning on 5,000 legal Q&A pairs, the model is great at legal questions but worse at general instructions and basic maths. What happened, and what helps?
questions.answer: Training only on one narrow distribution overwrites general behaviour. Mitigations: replay (mix in 10–30% general instruction data), a smaller learning rate and fewer epochs, parameter-efficient methods like LoRA, which change fewer weights, and an eval suite that includes general tasks, so you notice the regression before shipping.
options: Use a higher learning rate to finish faster.
The model was too small.
Catastrophic forgetting. Mix general instruction data back in, lower the learning rate or epochs, or use LoRA.
The legal data must contain wrong maths.

questions.title: Validation loss on your fine-tuning data keeps going down, but when people try the model, its answers are getting worse. What's the likely gap?
questions.answer: Validation loss uses teacher forcing: the model always sees the correct previous tokens. At inference it builds on its own outputs, and small errors compound. Lower loss can also come from learning the references' phrasing, without getting better at the task. Evaluate generated outputs on held-out prompts, with task metrics, human review, or a validated judge, and choose checkpoints by that.
options: The tokenizer changed.
Validation loss scores the next token on reference answers, which isn't the same as the quality of the model's own generated answers. Evaluate on generated outputs.
The model needs more epochs.
The validation set is too small.

questions.title: A fine-tuned chat model works in your training notebook but produces rambling text when served. What do you check first?
questions.answer: Chat models learn a precise format: role markers, special tokens, and an end-of-turn token. If the server's template differs, even by a missing end-of-turn token or a different system-prompt marker, the model sees an unfamiliar format and doesn't know where its turn ends. Use the tokenizer's chat template in training and serving, and test the served endpoint with a prompt from the training set.
options: That the server formats prompts with exactly the chat template and special tokens used in training.
The learning rate.
The GPU type.
Temperature.

questions.title: How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO?
questions.answer: RLHF with PPO trains a reward model on preference pairs, then optimises the policy with reinforcement learning against it, with a KL penalty to stay near the reference model: complex and finicky. DPO shows the same KL-constrained objective can be optimised directly, by raising the likelihood of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one (against the reference model). It's simpler and more stable, and widely used.
options: DPO only works for classification tasks.
DPO trains a bigger reward model.
DPO learns directly from preference pairs with a classification-style loss, with no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop.
DPO needs no preference data.

questions.title: You can fine-tune on 1,000 examples carefully written by experts, or on 100,000 scraped Q&A pairs of mixed quality. For teaching an instruction-following style, which is usually better?
questions.answer: For alignment-style tuning, the model already has the knowledge from pre-training. Fine-tuning mostly teaches the format and the manners. A small set of consistent, high-quality examples does that well, while large noisy sets teach inconsistency and errors. For teaching a genuinely new skill, you need more data, and quality still matters.
options: The 100,000 pairs, because more data always wins.
The 1,000 expert examples. For style and format, quality and consistency matter more than volume.
Neither. Fine-tuning can't change style.
Mix them equally.

questions.title: You move an RL job from one GPU to a cluster where the rollout engines and the trainers run on separate devices. The team wants generation and training to run at the same time, so that neither side waits for the other. Design the async setup: which knobs matter, what new failure appears, and what you watch in the logs.
questions.answer: Async training lets the engines generate the next batch while the trainer updates, at the price of samples that come from older weights. Two modes exist: one step ahead, where every sample is at most one weight version old with the default update interval, and fully async, where a worker keeps generating and the trainer drains a buffer, so the age depends on how fast the trainer drains it. Set a limit on sample age, decide what happens to running requests at each weight update, and lower the learning rate as you allow older samples. Watch the weight version of each sample, the share of dropped samples, the clip fraction, and the gap between the two sides.

questions.title: You have a small pretrained transformer and 800 labelled text messages, half of them spam. You need a binary classifier by tomorrow. Do you train only a new classification head, or do you update every weight? Defend the choice.
questions.answer: Swap the language-model head for a two-class linear layer and start with the body frozen. Head-only training is fast, costs almost no memory, and rarely overfits on this little data. Unfreeze the body only when the frozen run leaves accuracy on the table and the domain is far from the pretraining text.

questions.title: Your rater budget is gone. A colleague proposes to replace the human labelers with a model that reads a short list of principles and ranks the pairs, and to run the same RLHF pipeline on those labels. Is this just a cheaper RLHF? What changes?
questions.answer: It is the constitutional recipe, and it changes the failure modes rather than removing them. Phase one has the model critique and revise its own answers against sampled principles and trains on the revisions; phase two trains a reward model on pairs ranked by a feedback model and runs the usual RL stage. Rater psychology stops being the bias, and the reading of the principle set becomes the bias, applied uniformly over the whole dataset. Sycophancy toward a rater drops, and the proxy problem stays.

questions.title: A staff engineer argues that moving every alignment run from PPO to direct preference methods ends the reward-hacking problem, because there is no reward model left to hack. Make the counter-argument with the mechanism, and say what survives in your pipeline either way.
questions.answer: Direct methods remove the explicit reward model, not the proxy. The quantity they optimize is the log ratio of policy to reference, an implicit reward that the preference data pins down only where the data has coverage. Under optimization the policy queries that ratio out of distribution, and the published curves of gold reward against KL show the same peak and then collapse as reward-model pipelines, with the KL regularization failing to stabilize it. What survives: a blind held-out eval, early stopping, broader preference data, and ensembles of signals.

questions.title: During a DPO run the loss falls and the reward margin that the trainer logs grows every epoch. Yet the model's samples get shorter and less fluent, and the policy now gives the chosen training answers a lower probability than they had under the reference. Explain the mechanism and what you change.
questions.answer: The DPO loss cares only about the difference of two log ratios. It can lower the probability of the chosen answer as long as the rejected answer falls faster, and the margin still grows. This is the degraded chosen response failure: the policy moves probability mass away from both training answers, often toward short degenerate outputs. Log the absolute chosen log-probability, add a penalty on downward moves of the chosen term as the behavior-preserving variant does or switch to a loss with a bounded margin, and keep a generation eval next to the margin.

questions.title: DPO is often described as RLHF without a reward model. Walk me through where the reward went. Start from the RLHF objective with its KL term and end at the loss you would implement.
questions.answer: The penalized objective has a closed-form optimum: the optimal policy equals the reference policy times the exponential of reward over beta, normalized per prompt. Invert it and the reward equals beta times the log ratio of policy to reference, plus a term that depends on the prompt alone. Put that reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability and the prompt-only term cancels, because both answers share the prompt. What is left is a loss in the policy's own log-probabilities: minus the log sigmoid of beta times the difference of the two log ratios.

questions.title: A team of four engineers with eight GPUs has about 20,000 preference pairs for a customer support assistant and wants it aligned in three weeks. One engineer wants the full RLHF stack with a reward model and PPO. Another wants DPO. Which do you pick, and under what conditions would you reverse the choice?
questions.answer: Pick DPO. With tens of thousands of pairs it matches or beats the full stack, it trains one model against a frozen reference in a supervised loop, it needs about a third of the compute, and each experiment takes hours instead of days. Reverse the choice when the signal has several dimensions and needs a learned reward you can inspect and reuse, when you want an online loop that rates fresh samples, or when DPO plateaus on your eval.

questions.title: Your RL run shows a steady disagreement between trainer and rollout engine on the probability of each sampled token. One engineer wants to turn on a capped importance weighting right away. Another says it is a kernel artifact and should be ignored. Lay out how you decide, and what you would try first.
questions.answer: Match the method to the source of the gap. Five sources exist: tokens re-encoded between turns, expert routing on a mixture model, a sampler that cuts the vocabulary, numeric differences between kernels or precisions, and stale samples. The first three have corrections that remove the cause; try those first, because a reweighting such as truncated importance sampling leaves the gap in place and adds variance to the gradient. A flat gap on a dense model with plain sampling is the kernel floor of that setup; measure it, keep it inside your range, and reweight only what remains after the causes are gone.

questions.title: A GRPO run trains a small model on grade-school math with a binary reward. The reward per step jumps around, and the trend over many steps looks flat. The team wants to raise the learning rate. What do you read first, and what do you suspect?
questions.answer: Read the group statistics before you touch the learning rate. GRPO scores each answer against the mean of its group, so a group where every answer is right or every answer is wrong has a zero advantage for every member and teaches nothing. In the manual's runs, 10 of the 32 groups in the first step had one reward for all 8 answers, and about half of the groups did over 12 steps. If most groups are like that, the signal is thin, and the fix is the prompt mix or the dynamic sampling filter, not a bigger step.

questions.title: In the PPO stage of RLHF, the objective subtracts a KL term between the policy and a frozen copy of the SFT model. A new hire asks why the pipeline keeps a second copy of the model in memory for that one term. Explain the failure it prevents and how you tune its coefficient.
questions.answer: The reward model was trained on answers that look like SFT output. Without the term, PPO moves the policy into regions the reward model never saw and finds strings that score high but that people dislike. The term charges the policy for leaving the SFT distribution, so it is a regularizer, not a hard constraint. Tune beta from the measured KL: too low and the reward climbs together with the KL, too high and the policy barely moves from SFT.

questions.title: You start a GRPO run with a new model checkpoint. At step 0, the metric that compares the trainer's log-probabilities with the rollout engine's reads several times higher than on your earlier runs with the same model family. A colleague suggests turning on the engine's deterministic mode to close it. What do you do?
questions.answer: Stop the run before it trains on wrong numbers. At step 0 both sides hold the same weights, so a value far above your healthy range means the two sides do not compute the same model: a wrong checkpoint path on one side, or a format that one side reads differently. Deterministic inference does not help; in the manual's runs it left the gap unchanged at about 0.015 and made the engine repeat itself, which is a different property. Fix the setup, then compare the step-0 value with the range of your healthy runs.

questions.title: An attention projection in your model is a square matrix with 4,096 rows and 4,096 columns. You add a LoRA adapter of rank 16 to it. How many values does the adapter train, and what share of the frozen matrix is that? Then say what changes when you double the rank.
questions.answer: The adapter is two thin matrices: A with 16 rows and 4,096 columns, and B with 4,096 rows and 16 columns. Each holds 65,536 values, so the adapter trains 131,072 parameters. The frozen matrix holds 16,777,216, so the adapter is 0.78 percent of it. A doubled rank doubles the adapter, because its size is linear in the rank.

questions.title: Take-home. A company wants a support assistant built from an open 8B base model. They have about 50,000 past support conversations with customer ratings, two 24 GB GPUs, and three weeks. Write the post-training plan on one page: the stages, the data for each stage, the settings you start from, what you measure after each stage, and the three failure modes you guard against.
questions.answer: Three stages: first, SFT with QLoRA on the top-rated conversations in one chat template with the loss masked to the assistant turns, at a low learning rate for one to three epochs with a few percent of raw text mixed in, measured by held-out instruction loss, raw-text drift and a sample read. Second, DPO against the SFT checkpoint as the frozen reference, on pairs built from high- and low-rated answers to the same prompt with a conservative beta, measured by a blind pairwise eval and the absolute chosen log-probability, not the training margin. Third, a release gate: a fixed prompt set rated blind, a refusal set, and a comparison with the base model on tasks the data never covered. The guards are catastrophic forgetting, length and agreement exploits in the ratings, and over-optimization of the preference proxy.

questions.title: Four teams bring you four datasets. One has thumbs-up and thumbs-down clicks on single answers. One has paired comparisons whose preferred answers are mostly twice the length of the rejected ones. One has no SFT checkpoint and wants a single training stage from the base model. One has pairs where some preferences are near coin flips and others are unanimous. Which preference loss do you recommend to each team, and why?
questions.answer: The clicks team gets the prospect-theory loss that works on single labels. The length-skewed team gets the reference-free loss that normalizes by length and adds a margin, so a longer winner does not win by its token count. The team without an SFT stage gets the odds-ratio loss, which adds a preference term to the SFT likelihood and trains from the base in one pass; the team with mixed preference strengths gets the identity-mapping loss, whose margin is bounded. Each one repairs one assumption that plain DPO makes.

questions.title: You have one GPU with 24 GB of memory and want to fine-tune a 7B model on your own instruction data. Walk me through the memory for a full update, for LoRA and for QLoRA, and say what makes the last one fit.
questions.answer: A full update of a 7B model needs about 56 GB: the weights in half precision, the gradients, and two optimizer states per parameter, all in half precision. LoRA keeps the half-precision weights but trains only small adapters, so the gradients and optimizer states shrink and the run takes about 18 GB. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit, about 3.5 GB of weights, and trains the adapters in half precision, so the run takes about 6 GB and leaves room for activations on a 24 GB card.

questions.title: You need a reward model for a helpfulness objective. A product manager suggests asking raters to score each answer from one to ten and regressing on the scores. Why do most pipelines collect pairwise comparisons instead, and what loss do you train with?
questions.answer: People are poor at absolute scores and good at relative judgments, so pipelines show two answers to one prompt and ask which is better. The reward model is the SFT model with its vocabulary head replaced by a scalar head. It trains with the Bradley-Terry loss, the negative log of the sigmoid of the reward difference between the preferred and the rejected answer. The difference in reward becomes a log-odds of preference, which turns many relative judgments into one consistent scale.

questions.title: Four days into a PPO run, the mean score from the reward model keeps climbing. A blind human rating of samples from each checkpoint is flat, and the last two checkpoints read slightly worse. The team wants to keep training because the curve looks great. What do you say?
questions.answer: Stop, and treat it as reward hacking. The policy has found outputs that the reward model scores high but people do not prefer, because the reward model is a finite proxy with blind spots. Read the KL to the reference and the length and format of recent samples; a KL that climbs with the reward and answers that grow longer or more formulaic confirm it. Roll back to the checkpoint where the human rating peaked, raise the KL coefficient or stop earlier, and widen the reward model's training data to cover what the policy exploited.

questions.title: Take-home. The RL framework you use scores each sampled answer with a reward function that you swap in by import path. Write a reward for a task with a numeric final answer, write a test plan for it, and explain how you would prove that your reward does not break the GRPO advantages before a long run. Keep the function and the plan short enough to read in five minutes.
questions.answer: Write an async function that receives the run arguments and one sample, extracts the last number from the answer and from the label, and returns 1.0 for a match and 0.0 otherwise, comparing as values so that 142 never matches 42. Test it on ten answers you scored by hand, with a correct one, a wrong one, an empty one and one cut at the length limit, because a reward that crashes on an empty answer stops the rollout of the whole step. Then check the advantages: a group where every answer gets the same reward must get an advantage of 0 for every member, and a fractional reward can fail that through float32 rounding.

questions.title: You left a one-GPU RL training run alone for an hour. When you come back, the GPU is idle, the process is still alive, and the log file has grown to more than a hundred megabytes. Nothing reports a failure. What happened, how do you confirm it, and what do you put in place so that it cannot happen again?
questions.answer: The rollout engine died and the trainer never noticed. The engine failed during startup, and the rollout client kept sending requests to it, got a 503 from the router on each one, and retried. The failed run in the manual wrote 200,533 such error lines in 63 minutes and never reported a failure. Confirm it by counting the error lines per minute and by reading the engine lines above the first error, then run every unattended job with a watchdog that stops the container when the errors do not stop.

questions.title: An engineer shows you two RL training runs. The new one, with a changed offload setting, finished its rollouts twelve percent faster and ended with a reward a few hundredths higher than the old one. They want to ship the change as the new default. Design the review: what do you ask for before you trust either number?
questions.answer: Ask for the spread of the baseline before you read the change. In the manual's three baseline seeds the final reward ranged from 0.736 to 0.766, so a gain of a few hundredths on one seed is inside the noise. Then ask what else differed: the manual's first offload pair also changed the engine memory fraction and compared different step numbers, and its twelve percent shrank to one to three percent in a same-day pair that changed one setting. Require two seeds, one change per run, the same step numbers, and times from steps that no thermal pause touched.

questions.title: Your team has a budget to collect SFT data for a new assistant. One plan buys one million scraped question-answer pairs from the web. The other plan pays skilled writers for a much smaller set. Which plan do you pick, and how do you argue it?
questions.answer: Pick the smaller set from skilled writers. SFT teaches a behavior pattern, not new facts, so a few thousand to a few tens of thousands of clean examples are enough. The lesson's reference points are about 27,000 curated examples for the first SFT stage of a major open chat model, and 52,000 generated pairs that cost about 600 dollars and produced a usable assistant. Noise in scraped pairs is learned as behavior at the same weight as the good examples.

questions.title: A colleague copies the pretraining configuration into an SFT run: the same peak learning rate, the same warmup, three epochs over 27,000 examples. The loss on the SFT set drops fast and everyone is happy. What do you expect to see when you test the model, and what do you change?
questions.answer: Expect catastrophic forgetting: the model answers in the training format, but its loss on raw text rises and it gets worse at code, math and anything outside the set. Pretraining used a peak rate about fifteen times higher than the SFT value in the lesson, 3e-4 against 2e-5. Cut the rate into the 1e-5 to 5e-5 range, keep one to three epochs, and track raw-text loss next to the SFT loss.

questions.title: You fine-tune a base model so that it follows instructions. A teammate's training loop computes cross-entropy on every token of each sequence, the instruction tokens included. Is that a problem? What do you change, and why?
questions.answer: Yes. Count the loss only on the answer tokens. The user always provides the instruction at inference time, so a gradient on it teaches the model to write questions, not to answer them. Set the label of every instruction position, every padding position and the answer boundary token to the ignore index, so they add no loss and no gradient.

topics.title: Inference and serving systems
topics.about: Batching, the KV cache, prefix caching, schedulers and how to measure a serving engine.

questions.title: How do you measure and optimize Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT)?
questions.answer: Time to first token mostly reflects queueing plus the prefill phase that processes the prompt. Time per output token reflects the decode phase, which generates tokens one at a time. Measure them separately, using percentiles and not just averages. To reduce time to first token, shorten prompts and use prompt caching so a shared prefix reuses its KV cache. To reduce time per output token, use efficient batching, quantization, or a smaller model. Streaming tokens as they are generated also makes the response feel faster.

questions.title: Why does the KV cache bottleneck LLM serving memory, and how does PagedAttention solve it?
questions.answer: During generation, the model keeps the key and value tensors for every previous token in every layer, so that it does not have to recompute them. This KV cache grows with each token and each concurrent request, which often makes it the main GPU memory limit. Allocating contiguous memory for the maximum length wastes space and causes fragmentation. PagedAttention splits the cache into small fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, like virtual memory pages, so more requests fit and throughput rises. It can also share blocks between requests with a common prefix.

questions.title: When a model generates tokens one at a time for a single user, what limits its speed on a GPU?
questions.answer: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel: big matrix multiplications, compute-bound. Decode produces one token per forward pass: for each token the GPU streams every weight through for a few operations each, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound. That's why batching many users together makes decode far more efficient: the weights are read once per step and used for every sequence in the batch.
options: Network latency between the user and the server.
Compute: the GPU's FLOPs.
Memory bandwidth: every new token has to read all the weights from GPU memory.
The tokenizer.

questions.title: A 7B model in bf16 (14 GB of weights) runs on a GPU with 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. What's the theoretical maximum decode speed for one sequence? (Tokens per second.)
questions.answer: Each token reads every weight once: 2 × 10¹² bytes/s ÷ 14 × 10⁹ bytes = 143 tokens/s. Real numbers land lower (the KV cache is read too, and kernels don't hit peak bandwidth), but this ceiling is the right first estimate, and it's why 7B models feel fast and 70B ones don't.

questions.title: Same GPU, same model, but quantised to int4 weights (3.5 GB). What's the new ceiling for one sequence?
questions.answer: 2 × 10¹² ÷ 3.5 × 10⁹ = 571 tokens/s, four times the bf16 figure, because decode speed follows the bytes moved. Quantisation is mainly a memory-bandwidth optimisation for decode, which is why weight-only quantisation is so common in serving.

questions.title: With 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128, and bf16 (2 bytes), how much KV cache does one token take? (KiB.)
questions.answer: Each layer stores a key and a value for each KV head: 2 × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token. With full multi-head attention (32 KV heads) it would be 512 KiB. Grouped-query attention cuts the cache by 4× here.

questions.title: How much KV cache does one sequence with an 8,192-token context need? (GiB.)
questions.answer: 8,192 tokens × 128 KiB = 1,048,576 KiB = 1 GiB per sequence. Long contexts are expensive mainly because of the cache, not the weights.

questions.title: After loading the weights, 40 GiB of GPU memory is left for the KV cache. How many 8k-token sequences can run at once?
questions.answer: 40 GiB ÷ 1 GiB per sequence = 40 sequences. This is what really limits how many users one GPU can serve. It's why paged attention (allocating the cache in small blocks as sequences grow, instead of reserving the maximum up front) raises throughput so much: most sequences never reach 8k.

questions.title: Why do most recent open models use grouped-query attention (GQA)?
questions.answer: In decode, every step reads the whole KV cache. GQA lets groups of query heads share one key-value head, so the cache and the bandwidth it needs shrink by the group factor. Multi-query attention (one KV head) is the extreme case and costs more quality.
options: It improves accuracy over multi-head attention.
Several query heads share each key-value head, which shrinks the KV cache and the memory read per token.
It increases the context length.
It makes training faster.

questions.title: With static batching, a batch of 16 requests finishes only when the longest answer finishes. What does continuous batching change?
questions.answer: Output lengths vary widely. In static batching, a request that finishes early holds an empty slot until the longest one ends. Continuous (in-flight) batching schedules per decode step: it evicts finished sequences and inserts new ones straight away. Combined with paged KV caches, it's the main reason modern serving engines get several times more throughput from the same GPU.
options: Finished sequences leave the batch at every step and waiting requests join, so slots never sit idle.
It processes requests one at a time.
It makes each forward pass faster.
It compresses the KV cache.

questions.title: Users say answers take a long time to *start*, but once text appears it streams quickly. Which metric is bad, and what are the usual fixes?
questions.answer: TTFT covers queueing plus prefill of the whole prompt. Long system prompts and retrieved context make prefill slow. Fixes: prefix caching (keep the KV cache of a shared system prompt and reuse it), trimming retrieved context, chunked prefill so long prompts don't block everyone, and enough capacity that requests don't queue. Report TTFT and time per output token separately. They have different causes.
options: Throughput: add more GPUs.
Time to first token (TTFT): reuse shared prompt prefixes, shorten prompts, and reduce queueing.
Time per output token: quantise the model.
Accuracy: fine-tune the model.

questions.title: Every request starts with the same 3,000-token system prompt. Which optimisation targets that directly?
questions.answer: Prefill for 3,000 identical tokens on every request is pure waste. Prefix caching stores the KV blocks for a common prefix and maps new requests onto them, cutting TTFT and compute. Many API providers bill cached input tokens at a discount for the same reason. Put the stable parts of the prompt first and the variable parts last, so the shared prefix stays as long as possible.
options: Quantising the KV cache.
Prefix (prompt) caching: compute the KV cache for the shared prefix once and reuse it.
Speculative decoding.
Increasing temperature.

questions.title: In speculative decoding, a small draft model proposes 4 tokens and the large model checks them in one pass. Each draft token is accepted with probability 0.8, independently, and checking stops at the first rejection. On average, how many tokens does each pass of the large model produce? (Two decimals.)
questions.answer: The large model always produces at least one token (its own correction or continuation), plus each accepted draft token. The expected count is (1 − α^(k+1)) ÷ (1 − α) = (1 − 0.8⁵) ÷ 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per pass of the large model. Decode is memory-bound, so checking 4 tokens costs about the same as producing 1. That's where the speed-up comes from: about 3.4× fewer large-model passes, minus the draft model's own cost.

questions.title: With temperature 0 in production, the same prompt sometimes gets slightly different answers. What's the usual explanation?
questions.answer: Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token, but the logits themselves vary by tiny amounts depending on which other requests share the batch, because kernel choice and reduction order change. When two tokens are nearly tied, that's enough to flip the choice, and the rest of the text diverges from there. Batch-invariant kernels can make serving fully deterministic, at some cost in speed.
options: The model has a bug.
Temperature 0 still samples randomly.
The tokenizer is non-deterministic.
Floating-point results depend on how requests are batched together, so tiny numerical differences can change which token wins a near-tie.

questions.title: At 32 concurrent users your L4 chat service streams badly: the P99 inter-token gap is 613 ms, and your target is 100 ms or less per token with a first token within 1 second. A teammate proposes --max-num-seqs 16 so that each step holds fewer requests. What do you expect, and what does the measurement say?
questions.answer: A cap does not make room for more users; it only chooses who waits. With the cap at 16 and 32 users, each stream got a little smoother, a median ITL of 69.8 against 80.5 ms and a P99 ITL of 595 against 613, but half the users waited in the queue, the median first token went from 1.8 to 12.3 s, and output fell 38 percent to 171.8 tokens per second. At 64 users no cap that the manual tried brought the P99 ITL under 1.1 s, so the fix on this card is fewer users per replica, not a cap.

questions.title: A vLLM server runs Qwen/Qwen3-8B with an EAGLE3 draft of depth 3. Over a run of answers near 2,000 tokens at 8 users, the counters show that the draft at position one was accepted with probability 0.77, position two with 0.54, and position three with 0.38. Estimate the mean number of tokens that one verify pass commits, and say what you would check before you rely on that gain for long answers.
questions.answer: Each verify pass commits the accepted drafts plus one bonus token from the target, so the mean acceptance length is one plus the sum of the per-position acceptance rates. With 0.77, 0.54 and 0.38 that is about 2.69 tokens per pass, which is the value vLLM reported on GSM8K in that run. Before I trust it on long answers I would read the acceptance of the longest answers alone, with real output lengths and without ignore-eos, because another study saw the acceptance fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5 on answers that ran toward 20,000 tokens.

questions.title: Design the serving layer for a chat product on a fleet of L4 cards with Qwen/Qwen3-8B. The target is a first token within 1 second and 100 ms or less per token for the P99 user. Every request shares a 2,048-token system prompt, and sessions run for several turns. How many users per card, which precision, which caps, and what do you measure before launch?
questions.answer: Size from the pool and the knee, not from throughput. In BF16 the 24,094-token pool on an L4 holds about 37 requests of 640 tokens, and with a cache reset the P99 gap between tokens at 16 users was already 522 ms, so a BF16 replica meets the target for well under 16 users; the FP8 checkpoint with an FP8 cache grows the pool to 142,369 tokens and served 2.87 requests per second within the same target at 64 users, where BF16 served none. So I would serve FP8 after an accuracy check on our prompts, put the shared system prompt first so that the cache holds it, keep the pool large enough for the sessions that return, cap users per replica at the measured knee in the gateway, and run the sweep with a flush, a clock record and a mixed length distribution before launch.

questions.title: You turn on an EAGLE3 draft for Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 and must set num_speculative_tokens. The draft config suggests a value, but you want to set it yourself. How do you choose, and how does the right value move with the number of users?
questions.answer: Set the depth yourself and sweep it at your real concurrency, because the depth that pays falls as more users share each step. On our clock-locked L4 at 32 users, depth 3 gave 333.6 output tokens per second against 208.8 with no speculation, and depth 5 fell back to 289.5, so the extra guesses cost more than they returned. At one user depths 3 and 5 tied, so start at 3 and move only on a measurement.

questions.title: Your first concurrency sweep on an L4 shows a first-token median of 0.3 s up to 16 users and 1.8 s at 32, so you set the production limit at 20 users per replica. A second sweep with a reset before each run puts the first token at 1.6 s already at 16 users. Which sweep do you trust, and why do the two disagree?
questions.answer: Trust the sweep with the reset. The first sweep kept one server for all the user counts and sent the same first prompts at every count with a fixed seed, so below 32 users many requests found their prompt in the prefix cache and skipped the prefill. With the reset the median first token rose at every step, about 0.65 s at 4 users, 1.0 s at 8 and 1.6 s at 16, and the P99 ITL jumped from about 70 ms at 8 users to 522 ms at 16, so the knee on this card sits between 8 and 16 users, not between 16 and 32.

questions.title: Your server queues requests because the KV cache is full. Someone suggests --kv-cache-dtype fp8. What does it buy, what can it cost, and how do you check both before production?
questions.answer: An FP8 KV cache stores each key and value in 1 byte instead of 2, so the same memory holds twice the tokens: for Qwen/Qwen3-8B a token falls from 144 KiB to 72 KiB, and one GiB holds about 14,600 tokens instead of about 7,300. It can cost accuracy, because FP8 needs a scale per tensor and a checkpoint without scales runs with a scale of 1.0, and it can change the attention backend, which on our L4 broke the first start. Check it with an accuracy run on your own task and with the startup log: on 500 GSM8K questions our FP8 KV run scored 90.8 percent against 91.8 in BF16, with overlapping intervals.

questions.title: Your Qwen/Qwen3-8B server in BF16 fits on one L4, but only with a small KV pool. The model's publisher also offers an FP8 checkpoint. When does the FP8 checkpoint pay, what does it do to speed, and what does our GSM8K check say about the cost?
questions.answer: FP8 weights store most parameters in 1 byte instead of 2, so they free memory that the engine gives to the KV pool, and on a GPU with FP8 math they also speed up the matrix work. On our clock-locked L4 with the pool held fixed, the FP8 checkpoint gave 284.7 against 208.8 output tokens per second at 32 users, 36 percent more, and cut the time per token by 30 percent. On 500 GSM8K questions it scored 90.6 percent against 91.8 in BF16, 1.2 points lower with overlapping intervals, so the run did not show a loss and cannot rule out a few points.

questions.title: A teammate posts in the team channel that the server does 255 tokens per second. Is that a result? What would you ask for, and what single number tells you where to stop adding users?
questions.answer: It is a slogan, not a result, because a throughput number without the latency that came with it describes nothing a user feels. Ask for the concurrency, the median and P99 first token and time per token at that concurrency, the client and the temperature, and the clock. Goodput is the number that sets the limit: the requests per second, or the share of requests, that met every latency target at once, and on the manual's GB10 the BF16 server's goodput was highest at a cap of 4 while its throughput kept rising to a cap of 64.

questions.title: You serve a chat model on one GPU. A load sweep shows output throughput that still rises at a cap of 64 concurrent requests, so the team wants to set the cap to 64. The product needs the first token in under one second and a steady stream of text after it. Which cap do you pick, and how do you defend it?
questions.answer: Pick the cap from goodput, not from throughput. Goodput counts only the requests that meet every latency target, so it falls to zero long before throughput stops rising. On the sweep in the SGLang manual, BF16 goodput was highest at a cap of 4 and was 0 from a cap of 8. Use the throughput curve only to explain the choice.

questions.title: Speculative decoding promises several tokens per step with no change to what the model writes. Explain how the engine keeps that promise, where the speedup comes from, and why the gain shrinks as more users share the server.
questions.answer: A cheap proposer guesses the next few tokens, and the target model runs once over all the guesses and computes its own distribution at every position. A rejection sampler keeps each guess that the target supports, samples a correct token from the target at the first rejection, and stops, so one pass gives at least one token and at most the number of guesses plus one, with the same output distribution as plain decoding. The gain comes from idle GPU time: a small decode batch waits for memory, and as the batch grows that idle time goes away, so the checks of rejected guesses start to cost real compute.

questions.title: You serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one GPU with a maximum model length of 8,192 tokens. At startup the server prints a maximum concurrency of 2.94, and a manager asks if the GPU can serve only three users at a time. Your users send about 512 prompt tokens and get about 128 tokens back. How do you answer?
questions.answer: The startup number assumes that every user fills the full maximum model length, and real users hold much less. Count the KV bytes for one token, divide the KV pool by that number, and then divide the pool by the context that one user really holds. On the L4 in the vLLM manual, the pool of 24,096 tokens fits 37 users with 640 tokens each.

questions.title: A team runs long agent sessions on SGLang with hierarchical caching on. Their dashboards show #cached-token: 0 on requests that resend a long history. They have tuned the cache tiers and the write policy, and the hit rate barely moves. The prompt template looks stable to them. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find?
questions.answer: Look at the first tokens of the request as the server sees them, not at the template. A relay or a chat template often adds something that changes on every request near the start, such as a request ID, a session hash or the date, and the tree matches from the first token and stops at the first difference. In the manual's incident a random hash in the system prompt cost 27.6 points of hit rate, and removing it moved the engine hit rate from 66.8 to 94.4 percent.

questions.title: You have twenty fine-tunes of one base model, each a LoRA adapter, and you want to serve them from one vLLM server. What do you set, what decides the cost, and what else in the server changes when LoRA is on?
questions.answer: Turn LoRA on at startup with --enable-lora, name the adapters with --lora-modules, and let each request pick one in its model field. Three limits set the cost: --max-loras, which defaults to 1 and caps the adapters that run in one batch, --max-lora-rank, which defaults to 16 and reserves memory for the largest rank, and --max-cpu-loras for adapters kept in CPU memory ready to load. LoRA also changes the prefix cache, because the adapter is part of every block key, so two adapters never share cached blocks, and it adds CUDA graphs per adapter, so startup takes longer and uses more memory.

questions.title: Most explanations of continuous batching describe a prefill phase and a decode phase that take turns on the GPU. Describe what the vLLM scheduler does in one step instead. Where does chunked prefill come from in that design, and where do you read the value that controls it?
questions.answer: The scheduler asks the same question of every request: how many tokens does it still need to compute? Each step has a budget of tokens, set by --max-num-batched-tokens, and the running requests take their next token first. Waiting prompts fill the rest of the budget, so a long prompt is split over several steps, and chunked prefill needs no extra mechanism.

questions.title: Explain how vLLM keeps the KV cache in GPU memory. Why does it not give each request its own buffer, how does it recognize a prompt it has seen before, and what happens when the memory runs out?
questions.answer: The KV cache is one pool of 16-token blocks, and a request takes blocks one at a time as it grows, mapped by a small block table. A buffer per request wastes memory twice: on length that the request never reaches, and on gaps between requests of different sizes. Each full block gets a hash that is chained with the hash of the block before it, so one hash names a whole prefix, and a new request walks its chain and stops at the first miss. When no block is free, the scheduler preempts the newest request and computes it again later.

questions.title: A user sends a chat request to a serving engine and the answer streams back, slowly at first and then word by word. Describe what the GPU does from the moment the request arrives until the last token. Name the phases, and name the numbers you would put on a dashboard for each of them.
questions.answer: A request has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values into the KV cache, so the GPU is busy with math. Decode then writes one token per request per step, and each step reads all the weights to do it, so the GPU waits for memory. Four numbers measure them: TTFT for the wait before the first token, TPOT and ITL for the stream, and output tokens per second for the whole server.

questions.title: Every request to your service starts with the same long system prompt, and the prefix cache is on. The server reports almost no cached tokens, and the first token is slow. Last week a teammate added a request ID to the start of the system prompt for tracing. What happened, and what do you change?
questions.answer: The prefix cache matches a prompt from its first token and stops at the first token that differs. A new ID at the start makes every later token a miss, so the server computes the whole prompt again on each request. Move the parts that never change to the front and put the ID after them. Then prove the fix with the cached-token counters.

questions.title: Your first sweep on an L4 says that CUDA graphs do nothing: at one user the median per-token time is 103.4 ms with graphs and 103.4 ms without, and the three seeds at that cap spread from 10.0 to 14.9 tokens per second, half the median. What do you check before you report that graphs do nothing?
questions.answer: Check the GPU clock and the temperature during the run before you believe either number. The manual's L4 sat at 87 C with software thermal slowdown active and an SM clock of 360 MHz out of 2040 during that sweep, so the server under test was not the cause. A sweep with a cool-down to 72 C and the clock recorded gave 60.16 ms per token at one user against 103.38 hot, and 270.11 against 194.16 tokens per second at a cap of 32: the hot sweep reported up to 28 percent less throughput, with the same command on the same card.

questions.title: On one L4 with Qwen/Qwen3-8B and the same 24,096-token pool, a closed-loop sweep at 64 users gives vLLM 241 tokens of output per second and SGLang 257, so the engines tie on throughput. Yet the chat team says one of them is unusable at that load and the other is fine. What are they seeing, and which engine do you choose for chat?
questions.answer: They are seeing two different choices at a full pool. At 64 users vLLM ran 40 requests and kept 11 waiting with its pool 99.5 percent full, so its first token came 1.7 times sooner, 10,953 against 18,356 ms, but each new prefill shared the step with the running decodes and the P99 gap between tokens was 1,363 ms against 114 on SGLang, which ran 37 requests and kept 27 waiting. For chat, read the P99 ITL next to the first token at your real load and traffic shape, because the two engines pick different sides of that trade by default, and one flag on SGLang moved its side.

questions.title: Every request to your chat service repeats the same long system prompt, and the engine has prefix caching on by default. What decides whether the next request reuses the work of the last one? How would you lay out the prompt, and how do you show a hit with a number instead of a guess?
questions.answer: The cache matches tokens from the first one onward and stops at the first difference, so a hit needs the same tokens in the same order at the start of the prompt. Put the parts that never change first, the parts that change per session next, and the question, the time and any request ID last. Prove the hit from the server: the cached_tokens field in the usage block, the #cached-token count in the prefill log line, or the prefix cache counters in /metrics.

questions.title: Your RL trainer shares its GPUs with the vLLM server that generates the rollouts. Between rollout steps the trainer needs the GPU memory back, and after each step the server needs the new weights. What does vLLM give you for this loop, and what can go wrong at the pinned version?
questions.answer: vLLM has development-mode routes for the loop: sleep mode frees GPU memory on /sleep and takes it back on /wake_up, /pause and /resume stop and restart generation, and a weight transfer runs through /init_weight_transfer_engine, /start_weight_update and /finish_weight_update, over NCCL between GPUs or through CUDA memory handles on one machine. At level 1 the sleep keeps the weights, and at level 2 it drops them too, which suits a step where the trainer sends new weights anyway. Three problems are known at 0.31.0: a level 2 wake does not reload a speculative draft, a level 2 sleep clears calibrated KV scales, and a weight update during sleep stops the engine, so wake first, reload, reset the prefix cache and read the acceptance counters.

questions.title: Long prompts make the stream pause for the other users of your SGLang server. A tuning page says to lower --chunked-prefill-size, so that decode steps run more often between the pieces of a long prompt. Would you follow it? What did the manual find when it tried, and what would you try instead?
questions.answer: Not without a measurement, because the small chunk did not help on either card in the manual's runs. On the GB10 at a low arrival rate a chunk of 1,024 made the P99 ITL worse, 1,977 against 929 ms with the default of 8,192, and at higher rates all chunk sizes tied. I would first try --enable-mixed-chunk, which puts the decode tokens into the prefill batch, and measure its trade: on the GB10 it cut the P99 ITL by 15 to 19 percent and at 1 and 2 requests per second it raised the median first token by 49 to 74 percent.

questions.title: A teammate benchmarked EAGLE-3 on Qwen/Qwen3-8B on one L4 with the random dataset and saw the time per token fall by half at 8 users. In production, with 32 concurrent chat users, the output throughput did not rise and the first token came later. The acceptance length in the log looks fine. What happened?
questions.answer: Two things, and the acceptance length hides both. On a 24 GB card the draft weights took pool space: the KV pool fell from 24,094 to 9,951 tokens, about 15 of the 640-token requests, so at 32 users most requests waited for a slot and the median first token went from 2,970 to 8,040 ms. The dataset also matters: at 32 users EAGLE-3 gave 1.6 times the output on GSM8K and code prompts and no more output on the random set or on ShareGPT, because the draft only pays when the GPU has idle time to spend on guesses.

questions.title: You run the same evaluation twice at temperature 0 on a serving engine and the scores differ. You send one failing prompt alone and get one answer, then send it inside a busy batch and get another. Nothing in the request changed. Explain what did change, and what a seed can and cannot fix.
questions.answer: The batch changed the arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative, and the kernels split their sums by the batch size, so the same request adds its numbers in a different order in a batch of 3 than in a batch of 30; a change in the last bit can flip the top logit, and every later token then follows a different text. The prefix cache does the same, because a request that reuses cached blocks runs a different prefill path, and so does the dtype. A seed fixes only the random draws of sampling, so it is not enough: offline, run the engine in one process with the same order; online, use the batch-invariant mode and pay its speed cost.

questions.title: You have a model that does not fit on one GPU, or you need more throughput than one GPU gives. Walk me through how you choose between tensor, pipeline and data parallelism, and what each one costs in communication.
questions.answer: Ask three questions. If the model fits on one GPU with room for the KV cache you need, use data parallelism, one full copy per GPU, and the output grows with the copies. If it does not fit, split it: tensor parallelism inside one machine when the GPUs have a fast link and the GPU count divides the attention heads, and pipeline parallelism when they do not or when the model needs more than one machine. Tensor parallelism talks after every layer, pipeline parallelism once per stage boundary, and data parallelism not at all between copies.

questions.title: Two engineers benchmark the same server on the same day and report numbers that differ by a few percent. Both used standard benchmark clients. Before you look at the server, what about the clients could explain the gap, and what rules would you set for the team?
questions.answer: The client is part of the measurement. On one vLLM server the SGLang client read a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher and an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower than the vLLM client, the two clients sent different random prompts, and temperature 0.7 raised the time per token by 10 to 13 percent at one user against temperature 0. The rules: one client, one temperature, one prompt length distribution with the range ratio stated, a flush and a new seed per run, the clock recorded, and all of that written next to every number.

questions.title: Your evaluation team wants bit-identical outputs from the live server and asks you to enable batch invariance for all traffic. What does it change, what does it cost, and what would you say?
questions.answer: The mode replaces the kernels that split their sums by the batch size with kernels that keep one reduction order, so one request gives the same logits alone and in a batch. It costs speed, most at low concurrency: on our L4 the small model paid 2.4 times the time per token at one user and 1.4 times at 32, and Qwen3-8B paid 1.4 times at 8 users with 27 percent less output. I would turn it on for evaluation and rollout servers and leave it off for production traffic, after I measured the cost at the concurrency we serve, because on SGLang with the default backend it also turns prefix caching off.

questions.title: A teammate proposes --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 so that long prompts get their first token sooner. The server runs a model with mixture-of-experts layers on one card. Requests arrive at about half a request per second, with prompts between 1,024 and 4,096 tokens. What do you expect to change, and what would you measure before you accept the change?
questions.answer: A larger budget lets a long prompt finish its prefill in fewer steps, but each of those steps takes longer, and every running stream waits for it. At low load I expect a faster first token and a worse P99 ITL, and I would measure both with several seeds at the real request rate. On our GB10 at 0.5 requests per second, 16,384 raised the P99 ITL from 574 to 798 ms, while the first-token gain did not clear the seed spread.

questions.title: You add a second L4 to an SGLang server with --dp-size 2 and expect about twice the throughput. The sweep shows less than one card gave: at 64 users the pair peaks at 64 tokens per second and falls to 42, and the P99 first token is 391 seconds against 33.4 on one card. Both copies loaded the weights without an error. What do you check, and what went wrong?
questions.answer: Read the KV Cache is allocated line of every DP rank before you trust the sum. On that pair the second card ran two pods of another team, so its copy had 3.17 GB free after the weights against 6.59 GB and a pool of 2,925 tokens against 24,094, an eighth of the first. The round-robin controller does not look at pools, so it sent every second request to the small copy, where 4 ran and 59 waited, while the large copy held one to three requests and used 2 to 7 percent of its pool.

questions.title: Your chat users see a smooth stream until someone pastes a long document, and then every stream pauses while the server prefills it. A colleague proposes prefill-decode disaggregation: separate prefill servers and decode servers. When does that split pay, what does it not do, and how would you decide?
questions.answer: Split prefill from decode when the measured problem is the tail of the inter-token latency and long prompts cause it, because a prefill server then never shares a step with a stream. It does not raise throughput: the documentation says so, it costs a KV transfer for every request plus more servers and a router, and a 2025 study found that even the tail gain depends on the load and on the path that moves the cache. Decide with a measurement: one server first, then copies behind a gateway, and the split last, compared with the same GPUs run as plain servers at your real load.

topics.title: GPU memory, quantization and hardware
topics.about: Where GPU memory goes, how quantization frees it, and how work splits across GPUs.

questions.title: How do weight-only and weight-activation quantization techniques like AWQ, GPTQ, and FP8 work?
questions.answer: Weight-only quantization compresses just the stored weights, which reduces size and memory with a simple process, and is common for GPU serving. Weight-activation quantization also quantizes activations at runtime. It can reduce computation further, but activations contain outliers that hurt accuracy if they are quantized naively. Methods such as SmoothQuant and AWQ handle this by protecting the salient weights and channels. Smaller models also need less memory bandwidth, which speeds up inference, so always measure accuracy against your speed gain.

questions.title: How many parameters are in a fully connected layer from 4,096 inputs to 4,096 outputs, with a bias?
questions.answer: Weights: 4,096 × 4,096 = 16,777,216. Biases: 4,096. Total 16,781,312. A transformer block has several of these (the attention projections and the MLP), which is where most of a model's parameters live.

questions.title: A 3×3 convolution takes 64 input channels to 128 output channels, with a bias. How many parameters?
questions.answer: Each output channel has a 3 × 3 × 64 filter, plus a bias: 128 × (576 + 1) = 73,856. The image size doesn't appear anywhere. A convolution's parameters are shared across every position.

questions.title: How much GPU memory do the weights alone of a 7-billion-parameter model take in bf16? (In GB, where 1 GB is 10⁹ bytes.)
questions.answer: bf16 uses 2 bytes per parameter: 7 × 10⁹ × 2 = 14 GB. That's only the weights. Serving also needs memory for the KV cache and activations, and training needs far more.

questions.title: Training that 7B model with Adam in mixed precision: bf16 weights and gradients (2 bytes each), plus fp32 master weights and Adam's two moments (4 bytes each). How much memory before activations? (GB, 10⁹ bytes.)
questions.answer: Per parameter: 2 (weights) + 2 (gradients) + 4 (master copy) + 4 (first moment) + 4 (second moment) = 16 bytes. 7 × 10⁹ × 16 = 112 GB, before a single activation. That's why full fine-tuning a 7B model needs several GPUs or sharding (ZeRO, FSDP), and why LoRA is popular.

questions.title: Training runs out of memory at batch size 32. You want to keep an effective batch of 32. What do you do?
questions.answer: Activation memory scales with the micro-batch size. Gradient accumulation splits the batch, accumulates gradients over several forward/backward passes, then calls optimizer.step() once, which is mathematically the same update (apart from batch-norm statistics). Combine it with activation checkpointing (recompute activations during backward) and mixed precision if you need more room.
options: Lower the learning rate.
Use a smaller learning-rate warmup.
Gradient accumulation: run 4 micro-batches of 8, summing the gradients, then step once.
Train fewer epochs.

questions.title: Each GPU processes a micro-batch of 8, you accumulate gradients over 16 micro-batches, and you train on 4 GPUs with data parallelism. What's the effective batch size?
questions.answer: Effective batch = micro-batch × accumulation steps × GPUs = 8 × 16 × 4 = 512. This is the number to use when you reason about the learning rate.

questions.title: You need to train on 1 billion tokens. Each GPU processes 50,000 tokens a second, and you have 8 of them. How many minutes does one pass take, ignoring overheads?
questions.answer: Throughput is 8 × 50,000 = 400,000 tokens a second. 1 × 10⁹ ÷ 400,000 = 2,500 seconds = 41.7 minutes. Real runs add data loading, evaluation, checkpointing and communication, so a budget 20–40% above this is common.

questions.title: Why do most large-model training runs now use bf16 rather than fp16?
questions.answer: Both are 16-bit. fp16 spends its bits on precision (10 stored mantissa bits) with a small range (max about 65,504). bf16 keeps fp32's 8-bit exponent, so its range matches fp32, and stores only 7 mantissa bits. Neural network training is far more sensitive to overflow and underflow than to low precision, so bf16 trains stably without loss scaling.
options: bf16 uses less memory than fp16.
bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32, so it rarely overflows and doesn't need loss scaling.
bf16 is more precise than fp16.
fp16 isn't supported on GPUs.

questions.title: An image classifier scores 98% on validation and 81% on new photos. You find that augmented copies of the same originals appear in both the training and validation sets. What's the fix?
questions.answer: Any group of near-duplicates (augmentations, frames from the same video, photos from the same patient) must stay on one side of the split. Split first, by the group, then augment the training set only, ideally on the fly. Check for near-duplicates across splits with perceptual hashes or embedding similarity.
options: Stop augmenting.
Use a bigger validation set.
Use stronger augmentation.
Split by original image first, then augment only the training split.

questions.title: Your teammate starts Qwen/Qwen3-8B in BF16 on an L4 with no flags, and the start fails with an error about the KV cache and --max-model-len. The same command works on a larger card. Explain the failure with numbers, and say what you set.
questions.answer: The model config gives a context of 40,960 tokens, and vLLM takes that as the maximum length when you set none. At 144 KiB per token one request at that length needs 5.6 GiB of KV cache, and on a 24 GB card the 16.4 GB of weights can leave less than that, so the start check fails before the pool line prints. Set --max-model-len to the longest prompt plus answer that your users send; the pool stays the same size, and the limit only stops one request from claiming all of it.

questions.title: An SGLang server on a shared workstation ran for four minutes, and then a benchmark with 32 requests in flight crashed it with an out-of-memory error. The scheduler log just before the crash shows token usage: 0.05. Explain how the pool was 95 percent empty and the server still ran out of memory, and what you set.
questions.answer: The KV pool is sized once at startup from a snapshot of free memory, and the automatic fraction gave 87.2 percent of what was free to the weights and the pool. Thirty-two requests held 16,095 tokens, 5 percent of a 312,581-token pool, so the pool had reserved 33 GB and used under 2 GB, and the activations of the next forward pass needed memory outside the pool that the operating system no longer had. On a machine that runs anything else, pass --mem-fraction-static yourself; with 0.4 the same benchmark finished all 128 requests at concurrency 32.

questions.title: A teammate serves a model that uses latent attention (MLA) on eight GPUs with --tp-size 8 and asks why the server holds so few KV tokens on 640 GB of memory. Explain how a tensor-parallel split treats that cache, what the attention-group mode changes, and what it changes without a flag of its own.
