The most common root cause is skipping query condensation/rewriting before retrieval: embedding the raw follow-up as-is, rather than first rewriting it into a self-contained query using the conversation history, almost guarantees the retriever searches on an under-specified or ambiguous version of what the user actually meant.
options: The follow-up was embedded as written, instead of being rewritten into a standalone question using the conversation.
Top-k is too low.
The index is stale.
The embedding model is too small.

questions.title: How does CLIP's training objective enable cross-modal retrieval without any manually labeled image-text pairs?
questions.answer: It trains contrastively on hundreds of millions of naturally co-occurring (image, alt-text) pairs scraped from the web — no manual labeling involved — with a loss that pulls each image's embedding close to its paired text embedding and pushes it away from the other images in the same training batch. Because both encoders are trained to land in the same shared vector space, a text query can be embedded and compared directly against image embeddings by ordinary cosine similarity at retrieval time, with no classification head or extra alignment step needed.

questions.title: Early fusion vs. late fusion for multimodal RAG — which do production systems actually use, and why?
questions.answer: Early fusion combines raw multimodal inputs before encoding, requiring one architecture capable of processing both modalities jointly from the start. Late fusion encodes each modality independently with its own best-in-class encoder (text with a strong text embedder, images with CLIP) and combines the resulting vectors afterward — and this is what production systems overwhelmingly use, because it lets you swap in the best available encoder per modality without retraining anything else, index everything in one shared vector store with a single ANN query across modalities, and add a brand-new modality later (audio, say) by adding one new encoder rather than retraining the whole system.

questions.title: How would you index a corpus of PDFs that mix prose, figures, and tables?
questions.answer: Parse each document and route by content type: text blocks chunked and embedded with a text encoder; figures extracted as images and embedded with CLIP (or captioned via a vision-language model and embedded as text, for cases where a text query is more likely than an image query); tables linearized to Markdown and embedded as text. Store everything in one index with a modality metadata field so retrieval can span all three at once from a single text query embedding — and flag any figure that has no surrounding caption text for manual review, since those are the hardest content type for a plain text query to ever surface via semantic similarity alone.

questions.title: A retrieval pipeline uses one model to find candidate chunks and a second model to order them. Explain what each model sees as input, and why the second model does not run over the whole corpus.
questions.answer: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each document on their own and compares the vectors, so every document vector is computed once at index time. A cross-encoder reads the query and one document together as a single sequence and outputs one relevance score, so it can see how the two texts interact. That score costs one forward pass for each pair, so the cross-encoder runs only on a short candidate list.

questions.title: A team is about to index a new document corpus and asks you to review the chunker. They picked semantic splitting, 1000 tokens per chunk and 20 percent overlap, because a blog post recommended it. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: Start from the query type, not from a post. Factoid questions want 256 to 512 tokens, analytical or multi-hop questions 512 to 1024, and whole-section questions 1024 to 2048. Begin with recursive splitting at 512 tokens and no overlap, then measure recall at 5 on a 50-query set before you move any knob.

questions.title: You write the search step of a retrieval pipeline. A teammate wants to rank chunks by the raw dot product between the query vector and each chunk vector. What do you use instead, and when is the dot product the right choice?
questions.answer: Use cosine similarity, which is the dot product divided by the lengths of the two vectors. It measures only the angle, so a long chunk and a short chunk compete on direction and not on size. The raw dot product is right only when the vector length carries meaning that you want to reward.

questions.title: A proposal replaces the vector retriever with a cross-encoder that scores every chunk in a 10 million chunk index, so that nothing is ever missed. Estimate the work for one question, and say what you propose instead.
questions.answer: One forward pass per chunk means 10 million forward passes for one question, which no request budget allows. Keep a bi-encoder for the first stage, because its document vectors are computed once at index time, and run the cross-encoder on a pool of 50 to 200 candidates. The advanced RAG lesson puts the per-pair cost at 100 to 1000 times a bi-encoder comparison.

questions.title: Design a code search service that answers questions such as "how is the upload retry budget enforced" across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code, and that stays fresh on every push. What is different from document retrieval, and where does it break?
questions.answer: Chunk at syntax tree nodes, functions and classes, not at fixed windows, and give each chunk three retrievable forms: a dense code embedding, BM25 terms with the symbol name weighted above the body, and a one-sentence natural-language summary. Retrieve hybrid, rerank with a cross-encoder, and synthesize with mandatory file and line citations that a post-filter enforces. Freshness is the hard part: a push triggers a symbol-level diff so that only changed chunks re-embed and only affected cross-file edges recompute.

questions.title: Design a question answering service over a company's internal documents: wikis, policies, contracts and support articles, a few hundred thousand pages, with weekly updates. Users are employees with different access rights. Walk through the pipeline, the evaluation, and the first three things you would measure in production.
questions.answer: Build two sides. The ingestion side parses each document, chunks it per document with a structure-aware splitter, embeds the chunks, and indexes dense vectors and a BM25 index with metadata and access labels on every chunk. The query side filters by access first, runs hybrid retrieval with rank fusion, reranks a candidate pool with a cross-encoder, and generates a cited answer with a refuse path. Prove it with a golden set labeled by domain experts and a retrieval eval that reports recall at k per query class, then measure retrieval quality weekly, faithfulness and citation correctness per turn, and cost per query in production.

questions.title: After a release, the nightly RAG eval shows recall at 5 unchanged and still high, MRR down from last week, and faithfulness unchanged. Nobody touched the retriever. Which stage do you suspect, how do you confirm it, and what would other patterns have told you?
questions.answer: The reranker. On average the gold chunk still arrives in the top 5, so recall holds, but it sits lower in the list, so MRR falls, and the generator stays grounded in what it receives. Confirm it from the per-query trace: compare the rank of the gold chunk before and after the release, then look at what changed in the reranker, such as its weights, its candidate pool size, or the order of the query and the document in the pair.

questions.title: Support agents search the knowledge base with the exact error code from a ticket, such as E-4021. The vector search returns articles about error handling in general and misses the one article that contains that code. What is happening, and what do you add?
questions.answer: The embedding model treats a rare code as noise, so the query vector lands near articles about errors in general and not near the one exact match. Add a lexical index with BM25 next to the vector index, run both for every query, and merge the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion. The exact token wins on BM25, and the fused list puts that article first.

questions.title: Your RAG eval reports high recall, high MRR, high faithfulness and high answer relevance, and the weekly drift dashboard is flat. Support still forwards a stream of wrong answers from one business unit. As the staff engineer on the system, what do you conclude, and what do you change in the eval program itself?
questions.answer: Conclude that the eval set does not represent that unit's traffic: all four metrics can be high on queries that nobody asks. Add their real queries to the qrels, slice every metric by query class and document type, and check whether their documents are chunked by a splitter that fits their format. Then change the program: tier the qrels, review them on a schedule so they do not rot, and treat a per-slice drop as a release blocker.

questions.title: Two answer-grade metrics sit in your RAG eval report: faithfulness and answer relevance. A teammate says they measure the same thing and wants to drop one. Explain what each one grades, and give one answer that scores high on one and low on the other.
questions.answer: Faithfulness asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context. Answer relevance asks whether the answer addresses the question. A grounded summary of the retrieved chunks that never gets to the question scores high on faithfulness and low on relevance, and a short direct answer from the model's own memory scores high on relevance and low on faithfulness.

questions.title: A question asks what changed in the security policy last month. Your vector search returns a two-year-old security document because it is semantically close. Design the retrieval step so that this cannot happen, and say what else the same mechanism buys you in a regulated deployment.
questions.answer: Store metadata with each chunk, such as the source, the creation date, the category, the author and the version, and filter on it before the similarity search runs. For this question the filter is the security category and the last 30 days, so the old document is never a candidate. Under regulation the same pre-filter carries role labels and jurisdiction tags, so a user only retrieves chunks they are allowed to see.

questions.title: You turned on the hypothetical-answer rewriter for a code search assistant. Questions about one subsystem got worse: the gold document, which sat at rank 2 before, now falls out of the top 10 on the lexical side. The hypothetical passages read well. What happened, and what do you change?
questions.answer: The model wrote a function name that does not exist in the index. The real symbol that carried the lexical match is gone from the rewritten query, the rest of the passage is generic prose that scores across many documents, and the dense side returns a plausible neighbor for the invented token. Cap the hypothetical at two or three sentences, lower the BM25 weight in the fusion for rewritten queries, and route queries that already contain a literal symbol past the rewriter.

questions.title: Your faithfulness score comes from a model that reads each claim next to the retrieved context and answers yes or no. The score has sat near the top for a month, yet reviewers keep finding invented facts in sampled answers. The generator and the judge are the same model. What is going on, and what do you change?
questions.answer: A judge from the same family as the generator grades its own output as more faithful than it is, so the number stays high while the samples show the truth. Switch the judge to a different model family or hand-grade a sample, and add a sample-level review, because a per-sentence check can pass while the whole answer misleads.

questions.title: A regulated-domain assistant serves analysts in two jurisdictions from one index. In a red-team probe, a question asked under one jurisdiction returned a contract clause that belongs to the other. The reranker and the generator behave as designed. Where is the leak, how do you close it, and how do you prove that it stays closed?
questions.answer: The leak is in retrieval: the jurisdiction tag was not applied as a pre-filter before the similarity search, so a semantically close chunk from the other jurisdiction entered the candidate pool, and nothing downstream is built to remove it. Close it by tagging every chunk with role and jurisdiction at ingestion and filtering on both before hybrid retrieval runs. Prove it with a cross-jurisdiction probe set in the red-team suite, scored pass or fail with a severity, and run before every release.

questions.title: Your chunker keeps a 100-token overlap between neighbor chunks. After the last corpus refresh the index size and the embedding bill both went up, and a teammate says the overlap must stay because it protects sentences that a boundary would cut in half. How do you settle it?
questions.answer: Settle it with an ablation, not an opinion. Run the same recall at 5 eval with the overlap at zero and at the current value on a stratified query set, and keep the overlap only if the number moves. The recent studies found that overlap often adds no measurable benefit, while it adds index cost in proportion to its size.

questions.title: Your pipeline offers three query rewriters: write a hypothetical answer and search with it, write several paraphrases and merge, or decompose it into sub-questions and merge. A user asks "what does our team do when uploads fail and the budget is gone?" Which rewriter fits, and when would each of the other two be the right pick?
questions.answer: Split it, because the question joins two topics with a conjunction, an upload failure and an exhausted budget, and no single chunk holds both. The hypothetical answer fits a jargon-heavy question whose words do not match the corpus vocabulary. Paraphrases fit a short question that could be asked in many equally good ways.

questions.title: A product team wants an assistant that answers questions about the internal policy wiki. One engineer proposes to tune the model on the wiki pages. Another proposes to search the pages at question time and paste the matches into the prompt. Which do you pick, and in which case would you still tune the model?
questions.answer: Pick retrieval for knowledge. The model never changes, the document store updates in minutes, and you can show the passages behind each answer. Tuning fits when you need a style, a tone or a reasoning pattern that a prompt cannot reach, not when you need facts.

questions.title: A user reports that the document assistant gave a wrong answer. The pipeline has a chunker, a retriever, a reranker and a generator. You get one metric to look at before anything else. Which one, and why that one?
questions.answer: Recall at k on the retrieval stage. If the gold chunk is not in the top k, no reranker can bring it back and the generator usually lacks the evidence for the right answer, unless another chunk happens to hold it, so the later metrics are hard to read. Recall comes first in the order, but it is not a gate: when recall holds, or when another retrieved chunk holds the evidence, move on to the rank position and then to the generated text, because a failure there stays hidden otherwise.

questions.title: Your document assistant answers every question, including the ones the corpus does not cover, and the invented answers are the ones users remember. Design the path that lets the system say it does not know, and say how you measure that the path works.
questions.answer: Log the reranker's rank-1 score for every query and refuse when it falls below a corpus-specific threshold, instead of handing weak chunks to the generator. Tell the generator to answer only from the snippets, to cite every claim and to say it does not know when the snippets do not answer. Measure refusal calibration: on questions whose answer is not in the store, count how often the system refuses, and track the false confidence rate.

questions.title: You add a cross-encoder behind a hybrid retriever. The prompt receives K chunks. The team wants a rule for N, the number of candidates the reranker scores, and one engineer proposes a small N to protect the latency budget. How do you choose N, and what do you refuse?
questions.answer: Choose N from the recall curve of the reranked output and the latency budget together. Sweep N on a held-out query set; the lift saturates at a knee somewhere around 20 to 50 candidates, and past it every extra candidate costs a forward pass for nothing. Keep N at least three times K, because the reranker can only promote a chunk that the retriever put in the pool.

questions.title: A new cross-encoder reranker lifts MRR on the offline fixture to a near-perfect value. In production the same reranker makes the top result worse than the retriever alone. List the causes you check, in order, and say how each one shows up.
questions.answer: Check the training data first: if the hand-labeled training pairs include the eval queries, the eval is a memory test and the lift is fake. Then check the pair order in production, because a cross-encoder is not symmetric and a swapped query and document collapses recall. Then check the candidate pool, because production candidates come from the real bi-encoder, and its recall at N caps what the reranker can see.

questions.title: You have a BM25 ranked list and a vector ranked list for the same query. An engineer proposes to merge them as alpha times the BM25 score plus one minus alpha times the cosine. What is wrong with that, and what do you do instead?
questions.answer: BM25 scores are unbounded and change with the corpus, while a cosine sits between -1 and 1, so a weighted sum needs a new alpha every time you re-index. Reciprocal rank fusion merges by rank instead: each document gets the sum, over the lists, of one over k plus its rank, with k at 60. Ranks are comparable across the two retrievers, so nothing has to be calibrated.

questions.title: Take-home. You receive a corpus of a few hundred internal documents and a retrieval pipeline with two chunkers and two retrievers behind flags. Build the evaluation that tells the team which configuration to ship, and write up what the numbers mean. You have one evening.
questions.answer: Build a labeled query set first, stratified by query type, with gold document ids and gold answer text for each query. Run every configuration against the same set and report recall at 5 for each slice, plus MRR and the share of queries whose top 5 holds a chunk with the gold answer text, and read the spread between configurations. Label at document level so the same labels grade every chunker; if you label at chunk level, record the chunker in the qrels and relabel after any change of chunker.

topics.title: Prompting and structured output
topics.about: Prompt design, context engineering, schemas, constrained decoding and function calls.

questions.title: How do you guarantee strict schema-compliant JSON outputs from an LLM in production?
questions.answer: The strongest guarantee is constrained decoding, where a grammar or JSON schema masks any token that would make the output invalid. You define the expected structure with a schema, for example using Pydantic, and pass it to the model. You still validate every response in your application, because a valid format can contain wrong values. If validation fails, retry automatically with the error message, with a limit on the number of retries.

questions.title: When should you use chain-of-thought prompting and what engineering trade-offs does it introduce?
questions.answer: Use chain-of-thought for complex tasks that need several steps, such as multi-step maths, logic, or planning. It is rarely worth it for simple lookups or classification. It generates extra tokens, so it adds latency and cost. The written reasoning can also be wrong or may not reflect how the model actually reached its answer, so you should not treat it as proof. Keep the reasoning separate from the final answer, and evaluate whether it actually improves results on your task.

questions.title: A classifier uses constrained decoding with a schema of two fields, answer and reasoning, in that order. The output is always valid JSON and the accuracy is worse than the free-text version was. What is wrong?
questions.answer: The field order. The model commits to the answer before it writes any reasoning, so the reasoning tokens never shape the answer, and you lose the gain that step-by-step gives. Put reasoning first and answer last; the schema stays valid, and no validator will ever flag the difference, because the order is logic and not formatting.

questions.title: Your batch job sends the same 15,000-token rubric with each of twenty code reviews, spread over 40 minutes in uneven clusters, and some of the quiet stretches between clusters outlast the short cache. The provider bills a write at 1.25 times the input rate for a five-minute cache and at 2 times the input rate for a one-hour cache, and bills reads at one tenth of the input rate. Which cache do you pick, and show the break-even.
questions.answer: The five-minute cache pays for itself on the first read: a write costs 1.25 times and a read 0.1 times the normal input rate, so one write plus one read averages 0.675 times, a saving of 32 percent, and one write plus ten reads averages 0.205 times, a saving of 80 percent. Each read refreshes the five-minute lifetime, so the five-minute cache expires only in a gap longer than five minutes. This batch has such gaps, so the one-hour cache fits; its write costs 2 times the input rate and it needs only two reads to come out ahead, and twenty reviews give far more. The rule of thumb is to cache anything reused at least three times within the lifetime.

questions.title: Your team adds "think step by step" to every prompt in the product, including a high-volume classifier and the calls to a reasoning model. Where does that help, where does it hurt, and why?
questions.answer: It helps on multi-step problems, where each reasoning token becomes context for the next one and the model computes its way to the answer. It hurts on simple recall and single-step classification, where it adds 50 to 200 tokens of reasoning per query for no gain, and on reasoning models, which already run a chain of thought internally and can get worse with the extra instruction. Pick the technique per task from the accuracy requirement, the latency budget and the cost.

questions.title: Design the extraction service for purchase-order emails. The input is free text; the output is a typed record with a customer, line items and a total. Cover the schema, the enforcement mode, the retry and refusal handling, and how you prove it works before it touches the accounting system.
questions.answer: Write one JSON Schema 2020-12 with the constraints that matter: required fields, enums for closed sets, a minimum of zero on the total, additional properties forbidden, and any reasoning field ahead of any decision field. Run it in the provider's strict schema mode so that a response that finishes cannot have a parse error or a schema violation, check the stop reason so that a response cut at the token limit goes to the error path, and treat a refusal as a typed outcome that goes to a review queue. Prove it with a labeled set of real emails scored per field, a refusal check on inputs that must not extract, and a run beside the human process before any record is written.

questions.title: A team runs every question through the full escalation pipeline from the lesson: one deterministic chain, then five sampled chains with a vote, then a tree search when the vote is weak. Latency and cost are now the top complaint. As the staff engineer, how do you restructure the pipeline, and what do you measure to defend the new shape?
questions.answer: Make the pipeline earn each stage. Most questions should end at the cheap stage, so start the vote at the minimum of three samples and widen it only on disagreement, and reserve the tree search, which costs up to 39 calls at a branching factor of 3 and a depth of 3, for the questions where the vote fails. Measure accuracy against cost per question for each stage on a held-out set, and report the share of questions that each stage resolves.

questions.title: A classification prompt has eight output labels. One engineer wants twenty examples in the prompt to be safe, another wants none and a longer instruction. How many examples do you include, which ones, and what decides it?
questions.answer: Three to five for most tasks, and for a classifier with many labels one example per label, so eight here. Pick examples that are semantically close to the input and that cover every label, because similar examples beat random ones by 5 to 15 percent on classification. Below three the model has too little signal to extract the pattern; above five you pay context tokens on every call for diminishing returns.

questions.title: You own the memory layer for three products on one platform: a consumer chat assistant, a compliance review agent and a research retrieval agent. The memory system runs a vector store, a key-value store and a graph store in parallel and fuses their results. How do you configure the fusion for each product, and which one scoping mistake would get you paged?
questions.answer: The fused score is a weighted sum of relevance, importance and recency, and the weights are tuned per product: recency up for the chat assistant, importance up for the compliance agent, relevance up for the retrieval agent. Each store wins a query class the others miss, so the weights steer which class dominates without dropping a store. The paging mistake is a scope leak: every write picks the user, the session or the agent scope, and a retrieval that mixes scopes without per-scope weights tells one user about another user's project.

questions.title: A teammate turned on the provider's JSON mode and says the extraction output is now guaranteed. What does JSON mode guarantee, what does it not, and what do you turn on instead?
questions.answer: JSON mode guarantees that a finished output parses, nothing more; a response cut at the token limit can still fail, so check the finish reason first. It does not guarantee your keys, your types, your enum values or the absence of extra fields. Turn on the schema mode, where the provider takes a JSON Schema and constrains decoding to it, and keep a check on your side for the values that a schema cannot judge.

questions.title: You assemble a prompt from a system message, ten retrieved documents, the chat history so far and the user question. In which order do you place them, and what evidence decides it?
questions.answer: Put the system prompt and the critical instructions first, the current question and the most relevant context last, and the lowest-priority material in the middle. The evidence is the lost-in-the-middle finding: with one relevant document among 20, accuracy was 85 to 90 percent when it sat first or last and fell to 60 to 70 percent in the middle. If a key point has to sit in the middle, repeat it at the end.

questions.title: An extraction pipeline with strict schema enforcement has reported zero validation errors for a month. A finance review finds that a share of the extracted invoice totals do not match the source documents, and that a status field often holds a value that is allowed by the enum and wrong for the document. The engineers say the schema guarantees correctness. What do you tell them, and what do you build?
questions.answer: Schema enforcement guarantees shape, not truth. A total with the right type and the wrong number passes every format check, and an enum member can be allowed and still be the wrong one. Build a semantic eval: a labeled set of documents with gold records, exact match and field-level accuracy per field, plus a confidence signal from repeated extraction or token probabilities that sends low-confidence fields to human review.

questions.title: A math assistant samples five reasoning paths per question and takes a majority vote. Accuracy did not move compared with a single path, and the bill is five times higher. The team set the temperature to zero for reproducibility. What happened, and what else do you check before you keep the voting?
questions.answer: At temperature zero the samples should be identical, and only a nondeterministic serving stack makes them differ a little, so the five paths are close to one path counted five times and the vote changes almost nothing. The lesson samples at 0.7 so the paths differ enough for their errors to cancel. Then check that the final answer comes out in a fixed format, because without a line such as "The answer is" followed by the number the votes cannot be compared, and check that the single-path accuracy sits in the range where a vote helps, about 60 to 85 percent.

questions.title: An assistant's tail latency climbs because every turn also prunes, summarizes and reconciles its memory before it replies. A proposal moves that work to a second agent that runs while the user is idle. What does the split buy, what does it cost, and what new failure does it create?
questions.answer: The split takes the memory work off the critical path, so a reply never waits on consolidation, and the background agent can be a slower and stronger model because nobody is waiting on it. It costs a second agent, a shared block store and the coordination around them. The new failure is silent drift: the background agent rewrites a block and the primary agent never notices, so version the blocks, surface diffs in the trace, and treat the background writer as untrusted when it touches the persona or the safety block.

questions.title: You need two things from the same model: a typed summary of a support ticket, and the ability to look up the customer's account during the conversation. A teammate wants to build both as tools. Which mechanism fits each, and why does the distinction matter?
questions.answer: The ticket summary is structured output: the typed data is the final product, so use the schema mode and validate it. The account lookup is a function call: the model declares an intent to act, your code executes it and feeds the result back, so the output is an intermediate step. The two share the JSON Schema machinery but differ in what happens next, and mixing them hides which outputs are data and which are actions your code runs.

questions.title: Walk me through the three parts of a chat API call and what each one is for. Then tell me how you would get a model to return a JSON object with no preamble, without a structured output API.
questions.answer: The system message sets identity, rules and output constraints and persists across turns. The user message carries the task and changes every turn. The assistant prefill starts the model's reply for it, so a prefill of an opening brace makes the model continue as JSON with no preamble, on the providers that accept a partial assistant turn.

questions.title: Take-home. Build an agent memory with two tiers: a fixed-size main context and an unbounded searchable store, plus the tools that move facts between them. Show a trace where the main context fills, something is evicted, and a later question is still answered from the store. Standard library only. Explain your eviction and citation choices.
questions.answer: Treat the main context as RAM and the store as disk. Give the main context a cap, a pinned core section and a message list that compacts its oldest entries when the cap is passed; give the store records with an id, text, tags, a session id and a turn id, and a token-overlap search. Expose the memory tools, write three facts, overflow the main context, and answer the follow-up by searching the store and splicing the result into the next turn.

questions.title: An extraction service turns purchase-order emails into typed records. Name the ways a structured output call can fail, say which of them disappear under strict schema enforcement, and describe how the code should treat what remains.
questions.answer: Three ways: a parse error, where the output is not JSON; a schema violation, where it parses but breaks a type, a required field, an enum or a range; and a refusal, where the model decides the input does not fit the schema. Strict enforcement removes the first two by construction for a response that finishes. The refusal stays, and it must be a typed outcome that the code logs and returns, never a retry. A response cut at the token limit can still fail to parse, so check the stop reason before you read the output.

questions.title: You enabled prompt caching on a 15,000-token system prompt. The usage field for cache reads stays at zero on every request, while cache creation tokens are charged every time. What do you look for, and in what order?
questions.answer: Something above the cache breakpoint changes on every request. Look first for a timestamp or a request id at the top of the system prompt, then for tool definitions serialized in a changing order, then for near-duplicate text that differs by a byte between code paths, and then for a block under the minimum cacheable size. The cache matches prefixes only, so the first differing token turns everything after it into a miss.

questions.title: A coding assistant exposes 50 tools, each defined with a name, a description and a parameter schema. Estimate what the tool definitions cost on every call, and say how you would cut that cost without removing a single tool from the product.
questions.answer: Each definition costs 50 to 200 tokens, so 50 tools at 150 tokens each is 7,500 tokens before the conversation begins, repeated on every call. Classify the intent of the query and include only the tools that match it; the lesson puts the reduction at 60 to 80 percent, from about 8,000 tokens down to about 1,000. The product keeps every tool; only the per-call definition list changes.

questions.title: Design the execution layer for an agent that can query a database, run small code snippets and read files on behalf of a user. The model decides which tool to call. What rules does the executor enforce, and what does it never do?
questions.answer: The executor never passes model-generated SQL or shell text straight to a system. It exposes an allowlist of named functions with typed parameters, validates every argument against the schema before execution, sanitizes tool results before they return to the model, and caps the number of calls per conversation at 10 to 20. For code, an in-process filter is a teaching aid and not a boundary; untrusted code runs in a separate process or container.

questions.title: An agent has eight tools and keeps calling the wrong one. The tool descriptions are one or two words each, such as "gets weather". What does the description do, and how do you rewrite one?
questions.answer: The model reads the description to decide when and how to call the tool, so the description is a prompt for tool selection. Rewrite it as a full sentence that says what the tool does and what it returns, for example that it gets the current weather for a city and returns the temperature in Celsius and the conditions, and describe each parameter with an example value and an enum where the set is closed. Then validate the arguments against the schema before anything executes.

topics.title: Evaluation
topics.about: Metrics, eval harnesses, judges, calibration and how to trust a score.

questions.title: How do you design an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation harness and mitigate systematic biases?
questions.answer: Start with an explicit rubric and a clear scoring scale, with examples of each score, instead of asking which answer is better. Judges have known biases, so swap the order of answers to cancel position bias, and control for verbosity bias, where longer answers get higher scores. Avoid self-preference by using a judge from a different model family than the one being tested. Finally, calibrate the judge against a human-labelled set and track agreement over time.

questions.title: How do you evaluate RAG systems for hallucination using the RAG Triad?
questions.answer: The RAG Triad checks three links. Faithfulness, or groundedness, asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, and this is the direct check for hallucination. Context relevance asks whether the retrieved passages are relevant to the question, which tests the retriever. Answer relevance asks whether the answer actually addresses the question. Scoring all three separately tells you whether a failure came from retrieval or from generation.

questions.title: What architectural and prompting patterns prevent and intercept hallucinations in production?
questions.answer: Prevention starts with grounding: instruct the model to answer only from provided context, require citations, and allow it to say it does not know. For factual tasks, lower the temperature to reduce random output. To intercept errors, sample several answers and check whether they agree, because disagreement is a useful warning sign. You can also verify claims against sources with a separate check, and route high-risk or low-confidence answers to a person.

questions.title: What does building a real golden evaluation dataset actually involve, beyond “write 20 questions”?
questions.answer: Real query sampling (drawn from actual production logs or a representative spread of query types, not just whatever's easy to think of), relevant-passage labeling (manual annotation is the gold standard but expensive; LLM-assisted labeling scales further but is noisier and needs spot-checking), measuring inter-annotator agreement if multiple people label (low agreement means your "ground truth" itself is ambiguous, which is useful information, not noise to ignore), and wiring the resulting set into CI so every pipeline change gets measured against it automatically rather than relying on someone remembering to run an eval manually before merging.

questions.title: Beyond RAGAS, what other LLM-judge evaluation frameworks exist, and when would you reach for each?
questions.answer: ARES adds calibrated confidence intervals to judge scores at the cost of needing domain fine-tuning and a few hundred human labels — worth it when you need statistically defensible scores, not just a point estimate. RAGChecker gives claim-level diagnostics that separate retriever failure from generator failure, useful specifically when RAGAS or production has already flagged *that* something's wrong but not *which stage*. ConsJudge trains a judge model from judgment-consistency signals rather than human labels or a stronger reference model, useful if you want your own judge without depending on either. FaithJudge is a human-aligned hallucination-rate leaderboard, useful for picking a generator (or judge) model with an independent, pre-validated hallucination-rate comparison rather than trusting a vendor's own benchmark.

questions.title: How do you measure citation quality in a verifiable RAG system, beyond “does it have citations at all”?
questions.answer: Three genuinely separate metrics, because they catch three different failure modes: citation precision (of the passages actually cited, what fraction genuinely support the claim next to them — measured via NLI entailment between the cited passage and the specific claim); citation recall (of the claims the response makes, what fraction have any citation at all — requires segmenting the response into atomic claims first); and attribution accuracy (does the cited passage actually say what the response claims it says, which is distinct from hallucination detection, since hallucination checks if *any* passage supports a claim, while attribution accuracy checks specifically whether *the cited one* does).

questions.title: How do you evaluate RAG answers for open-ended questions where there's no single correct reference answer?
questions.answer: Automated exact-match metrics are useless here, so lean on two complementary LLM-judge patterns instead: rubric-based absolute scoring (define explicit dimensions — relevance, completeness, accuracy, citation quality — and have a strong judge model score each independently, which forces reproducibility and makes variance explainable) and pairwise preference (show the judge two responses — a baseline and a candidate — and ask which is better overall; pairwise judgments are empirically more reliable than absolute scores because they anchor the judge to a concrete comparison rather than an abstract scale). Always calibrate whichever you use against a small set of human-labeled examples before trusting it at scale.

questions.title: How do you evaluate a RAG system when you have no ground-truth labels at all?
questions.answer: "You can't" is the wrong answer here. Reference-free LLM-as-judge techniques genuinely work for faithfulness specifically, because checking whether an answer's claims are supported by the retrieved context only needs the context and the answer — it never needed a gold reference answer in the first place. Combine that with behavioral signals from live traffic (regeneration rate, rephrase rate, escalation rate) to triangulate overall quality without any labeled data at all.

questions.title: Your thumbs-up rate is 92%. Does that mean your RAG system is actually good?
questions.answer: Not necessarily, and taking it at face value is a real mistake — explicit feedback like thumbs typically comes from under 5% of users, and that sliver is heavily skewed toward either very angry or unusually engaged users, which says very little about the silent majority who never clicked anything. A more reliable read comes from composite implicit signals instead — no regeneration, no rephrase, no escalation within the session, taken together — rather than trusting one small, self-selected explicit metric.
options: No, because a good system scores 99%.
Not necessarily. Few users rate at all, and those who do are skewed. Look at implicit signals too.
Yes. 92% is high.
Yes, as long as thousands of people rated it.

questions.title: Your offline eval scores improved after a change, but users are complaining more. What's going on?
questions.answer: Don't default to blaming the users or assuming the eval was wrong — this is the classic online/offline divergence, and it has a few concrete, checkable causes: the golden dataset is cleaner and narrower than real live traffic (distribution shift), the change may have overfit specifically to the fixed golden set without generalizing (Goodharting), or live traffic includes genuinely unanswerable questions that never show up in a curated offline set at all. Check the unanswerable-question rate and compare query distributions between the golden set and live traffic before concluding anything about the model itself regressed.
options: Roll back and move on.
The offline set doesn't look like live traffic, or the change overfit to it. Compare the query mix and the unanswerable-question rate.
The eval has a bug, so ignore it.
Users don't like change.

questions.title: What should you actually log per request in a production RAG system, beyond the question and the final answer?
questions.answer: The full trace: the raw query and the rewritten/condensed version if query transformation ran, retrieved chunk IDs and their scores, reranked chunk IDs and scores if reranking ran, the final assembled prompt that actually went to the model, model parameters and token usage, and any sampled judge scores for that request. Without per-stage chunk IDs and scores specifically, you cannot localize a production failure to retrieval, reranking, or generation after the fact — you're stuck guessing.

questions.title: Your LLM-judge scores dropped 5% overnight with no deploy on your side. What do you check first?
questions.answer: Don't assume your system broke — the drop could be coming from the *judge* itself. Providers silently update underlying judge models, and that alone can shift every score without any genuine change in your system's output quality. The fix is scoring a fixed sentinel set daily (same inputs, same expected scores, run every day regardless of anything else) — a shift in the sentinel set's scores isolates judge drift from a genuine system regression immediately, instead of you spending hours investigating a system problem that doesn't exist.
options: Raise the judge's temperature.
Whether the judge changed: score a fixed sentinel set every day to separate judge drift from a real regression.
Roll back the last deploy.
Retrain the retriever.

questions.title: How would you know your RAG system's quality regressed after a deploy, in a real production setup?
questions.answer: Four layers, and naming all four (in order) is what separates a senior answer from "we have an eval set": a pre-deploy CI gate running the golden-dataset eval that blocks the deploy on any metric regression beyond threshold; a canary rollout to a small traffic slice, comparing guardrail metrics (latency, error rate, refusal rate) and judge scores canary-vs-control before full rollout; post-rollout online signals (regeneration rate, rephrase rate, thumbs ratio, escalation rate) watched against a pre-deploy baseline window; and trace-level triage when any signal fires — pulling the actual failing traces, localizing which stage broke using per-stage scores, and promoting those failures into the golden set so the exact same regression gets caught pre-deploy the next time around.

questions.title: A leaderboard ranks your candidate models by one aggregate score, and the top model wins by a small margin. A colleague on the code team says that the top model is the worst of the three on their work. Both read the same report. How is this possible, what does the aggregate hide, and how do you publish so that both readers are served?
questions.answer: The aggregate is a weighted mean, so a model can win overall and lose in one category, and a small margin can sit inside the interval on the mean. Publish the per category means next to the aggregate, with intervals, and print the weights. If the leaderboard also mixes scales, a task with a wider range dominates the mean without anyone noticing.

questions.title: Two engineers ran the same judge on the same 100 answers with the instruction "rate from 1 to 5 how good the answer is" and got means almost a full point apart. How do you rewrite the rubric so the scores become reproducible, and what else goes into the judge prompt?
questions.answer: Anchor every level to behavior a reader can check. A rubric that states what a 5, a 4 and a 3 look like reduces judge variance by 30 to 40 percent compared with an unanchored scale. Score several criteria separately, give the judge the input, the output and the reference, and ask for the reasoning next to the number.

questions.title: A model you fine tuned jumped eight points on a public benchmark after you added a new web scraped corpus to the training mix. Leadership wants to announce it. Design the audit that tells you whether the jump is capability or leakage, and say what you would publish instead if it is leakage.
questions.answer: Audit for contamination before anyone announces anything. Search the new corpus for the benchmark questions and their close paraphrases and report the share found, then rerun the model on a versioned custom eval that the corpus cannot contain and diff the individual test cases against the previous model. If the overlap is material and the custom eval did not move, the jump is memorization, and you publish the custom eval result with the contamination share.

questions.title: A vendor shows you that their new model scores 89 percent on a public multiple choice benchmark and the model you run today scores 87. They say the gap proves the new model is smarter. Why are you not convinced, and what do you ask for instead?
questions.answer: Public benchmarks stop telling models apart once every frontier model sits in a narrow band near the top. Three mechanisms cause this: training data that contains the test, training mixes tuned to the test format, and saturation, where the questions that remain are ambiguous or mislabeled. A gap of two points in that band is noise or memorization. Ask for a run on your task with your data.

questions.title: You must score generated code by running it. A teammate proposes a call to the interpreter's eval function inside the harness process with a try block around it. Design the execution contract instead, and say how a timeout, a crash and a denylist hit each appear in the result.
questions.answer: Run every candidate in a fresh interpreter subprocess with a wall clock timeout, an output cap and an import denylist, never in the harness process. The score is the fraction of assertions that pass. A timeout, a syntax error, an assertion failure and any other crash each map to a distinct exit reason, so a reviewer can tell a slow solution from a wrong one while the score for most of them is zero.

questions.title: Your multiple choice eval reports an expected calibration error of 0.02 on a hundred predictions with ten bins, and the team calls the model well calibrated. What does that number measure, what does it miss, and which second number do you add?
questions.answer: ECE bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy, weighted by bin size. With ten bins and a hundred predictions you cannot tell 0.02 from noise, and inside one bin overconfident and underconfident predictions can offset each other in the bin average. Add the Brier score, the mean squared error between confidence and outcome per prediction, and report how many bins were populated.

questions.title: Your team will adopt a new model next quarter and needs a long context evaluation that runs again on every future upgrade. Design the battery for a product that answers questions over long documents and sometimes has to combine facts from several places: the tests, the sampling grid, the metrics, the cutoffs and the regression procedure.
questions.answer: Build a fixed in house harness with three parts: a needle grid over depth and length on your own documents, a multi hop variable tracing task at the same lengths, and a slice of real long document questions. Sample five depths at each length and record pass rates, time to first token and cost per query. Publish two cutoffs, the effective retrieval length at a 90 percent pass and the effective reasoning length at 70 percent, and rerun the same harness on every upgrade.

questions.title: Take home. We give you a small instruction tuned model, a held out corpus, a set of short factual prompts with gold answers, a set of open form prompts with reference answers, and no network access. Build an evaluation pipeline that reports more than one number and explains its aggregate, and describe how it would run in CI once a network and a judge model are available. What do you deliver, and what do you leave out on purpose?
questions.answer: Deliver one runnable file with four evals: held out perplexity with honest token accounting, normalized exact match on the factual set, token F1 on the open form set, and a deterministic mock judge on a 1 to 5 scale with the same interface a real judge will have. Report every per eval number, a weighted aggregate with the weights in a config, and per example records for diagnosis. Leave out the real judge, intervals on the aggregate and anything that needs a network, and say so in the readme.

questions.title: Your question answering system returns "June 29th, 2007." The reference says "June 29, 2007." A teammate reports that this case gets a zero and asks you to replace the whole eval with token F1. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: Both metrics are right for different answer shapes. Exact match compares the whole string after normalization, so one extra character makes it zero. Token F1 compares the bags of tokens, so this pair scores about 75 percent. First add normalization to exact match, then pick the metric by the shape of the answers you grade.

questions.title: A prompt change scores 90 percent on your 50 case golden set, and the baseline scored 86 on the same set. The author wants to ship it as a four point win. How sure can you be, and what sample size would you need to make this call?
questions.answer: At 50 cases and 90 percent observed accuracy, the 95 percent interval runs from 78 to 97 percent, a 19 point spread. A four point gap sits well inside that spread, so the win cannot be told from noise. You need about 200 cases to detect a 5 percent change, and 500 or more when two systems are close.

questions.title: You wrote a rubric, and a judge model now scores faithfulness for your retrieval system. The dashboard shows a high mean, and the team wants to use it as the release gate from Monday. What has to happen before this number can block or approve a release?
questions.answer: Calibrate the judge against people first. Hand label about 100 cases, score them with the judge, and compute the Spearman correlation between the two rankings. Below 0.7 the rubric needs work and the number is noise. Then freeze the judge model and version, and read the bottom scores as well as the mean.

questions.title: Overnight every metric on the eval dashboard moved by several points, up for some criteria and down for others, with no prompt change and no model change in the product. The last merged change switched the judge to the newest version of its model. What happened, and how should such a change be made?
questions.answer: The judge is part of the measurement, so a new judge version changes every metric at once while the product stands still. Freeze the judge model and version in the pipeline. When you upgrade, run the old and the new judge on the same baseline in parallel, calibrate the new judge against the human labeled set, and reset the baseline before you compare anything new.

questions.title: A faithfulness dashboard reports a mean of 0.85 over a thousand cases, above the 0.8 release threshold. Support tickets say the assistant invents policy details in some answers. The eval owner says the metric is green. Where do you look, and what do you change in the report?
questions.answer: A mean hides the tail. A mean of 0.85 is consistent with a 5 percent slice of catastrophic failures, and that slice is what becomes tickets. Sort the cases by score and read the lowest 10 percent. Then add a pass rate at a threshold and a bottom quantile alert to the report, next to the mean.

questions.title: Your judge returns a JSON object with a score for each case. The pipeline parses it, and mean faithfulness rose from one week to the next with no change to the product. The logs show that the judge's output failed to parse on a growing share of cases. Explain the rise and fix the pipeline.
questions.answer: A parse failure becomes a missing score, and the aggregate silently drops missing scores. The cases that fail to parse are often the worst outputs, so dropping them lifts the mean. Catch the failure explicitly, record it as its own outcome, count it against the score or report it next to the mean, and alert when the failure share grows.

questions.title: A model card advertises a context window of one million tokens and a perfect score on a needle in a haystack test at that length. Your product asks the model to reconcile figures that appear in several places across a long contract. Does the card answer your question, and what do you measure instead?
questions.answer: No. A single needle test measures retrieval of one planted fact, and frontier models saturate it. Your task is multi hop aggregation, which degrades sharply past about 128k tokens on most models. Run a multi hop test at your target length and report two numbers: the effective retrieval length and the effective reasoning length.

questions.title: You run three candidate models on the same fifty tasks and must publish a leaderboard with a winner. The means are 0.78, 0.75 and 0.10. The second team says their model is tied with the first. Design the aggregation and the statistics that settle it.
questions.answer: Report a mean with a bootstrap interval, a win rate, and a paired interval on the difference for each pair of models. Resample the tasks with replacement to get the interval on each mean. For the tie claim, bootstrap the per task difference between the first two models; if that interval includes zero, the leaderboard shows them as tied.

questions.title: You compare two prompt versions by showing a judge model both outputs and asking which one is better. Version B wins 70 percent of the pairs. You then swap the two outputs and version A wins most of them. What went wrong, and how do you run the comparison?
questions.answer: The judge has position bias: it prefers the option it reads first. Your first run measured the order, not the prompt. Score every pair in both orders, count a win only when the same version wins twice, and treat split decisions as ties. Then report the win rate with a confidence interval.

questions.title: Your coding agent scores a pass at one of 0.6 on the fixture suite and a pass at five of 0.95. One manager reads this as a failing agent; another reads it as a passing agent. What does each number tell you, and what do you put in the report?
questions.answer: Pass at one says the first sample fixes the task on about six tasks in ten. Pass at five says that at least one of five samples passes on almost every task, so the right answer is usually within reach and the gap is selection. Report both, with the raw pass counts per task, because pass at k alone hides an agent that succeeds once in twenty tries.

questions.title: A colleague reports that the new checkpoint reaches a perplexity of 10 on the held out text, better than last week, and wants to ship it as the stronger model. What does the number mean, and what does it not tell you?
questions.answer: Perplexity is the exponential of the mean negative log likelihood per token. A value of 10 means that at each position the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among 10 options. Lower is better only while the test set and the tokenizer stay fixed. It says nothing about instruction following, reasoning or factual accuracy, so treat it as a sanity check and run the task evals before you ship.

questions.title: A colleague's perplexity eval computes the cross entropy at every position of every padded batch, averages it over the batch, exponentiates, and then averages the per batch values. The reported perplexity looks very good and gets better whenever the batch size grows. Read the description, name the bugs and give the correct computation.
questions.answer: There are three bugs: pad positions sit in the denominator, so the loss is diluted and the number improves with more padding, which is what a larger batch brings. Averaging per batch gives each token of a short batch more weight than each token of a long batch. And the targets must shift by one, because the logits at a position predict the next token. Sum the loss over real target positions across the corpus, count those positions, divide once, and exponentiate.

questions.title: You can score a summarization feature in three ways: n-gram overlap against a reference, a strong model that grades with a rubric, or human experts. The team has one afternoon and a small budget. How do you decide which to use, and for what?
questions.answer: Use all three, each for a different job. Overlap metrics are free and instant but agree with people only 40 to 60 percent of the time, so they serve as a baseline and a smoke test. A judge model costs a few dollars per thousand cases and agrees 82 to 88 percent with people on a well anchored rubric, so it is the default scorer. People are the ground truth, so spend them on calibrating the judge and on edge cases, not on every commit.

questions.title: Design the evaluation gate that runs on every pull request that touches prompts or model code for a support assistant. Say what runs, what blocks the merge, what it costs per month, and how you stop the gate from blocking on noise.
questions.answer: Trigger on changes to the prompt and model paths, run a fixed versioned suite of about 200 cases through the proposed prompt, score four anchored criteria with a frozen calibrated judge, and compare with the stored scores of the last known good baseline. Block when any criterion drops beyond the threshold and the interval on the difference excludes zero, and store the results as artifacts. With a small judge tier a 200 case run costs about 4 dollars, so ten merges a week cost about 160 dollars a month.

questions.title: Your product generates answers with one model, and your eval pipeline grades them using that same model plus a rubric. Scores rose after the last release and the team is pleased. A reviewer asks why the gain might not be real. What is the risk, and what do you change?
questions.answer: A model that grades its own family prefers its own style, so self evaluation inflates scores by about 10 to 20 percent. The rise can mean the judge likes the new outputs more, not that users do. Move the judge to a different model family, calibrate it against human labels, and score the baseline and the new version again under that judge.

questions.title: Two papers report BLEU on the same test set. One says 28.3 and the other says 0.283. A third team reports a ROUGE-L score ten points below yours on the same outputs. Your manager asks which number is right. How do you answer?
questions.answer: All of them can be right for different metric setups. BLEU is a fraction, and one paper multiplies it by a hundred. ROUGE-L moves by ten points when one library lowercases and the other does not, or when the two tokenize differently. Read the metric setup before you compare, and in your own harness fix one tokenizer and one smoothing rule and pin them with tests.

questions.title: Two harnesses in the repository compute pass at k. The first takes the empirical pass rate p and returns 1 - (1 - p) ** k. The second takes the sample count n, the pass count c and k, and returns 1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k). Read both. When do they agree, when do they differ, and which one goes in the report?
questions.answer: The first formula treats every draw as independent with success probability p and is a plug in estimate. The second counts the exact chance that k samples drawn from the n you ran contain at least one pass, and it is the unbiased estimator that code generation benchmarks use. They agree only as n grows large; for the samples you ran, the plug in is lower and noisier, and it extrapolates when k exceeds n. Report the unbiased one with the raw counts next to it.

questions.title: Your eval report shows two kinds of numbers: a pass rate, which is the share of cases that scored 4 or more, and a mean judge score on a 1 to 5 scale. A reviewer asks for error bars on both. Which interval do you use for each, and why not the same one?
questions.answer: Use a Wilson interval for the pass rate and a bootstrap interval for the mean score. A pass rate is a proportion, and the Wilson interval stays correct at small samples and near zero or one, where the normal approximation breaks. A mean of ordinal judge scores has no clean closed form, and the bootstrap resamples the scores with replacement and works with any distribution.

topics.title: Multimodal
topics.about: How vision and language models join images and text, and how they are trained.

questions.title: You pretrain an early-fusion model on interleaved text and image codes. The small runs are fine, but the large run's loss spikes and diverges after a while, and the attention scores climb from layer to layer. What is happening, and what did the published recipe change to make such a run converge?
questions.answer: Early-fusion training at scale is unstable because image codes and text tokens share one softmax and one residual stream, and their gradients and norms differ; the attention logits grow with depth until the softmax saturates and the loss blows up. The published recipe at 34B parameters diverged at several checkpoints without three changes: normalization of the query and key projections before the dot product, dropout after every residual addition rather than only after attention and the MLP, and pre-normalization on the residual branch plus an extra normalization on the skip connection of the last block. The training recipe is as much of the contribution as the architecture.

questions.title: A product needs a model that reads screenshots and answers questions today, and might need to draw diagrams later. Two designs are on the table: an adapter model, where a vision encoder feeds projected tokens into a text-only decoder, and a model that turns images into discrete codes in the same vocabulary as text and trains one next-token loss over interleaved sequences. Compare them and pick for this product.
questions.answer: The adapter design is late fusion: images enter as projected continuous tokens or through cross-attention, the decoder reuses all its text pretraining, and the output is text only. The shared-vocabulary design is early fusion: a quantizer maps an image to discrete codes, the transformer trains one loss over text and image codes, and it can emit image codes, so it generates pictures. For a product that must read screenshots now, pick the adapter: it reuses more pretrained compute, has no quantizer ceiling for understanding, and is cheaper to serve; add the early-fusion model only when drawing becomes a real requirement, because its image quality is capped by the quantizer and each generated image costs a decoder pass over a thousand or more codes.

questions.title: A unified next-token model generates a 512 by 512 image as a sequence of discrete codes. Estimate how long one image takes at a typical decode speed, compare it with a diffusion model, and say what a four-second video clip at low resolution costs in codes. Then name the levers that change the answer.
questions.answer: The reference model's tokenizer reduces 8 by 8 pixels to one code, so a 512 by 512 image is 4096 codes; at about 30 codes per second that is about 2 minutes per image, against 2 to 5 seconds for a diffusion model of the same quality tier. A 4-second clip at 8 frames per second is 32 frames; with the same 8 times spatial reduction and a 4-frame temporal reduction, a 256 by 256 clip is 32 times 32 times 8, which is 8,192 codes. The levers are the codes per image, the decode speed through speculative decoding or the KV cache, and a different decoding scheme such as masked parallel decoding, which needs about 16 passes instead of one pass per code.

questions.title: You fine-tune a model built like Flamingo, with a gated cross-attention block after every few layers of a frozen language model, on a small captioning dataset. Captions improve, but text-only quality degrades: the model rambles on plain prompts and loses facts it knew. What is the likely cause, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: The gates opened too wide too fast. Each gated layer adds the hyperbolic tangent of a learned scalar times the cross-attention output to the residual stream; at zero the layer is a no-op and the model is the pretrained text model. A high learning rate on the gates, or no regularization, lets visual noise flood the residual stream even when the prompt has no image. Confirm it by reading the gate values per layer against the base and by running a text-only eval with the gates forced to zero; fix it with a lower rate or a schedule on the gates, a text-only data mix, and a check that the layers add nothing when no image is present.

questions.title: You can spend your data budget on one of two things: have a strong proprietary model write captions for two million images, or pay people to describe seven hundred thousand images in detail by speaking for a minute or more about each one. Which do you choose for a new vision-language model, and what is the evidence?
questions.answer: Pay the people. The reference result is a model trained on 712K densely captioned images and no distilled captions that beat a much larger model on 11 of 11 benchmarks. Dense human captions carry 5 to 10 times the information of a short web caption and stay grounded in the image, while distilled captions inherit the hallucinations of the model that wrote them; about 12 percent of crawled pairs already describe things that are not in the image. Caption density beats caption quantity, which beats distillation convenience.

questions.title: A product manager asks how much of the context window one image uses in a LLaVA-style model with a 336-pixel encoder. Give the number, say where it comes from, and say how it changes with high-resolution tiling or with a query-based bridge.
questions.answer: One image costs 576 tokens: the encoder cuts the 336-pixel image into 14-pixel patches, a 24 by 24 grid, and the projector passes every patch token through. In a 2048-token context that leaves 1472 tokens for text; at 32k or 128k it is a small share. Tiling multiplies it: a 2 by 2 grid of 336-pixel crops plus one global thumbnail gives about 2880 tokens per image, and a 1 by 3 grid plus the thumbnail gives fewer, because it has one crop less. A query-based bridge compresses any image to a fixed 32 tokens, and a resampler to 64.

questions.title: Your 7B vision-language model trails a competitor on a multimodal reasoning benchmark by several points. The team's plan is a new connector design. Argue for or against, using what the ablation literature says about where the score comes from.
questions.answer: Against. Across the controlled studies, swapping the connector moved a reasoning benchmark by less than a point at a fixed token count, while swapping the encoder moved it by three or more, and doubling the language model from 7B to 13B added two to four points. The reasoning ceiling of such a model is the text reasoning ceiling of its language model; the visual side can only feed it. Spend the effort on the language model size, the encoder, the token count and the data before the connector.

questions.title: Design a vision-language model for an on-device mobile assistant that reads the phone screen and taps, types and scrolls. Keep the language model at about 2B parameters. Choose the encoder, the bridge, the resolution plan and the data mix, justify each choice with the ablation evidence, and name the capability you would guard against over-promising.
questions.answer: Encoder: the stronger contrastive encoder at native resolution, with a self-supervised encoder's features concatenated for a dense spatial signal, because the encoder explains about 20 percent of the variance and self-supervised features lead vision-centric tests. Bridge: a two-layer MLP, since the connector explains about 5 percent, with features from several encoder depths stacked so that fine position reaches the language model. Resolution: a ramp from low to high, with dynamic resolution up to about 1280 pixels on the long side, because screens are text-dense and reading gains most from pixels. Data: dense human descriptions of screens plus grounded action traces, not distilled captions; and guard the promise on spatial relations, where general models score 50 to 60 percent and the agent must hit the right element every time.

questions.title: A model must take a prompt with any number of images, some small and some large, interleaved with text, and then caption the last image from a few in-context examples. Explain the module that makes the number and the size of the images manageable, and how a text token knows which image to look at.
questions.answer: A resampler with a fixed set of learned latent vectors turns the patch tokens of each image into a fixed number of visual tokens. In the reference design, 64 latents attend over however many patches the encoder produced, 196 for a small image or 900 for a large one, through six blocks of cross-attention and self-attention, and every image exits as 64 tokens of one width. Text tokens then read those tokens through gated cross-attention layers inserted between the frozen language model blocks, and a mask lets each text token attend only to the latents of the most recent image before it in the sequence.

questions.title: A design tool wants to ship, with open weights it can host, one model that answers questions about a user's image, edits a region of it on request, and generates a new image from text. The latency per image must stay in seconds, not minutes. Lay out the families you would consider, pick one, and state the test that would make you change the pick.
questions.answer: Three open families cover understanding and generation in one model: next-token prediction over discrete codes, which does everything with one loss but spends one pass per code and minutes per image; continuous patches with a diffusion loss next to the text loss, which gives the best fidelity in about 20 passes but trains two losses; and masked discrete decoding, which keeps one loss, fills an image in about 16 passes, and gets region editing free from its masking objective. For a tool that needs editing and a seconds-level latency with open weights, start with the masked discrete family. Change the pick if a fidelity eval on your own prompts shows the quantizer ceiling hurting, or if the latency budget cannot afford sixteen full passes; the continuous two-loss family then takes over, with editing done through conditioned denoising of the region.

questions.title: Take-home. You get a frozen vision encoder that emits 197 tokens of width 768 per image and a frozen text embedding table of width 512. Build the smallest module that lets the two talk, train it on paired samples, and ship tests that prove it works. Describe the design, the loss, how you train it, and the tests.
questions.answer: Pool the 197 image tokens to one vector, pass it through a two-layer MLP, 768 to 1024 to 512 with a GELU between, and compare it with the mean-pooled caption embedding through a cosine alignment loss, one minus the cosine. Train only the MLP, about 1.3M parameters, with the encoder and the table frozen, for a few hundred steps over a few dozen pairs. The tests: the output shape equals the text width, the frozen parts have no trainable parameters, the loss is zero on identical vectors and two on opposite vectors, a gradient reaches the projector after one backward pass, and the loss at the last step is lower than at the first.

questions.title: You are choosing the bridge between a frozen vision encoder and a language model that stays frozen, for a new product. One architect wants a query-based transformer that compresses each image to a fixed set of tokens. Another wants a plain MLP that passes every patch through. How do you decide?
questions.answer: Decide on the token budget, not on quality in the abstract. At a fixed number of visual tokens, the ablation studies find the connector architecture a wash, within about a point between an MLP on mean-pooled patches, a query bridge and a resampler; a full-patch MLP spends more tokens, so it sits at a different budget. The query bridge caps an image at 32 tokens whatever its resolution and costs 188M parameters plus a two-stage pretraining of its own; the MLP emits every patch, 576 for a 336-pixel image, with about 22M parameters and one language-modeling loss. Pick the compressing bridge when context binds, as with long video or many images; pick the MLP when quality per token and simplicity matter and the context is long enough.

questions.title: Your team needs one open model for answering questions about images, text-to-image generation and inpainting, with a usable generation latency. One candidate generates images one code at a time; another denoises continuous patches; a third stays with discrete codes and fills them in parallel over a few passes. Compare the three on passes, training complexity and what comes for free.
questions.answer: Next-token generation over codes needs one pass per code, 1024 to 4096 passes per image, with one simple loss. Continuous diffusion in a shared transformer needs about 20 passes, but it trains two losses on different scales. Masked discrete decoding keeps codes and one cross-entropy loss, predicts all masked positions at once and commits the most confident ones each pass, so an image takes about 16 passes; inpainting is free, because the training objective is to fill masked codes from the rest. For a product that wants all three tasks in one open model at a usable latency, the masked discrete design is the fit, and the continuous design is the pick when fidelity is paramount.

questions.title: A warehouse team wants a general vision-language model to answer "which shelf is the item on" and "is the box on top of or under the pallet" from camera frames. They plan to ship as soon as a demo works on ten images. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: Spatial relations are the weak spot of today's general-purpose vision-language models: on benchmarks of above and below, left and right, counting and distance they score about 50 to 60 percent, below human level. A demo on ten images proves nothing about that distribution. Build a labelled eval of a few hundred frames with the exact questions first, measure the model, and compare it with a specialised detection or depth model whose box geometry you post-process; if the general model stays, fine-tune it on the task and keep a human-review route for low-confidence answers.

questions.title: In the first training stage of most open vision-language models, both the vision encoder and the decoder are frozen, and only the small projector learns. A junior engineer asks why anyone would train the smallest part first instead of the parts that matter. Answer them.
questions.answer: The two big parts already work: the encoder represents images, and the language model writes text. What is missing is a translation between their two vector spaces, and that translation is small. Training only the bridge costs a few hundred steps on one GPU, cannot damage either pretrained part, and gives the language model inputs it can read before anyone unfreezes it. Unfreezing the language model comes in the second stage, once the bridge produces tokens that look like language.

questions.title: Explain how a single transformer can train the text objective of next-token prediction together with a denoising loss on images in one gradient step. Cover the input representation, the attention mask, how the loss is routed per position, and the balance problem that follows. Then say what a sibling architecture changed.
questions.answer: Text enters as discrete tokens through the embedding table; images enter as continuous 16 by 16 pixel patches through a linear projection, bracketed by image start and end tags. One forward pass runs over the mixed sequence, and the loss is picked per position: cross-entropy on the vocabulary head for text positions, and a flow-matching regression for image patches, which predicts the velocity from a noised patch toward the clean one at a sampled time.
