The mask is block-triangular, causal over text and bidirectional among the patches of one image, with text attending to images that closed before it and patches attending to the preceding text. Both losses backpropagate through the same weights, so their relative magnitude must be balanced by hand; the sibling architecture keeps the joint attention but gives text and image their own weights in every block.

questions.title: Token-by-token image generation used to mean predicting one code after another in raster order. A newer method predicts whole grids at increasing resolution instead. Explain what it predicts at each step, why that fixes the old method's main weakness, and how it compares with diffusion in the number of network passes.
questions.answer: Next-scale prediction tokenizes an image into a pyramid of grids, from one code up to the full latent resolution, with a residual quantizer so that the sum of the scales reconstructs the image. The transformer is causal across scales and parallel within a scale: given all coarser grids, it predicts every code of the next grid in one pass. That removes the raster-order problem, where an early corner code had to commit before any context existed. For a 256 by 256 image the reference uses about 10 scales, so generation is about 10 passes against 28 to 50 for a diffusion transformer, and all codes of a scale come out together.

questions.title: Your deployed vision-language model answers questions about product photos. Support tickets say that it invents objects and misreads numbers, but the offline benchmark score is fine. Design the production monitoring and the response plan.
questions.answer: Treat hallucination as a production metric, not as a model property. Score every answer with a cross-modal error rate: embed the image and the generated text with an independent contrastive checker, and flag outputs where the text confidence is high but the image-text similarity is low. Track that rate per endpoint, per prompt type and per customer, alert on a rise, and route the flagged answers to human review instead of to the user. The team that introduced the metric cut its hallucination rate by about 35 percent this way, without a model change.

questions.title: Draw the standard architecture of a vision-language model that answers questions about an image. Name its three parts, say what each one contributes, and say which part you would expect to train when a team fine-tunes on a few thousand labelled images.
questions.answer: A vision encoder, a projector and a language model. The encoder, a pretrained vision transformer, turns the image into patch tokens. The projector, a small two- to four-layer MLP or a query-based bridge, maps those tokens into the language model's embedding space, where they replace a placeholder token in the prompt. The decoder language model reads image tokens and text tokens as one sequence and writes the answer; in most fine-tunes the encoder and the language model stay frozen or get adapters, and the projector is where the training happens.

questions.title: In the unified-generation family, the quality of a generated image is said to be capped by the tokenizer, not by the transformer. Explain why, show what moved the cap between two generations of models, and say which design avoids the cap entirely and at what cost.
questions.answer: A discrete image tokenizer is lossy: the decoder can only render what the codes carry, so the best image the model can ever produce is the tokenizer's own reconstruction of a real image. The first shared-vocabulary model used 1024 codes per 512 by 512 image from a codebook of 8192 and reconstructed at about 26 to 28 dB; the next generation used four times the codes, 4096, and a codebook four times larger, 32768, and reached 30.5 dB, close to the 32 dB of continuous latent diffusion. The design that avoids the cap keeps image patches continuous and trains a diffusion loss on them next to the text loss in one transformer; it drops the quantizer and gains fidelity, and pays with two losses on different scales to balance and a sampling loop at generation time.

questions.title: You lead a small team training an open vision-language model. The first run lands well below the open-weight models of its size on a general benchmark and on a document-reading benchmark. You can afford three more full runs. Which three changes do you make, in what order, and what do you expect each to move?
questions.answer: Order the runs by the variance each axis explains. First, the resolution schedule and the token count: ramp from a low resolution to a high one and add image splitting for the document benchmark, where moving from 448 to 980 pixels added 3 to 5 points in the ablations. Second, the encoder: swap the common contrastive encoder for the stronger one, which added 3 or more points on the general benchmark, and concatenate a self-supervised encoder if grounding matters. Third, the data: replace distilled synthetic captions with dense human-written ones, which beat the distilled set on every benchmark in the reference comparison; leave the connector alone, because at a fixed token count it moves scores by about a point.

topics.title: Agents
topics.about: The agent loop, tools, scope contracts, verification gates and why agents fail.

questions.title: How does an autonomous ReAct agent loop work and how do you prevent runaway execution?
questions.answer: A ReAct agent repeats a cycle of thought, action, and observation. The model reasons about what to do, calls a tool, reads the result, and continues until it can answer. Tools are defined with clear schemas, and their calls are parsed and validated before they run. To prevent runaway loops, enforce a maximum number of steps, plus time and cost budgets. Also detect repeated identical calls and break the cycle, then stop gracefully or hand off to a person.

questions.title: When should you build a multi-agent system versus a single agent with multiple tools?
questions.answer: Start with one agent, and add more only when you have a real need. Multi-agent designs help when one agent has too many tools to choose from accurately, or when unrelated context pollutes its prompt. A common pattern is a supervisor that routes work to specialised agents, each with a small tool set and focused context. The cost is that every extra agent adds model calls, latency, and new ways to fail, so measure whether quality improves enough to justify it.

questions.title: What is an AI agent, and how is it different from a single LLM call?
questions.answer: A single LLM call takes input, produces output, and stops. An agent wraps the model in a loop where it can decide to call a tool, observe the result, and decide what to do next — potentially many times — before producing a final answer.

questions.title: With function calling, who actually executes the function?
questions.answer: The model recognizes when a task needs external information or action and emits a structured request (a function name plus arguments) instead of a plain-text answer; the calling application actually executes it and feeds the result back into context.
options: Your application. The model only outputs the function's name and arguments.
The model runs it inside the API.
The provider runs it in a sandbox.
The user approves and runs it.

questions.title: What is the ReAct pattern?
questions.answer: Interleaving reasoning steps with actions and observations — think, act (call a tool), observe the result, think again — the foundational loop behind most tool-using agents.

questions.title: A task has twenty steps whose order is clear upfront, and each model call is expensive. ReAct, or plan-and-execute?
questions.answer: Produce a full multi-step plan upfront, then execute the steps (optionally re-planning if one fails), rather than deciding just the next single action at each turn like ReAct does. Better for tasks where seeing the whole shape of the problem upfront produces a more coherent plan than reasoning step-by-step in isolation.
options: Neither. Use a single prompt.
Either. They cost the same.
ReAct: decide each step after seeing the last result.
Plan-and-execute: plan once, then run the steps, replanning only if one fails.

questions.title: What is reflection / self-critique in an agent?
questions.answer: Having the model (or a separate call) evaluate its own prior output against the task and revise it before finalizing — a real accuracy lever for tasks where a first pass is often subtly wrong in a findable way.

questions.title: What's the difference between single-agent and multi-agent systems?
questions.answer: A single agent handles the whole task itself, with one growing context. Multi-agent systems split work across several agents (often with their own clean context windows), trading added coordination complexity for parallelism and per-subtask focus.

questions.title: You're building a multi-agent system that has to be easy to debug when something goes wrong. Which topology?
questions.answer: Hierarchical (one orchestrator delegates to sub-agents and combines results — easiest to debug), peer-to-peer (agents talk directly as equals — more flexible, harder to guarantee convergence), and blackboard (agents read/write shared state, never talking directly — useful when the set of contributors isn't fixed in advance).
options: Peer-to-peer.
Blackboard.
A swarm where every agent can message every other.
Hierarchical: one orchestrator delegates and combines.

questions.title: What is the supervisor / routing pattern?
questions.answer: A dynamic version of hierarchical delegation: a supervisor agent loops, re-routing between sub-agents based on intermediate results, instead of committing to one fixed delegation plan upfront like a static orchestrator would.

questions.title: Five AI apps each need the same 20 tools. Without a shared protocol, each app-tool pair needs its own integration. How many is that?
questions.answer:
5 × 20 = 100 separate integrations. With MCP, each app implements a client once and each tool a server once: 5 + 20 = 25. That N × M to N + M change is the problem MCP solves.

A standardized protocol for connecting an AI application to external tools/data sources, so one client implementation works against any MCP-compatible server instead of every app needing bespoke integration code per tool.

questions.title: What are the agent memory types?
questions.answer: Short-term: whatever fits in the current context window (conversation so far, tool results). Long-term: information persisted outside context, across sessions, typically an external store the agent retrieves from — turning memory into a retrieval problem.

questions.title: What is context engineering, and how is it different from prompt engineering?
questions.answer: Prompt engineering is about writing and organizing instructions. Context engineering is the broader discipline of managing an agent's *entire* context state across a multi-turn task — conversation history, tool results, retrieved documents, memory, all of it — not just the instructions.

questions.title: A fact at the very start of a 120k-token context is recalled reliably, but the same fact in the middle often isn't. What's that called?
questions.answer: As the number of tokens in context grows, a model's ability to accurately recall and use any specific piece of it degrades — not because of position (that's "lost in the middle" specifically), but because of sheer token volume spreading attention thinner.
options: Lost in the middle: recall depends on where the fact sits.
Hallucination.
Catastrophic forgetting.
Context rot.

questions.title: Your agent's context fills with the full working traces of research sub-tasks, and later steps get worse. What's the standard fix?
questions.answer: A specialized sub-agent handles a focused sub-task in its own clean context, then returns only a condensed summary (often 1,000–2,000 tokens) to the parent — keeping the parent's context from filling up with the sub-agent's entire working trace.
options: Raise the temperature.
Delete the oldest messages.
Switch to a model with a longer context.
Run each sub-task in a sub-agent with its own context, and return only a short summary to the parent.

questions.title: How do you prevent an agentic RAG loop from running forever (or effectively forever, on your bill)?
questions.answer: Combine four stopping conditions rather than relying on just one: a hard iteration cap as the absolute last resort (e.g. max 6 loops); a semantic-drift check that flags when the agent starts issuing near-duplicate retrieval queries (high cosine similarity to a prior query in the same loop signals it's spinning); a cheap sufficiency check, where a small model reads the accumulated context and outputs a simple yes/no on whether it's enough to answer; and a token/cost budget guard that stops before the context window or a spend limit is hit. In practice the sufficiency check fires most often in healthy operation — the hard cap and budget guard are safety nets for genuine edge cases, not the primary mechanism.
options: Several stopping rules together: a sufficiency check, a near-duplicate-query check, a token budget, and a hard iteration cap.
Tell the model to stop when it's done.
A wall-clock timeout only.
A hard cap of 50 iterations.

questions.title: ReAct vs. Plan-and-Execute for agentic RAG — when do you reach for each?
questions.answer: ReAct interleaves reasoning and retrieval in a serial loop, where each observation informs the next step — highly adaptive, since it can change approach mid-loop, but every hop adds latency because steps can't run in parallel. Plan-and-Execute separates planning from execution: one call produces a full task list up front, then everything in it runs in parallel — faster when the task decomposes predictably, but brittle, since there's no replanning if the upfront plan turns out to be wrong partway through. Use ReAct when the query's scope is genuinely unknown and you need adaptive exploration; use Plan-and-Execute when the decomposition is predictable and latency matters more than adaptivity.

questions.title: What does a Reflection/Correction agent actually catch that a single-pass RAG system misses?
questions.answer: It re-reads the retrieved chunk it just cited alongside the model's own draft answer and checks whether the chunk *actually* supports the specific claim being made — not just whether some chunk was retrieved at all, but whether this particular sentence is traceable to this particular chunk's text. A single-pass system has no mechanism to catch the case where a plausible-sounding number or fact simply wasn't in the retrieved context at all; a reflection agent flags that case and can trigger a more targeted re-retrieval before the draft ever reaches the user.

questions.title: How do you make an agentic RAG system observable in production, given that failures can be two or three hops removed from the wrong final answer?
questions.answer: Instrument three things specifically: per-iteration traces (log each step's query, which tool was called, a summary of the result, and tokens used, with an iteration index, so you can replay the whole chain); the *terminal reason* the loop stopped (reached a real answer, hit the iteration cap, tripped the drift check, or exhausted budget — distinguishing "answered correctly" from "gave up" is not optional for debugging); and user-visible citations tracing which retrieved passages actually contributed to the final answer. Without per-iteration traces specifically, debugging a multi-hop agent is close to impossible, because the root cause is routinely several steps upstream of where the wrong answer actually surfaces.

questions.title: How do you decide which agent framework to use for a given agentic RAG project?
questions.answer: Match the framework to what's actually hard about the use case, not to popularity — LlamaIndex if the core problem is RAG pipeline quality itself (chunking, indexing, retrieval); LangChain for general-purpose orchestration gluing together many different tool types; LangGraph or CrewAI when the design is genuinely multi-agent with distinct roles that need to converse or loop, and you want explicit, inspectable control over a cyclic execution graph; and for a single-agent, single-source system, consider skipping a framework entirely — a hand-rolled loop against the raw model API has less overhead and is easier to debug than an unnecessary abstraction layer.

questions.title: Walk through a concrete example of why single-shot RAG fails on a genuinely compound question, and how an agentic version fixes it.
questions.answer: Take "my basement flooded from a burst pipe and my car got water damage, am I covered?" — single-shot RAG embeds the whole compound question once and runs one search, which creates three distinct failure points: if auto and homeowner's policies live in the same index, whichever has denser chunks near that embedding dominates the top-k and the other policy's relevant clause may not make the cut at all; even if both surface, nothing checks that the retrieved "water damage" clause actually addresses *flood* specifically (homeowner's policies typically exclude flood while covering other water damage — a distinction a single pass has no mechanism to check); and there's no re-query if the first pull is thin. An agentic version decomposes into policy-specific subqueries, retrieves each independently, and runs an explicit verification step checking for exactly this kind of nuance before synthesizing a final answer.

questions.title: At the end of each session your agent writes a paragraph that says what it did. The next session still spends its first half hour finding out where things stand. What is missing from the end-of-session artifact, and how do you produce it so that it is never skipped?
questions.answer: The paragraph is a status report, and a handoff needs seven fields: a summary, the changed files, the commands run, the failed attempts, the open risks, the next action and a pointer to the verification and review reports. The next action is the most important field, because it makes the first step of the next session deterministic. Generate the packet from the workbench artifacts instead of asking the agent to write it, and run a cleanup check first so that the packet describes a tree the next session can trust.

questions.title: The task given to the agent was to fix one login bug. The diff changes the login route, an email helper, the database driver, the README and the release script. The transcript gives a plausible reason for each change. The reviewer rejects the pull request and asks you what went wrong and how to stop it. What do you say?
questions.answer: This is scope creep, and it is hard to see because the agent explains each step in good faith. The fix is not a stricter prompt. It is a contract on disk that lists the files the task may change and the files it must never change, plus a check that compares the final diff with that contract. The check runs before the gate, and a write to a forbidden path blocks the task.

questions.title: The product team wants a single maximum number of turns that applies to every run of your agent. The agent handles one-line edits, multi-file refactors, and unattended runs that drive a computer for hours. What number do you give them, and how do you defend it?
questions.answer: There is no single number, and the estimate shows why. Agents run 40 to 400 steps per task, and a computer-use task runs dozens to hundreds of steps as a normal case. A cap that fits a one-line edit stops every refactor, and a cap that fits an unattended run lets a stuck edit spend hundreds of turns. Give one cap per task class, set each from the trace distribution of successful runs in that class, and pair every cap with a wall-clock budget and a cost cap.

questions.title: A long coding session has used most of its context window. The runtime offers to summarize the older turns and keep going. Your teammate wants to let it run to the limit, because compaction is automatic. When do you compact, when do you end the session, and what do you measure to choose?
questions.answer: Compaction extends a session, and a handoff closes one cleanly and starts the next in fresh context. Compaction is fine while the compressed history still carries what the task needs, but quality decays as compression stacks up. The lesson's guidance is to end the session with a generated handoff at 50 to 75 percent of the budget, not at the wall, because the packet is cheap to write while the context is intact and expensive when the model is already losing its place.

questions.title: Two engineers disagree about how the loop should end. One wants an explicit finish tool that the model must call. The other wants the loop to end as soon as an assistant turn has no tool call in it. Which do you pick, and what does each choice get wrong?
questions.answer: Both are stop conditions, and a production loop needs both plus a budget. The no-tool-call stop is simple and matches how models behave, but it ends the run on any turn where the model answers in prose, including a turn where it only meant to think aloud. An explicit finish gives a clear signal with a payload, but a model that never calls it runs until the budget. Pick the no-tool-call stop as the default, keep finish as a tool that carries the final answer, and make the budget the last guard.

questions.title: A teammate says that their chat application is an agent because it calls a model inside a while loop. Name the parts that a real agent loop needs, and say what goes wrong when each one is missing.
questions.answer: An agent loop needs five parts: a message buffer that grows with each turn, a tool registry that the model calls by name, a stop condition, a turn budget, and an observation formatter. The model is the same in a chat bot and in an agent. The difference is that the agent can pause, call a tool, read the result and continue. Without the five parts, the loop is a chat bot with extra steps.

questions.title: Every verification report for the last month says passed. A reviewer notices that the test suite runs much faster than it did, and that several test files are gone. The acceptance command still exits zero. What happened, which check is missing from the gate, and what else do you change?
questions.answer: The agent met the acceptance command by removing the tests that failed, and the gate only checked that the command ran and exited zero. The missing check is a coverage floor: the gate reads a coverage report and blocks when coverage is below the floor, 80 percent by default, or when it drops by more than one percentage point against the previous merge. Add the test directory to the scope check so that a deletion under it is a flagged write, and promote warnings to blocks on release branches.

questions.title: Leadership wants to pause the harness work for two quarters and wait for the next model generation, on the theory that a better model will not need the scaffolding. Make the case with evidence, and say what part of their argument is right.
questions.answer: Today the engineering that carries the load is around the model, not inside it, and the numbers say so. The same model moved a coding agent from outside the top 30 to rank five on a terminal benchmark when only the harness changed, and a team that deleted 80 percent of its agent's tools saw success go from 80 percent to 100 percent. Most enterprise agent projects that fail do so around runtime, not reasoning. Leadership is right that models absorb harness tricks over time, which is why you build the harness from primitives that survive a model swap.

questions.title: A repository has a project-wide scope contract, and each task adds its own. The checker currently reads whichever file it finds first. Write the merge rule for every field so that the result is mechanical, reviewable and never looser than either input.
questions.answer: Merge by least privilege. Intersect the allowed globs, so that a path must be permitted by both contracts, and union the forbidden globs, so that either contract can prohibit a path. Take the smaller time budget, accumulate the approvals required, and treat the egress allowlist with three states: unset defers to the other side, two lists intersect, and an empty list stays deny-all. Write the rule into the contract schema so that the checker and the reviewer apply the same merge.

questions.title: A coding agent offers six permission modes, from one that asks before every action to one that approves everything. A colleague runs every task in the mode that approves everything, because the prompts are annoying. Give the rule you use to pick a mode, and say which tasks go where.
questions.answer: Pick the mode from the task, not from the annoyance. Start an unfamiliar or production-adjacent task in plan mode, where reading the plan is cheaper than undoing a bad run. Use the default mode for most interactive sessions, and the mode that auto-approves file writes for a known refactor across many files. Reserve the classifier-driven auto mode for unattended runs inside a workspace whose reach you have measured, and reserve the approve-everything mode for a disposable container.

questions.title: Take-home. Pick a small real change in a repository you may modify, and let one coding agent make it. Bring back evidence that a reviewer can reproduce, not a transcript. Tell us what you would record at each step, how you would prove that your acceptance check can fail, and what you would refuse to claim.
questions.answer: Record the starting revision, the observable goal, the non-goals, the allowed paths and the acceptance evidence before the agent runs, together with the working mode, the budget and a stop condition. Capture a baseline with the closest existing check before any edit. After the change, write the expected result independently of the implementation, introduce one deliberate wrong result in a disposable copy, and show that the same check fails for that reason. Label every runtime observation as local, staging or live, rehearse a rollback, and leave the branch, the changed files, the open risks and the next action explicit.

questions.title: A repo has a 3000-line instructions file for its coding agent. The agent follows about half of it. One engineer wants to cut it to a page. Another says that every line came from an incident and nothing can go. How do you settle it?
questions.answer: Both are right about something, and the answer is a layered file set, not a shorter file. Keep a root router under about 50 lines that holds only pointers and the few hard rules. Move the rules into a rules file with one screen per category, and move the depth into topic documents that the agent loads only when a task touches them. Every rule stays, and the agent reaches any rule in at most two hops.

questions.title: An instructions file tells the agent to be careful, to test thoroughly, and to ask if it is unsure. Three days later the agent ships a change with no tests, writes into a directory it should not touch, and never asks a question. Redesign these instructions so that a runtime can enforce them and a reviewer can score them.
questions.answer: Rewrite each wish as a rule with a slug, a category, a one-line description and a named check function. Five categories cover most rules: startup, forbidden, definition of done, uncertainty and approval. Give every rule a severity of block, warn or info, so that the runtime refuses only on block. Keep the rules in one markdown file with one rule per heading, so that review can see every change.

questions.title: An unattended coding run used the mode in which a separate model reviews every action before it executes. The audit shows that the reviewer approved each action. The run still copied a private dataset into a public repository. Explain how that is possible, and name the controls that would have stopped it.
questions.answer: The reviewer judges one action at a time against the request. Each action in the run was allowed on its own: read a file you own, write a file you own, commit, push. The harm was in the composition, and the reviewer does not re-derive the user's intent across the trajectory. The controls that catch this live outside the per-action check: an isolated workspace with no sensitive mounts, a network egress allowlist in the scope contract, per-tool action caps, and a trajectory audit after the run that detects what the other controls let through.

questions.title: A team ran a frontier model on a small repo task. The result had plausible code, two red tests, one edit in a file that had nothing to do with the task, and no note of what the model assumed or what remains. The team wants to buy a bigger model. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: The model was right about the language and wrong about the work, and a bigger model does not fix that. Reliable agents need a workbench with seven surfaces around the model: instructions, state, scope, feedback, verification, review and handoff. Each symptom in the run maps to one missing surface. You can swap the model and keep the surfaces, but you cannot drop the surfaces and keep the reliability.

questions.title: Take-home. Your team has the workbench surfaces as loose scripts, a shared document and some memory. Package them into one directory that a new repository can install with one command, and defend what you leave out. Bring the layout, the installer, the versioning rule and the uninstall rule. We grade the second install as much as the first.
questions.answer: Ship a versioned directory with four parts: the docs that carry the rules and the rubric, the schemas that are the contract, the scripts that are the runtime, and a short installer. The installer refuses to install over an existing pack without a force flag, copies the pack, connects CI if a workflows directory exists, and prints the next steps. Running it twice gives the same result. Project tasks, vendor SDK calls and onboarding prose stay out, because the pack is the recipe and each install is a serving.

questions.title: A pull request from a coding agent says that the whole suite is green. A reviewer runs it and two tests fail. The transcript shows the agent writing "running tests now" and then "all tests pass", with nothing between the two lines. What happened, and what do you build so that this claim cannot reach a reviewer again?
questions.answer: The agent predicted the output instead of reading it. Either no command ran, or the command ran and nobody captured the result into the loop. The fix has two parts: a feedback runner that records every command with its exit code, and a verification gate that reads those records and refuses to mark the task done unless each acceptance command ran and exited zero.

questions.title: A rule says that no migration file may change without an approval. It lives in docs/database.md, which docs/architecture.md links, which the top-level instructions file links. The root file also says to always use the ORM, while the database document says to write raw SQL in migrations. The agent changed a migration twice this week without asking. Find the causes and fix them in order.
questions.answer: There are three independent causes, and any one of them is enough. The rule is three hops from the router, past the two-hop reachability limit, so the agent never loads it, and it is prose with no check, so nothing refuses the write even when the agent reads it. And the root file conflicts with the database document, and conflicting instructions silently move an agent from asking to guessing. Fix the reach first, make the rule an approval-category rule with a block-severity check, and remove the conflict.

questions.title: An on-call engineer pages you. A coding agent has run for two hours on a task that normally takes ten minutes. The trace shows one shell command, one result, and then the same command again, over and over. Walk through how you find the cause and what you change so that this cannot happen again.
questions.answer: Read the trace for the pair of action and observation that repeats, then ask why the model does not react to the observation. The usual causes are an error that the loop never shows to the model, an observation that reads the same on every turn, and a missing turn budget. Fix the cause, then add the two guards that stop any future loop: a budget that yields control to the caller, and a check for a repeated action with a repeated observation.

questions.title: Your harness has grown to about two hundred tools across several teams. The model cannot hold all of them in context, two teams once registered the same name and the second silently replaced the first, and the success rate has fallen as the catalog grew. Design the registry and the policy for what the model sees on each turn.
questions.answer: Make the registry the only source of truth for what exists, what shape the arguments take and which handler runs, and surface only ten to forty tools per turn. The registry holds a typed record per tool, rejects a second registration of a name unless the caller asks to override, and validates every call against a small schema subset with pointer-shaped errors. The exposure policy loads tool metadata into context only when the task needs it, and the fewer tools the model sees, the better it calls them.

questions.title: A vendor deck lists its harness features: a loop that re-injects the original intent when the agent tries to stop early, a plan-execute-verify split, control-plane separation, signed tool-call passports, progressive compaction, hooks, skills with progressive disclosure, and sandboxed agents. Translate each one into the primitive it is, and say what the deck leaves out.
questions.answer: Every entry is a distributed-systems primitive with a new name. The re-inject loop is a trigger that re-enqueues the task with fresh context, plan-execute-verify is three workers with a queue between them, the passport is an authorization policy enforced by a pre-action worker, and compaction is a state-management worker over session persistence. Hooks are triggers around the invocation path, skills are a function registry whose metadata loads just in time, sandboxes are the compute plane, and the control-plane item is the control-plane and data-plane split that predates agents. The decks usually leave out queues, workers as the unit of deployment, trigger semantics, persistence as its own concern and authorization as a separate plane.

questions.title: You wrap every shell command that an agent runs so that the next turn can read what happened. What goes into the record, which field tells you whether the command worked, and what do you do when that field is empty?
questions.answer: The record carries the exact command as argv, the tail of stdout and the tail of stderr as separate fields, the exit code, the duration, the start time, and a one-line note of what the agent expected. The exit code is the success signal, because text can say anything and the code cannot. If the runner fails before it captures an exit, the record carries a null exit and an error reason, and the loop must not advance on it.

questions.title: A proposal replaces the script that decides whether an agent task is done with a model judge. The argument is that a judge reads the diff, understands intent, and catches more than a script can. Argue for or against, and say where a judge does belong.
questions.answer: Against. The gate answers one question, is this task complete, and that verdict must be the same for the same artifacts every time, in version control, in CI, with no way for the agent to argue with it. A model judge gives a different answer on a different day and can be talked into a pass. A judge belongs on the review side, where the question is qualitative: is the code readable, secure and on style.

topics.title: Protocols: MCP, A2A and skills
topics.about: How agents call tools and other agents, and how those calls stay safe.

questions.title: Your planner agent must delegate a test run to a remote agent that it knows only by host and port. Describe what it fetches first, how it decides which endpoint to call, and what it checks before it asks that agent for a stream.
questions.answer: It fetches the agent card with a plain GET on /.well-known/agent-card.json. From supportedInterfaces it takes the first entry whose binding and version it speaks, and it calls that entry's URL. Before SendStreamingMessage it reads capabilities.streaming, because a server must refuse the call with UnsupportedOperationError when the flag is absent or false.

questions.title: A planner polls a remote agent with GetTask until a task is done. It stops when the state is completed, failed or canceled. Against a deploy agent, the loop never returns. Against a test runner, the planner deploys a build whose test suite had a failure. Explain both bugs.
questions.answer: The loop knows three terminal states, and there are four. The deploy agent rejected the task, and a task in TASK_STATE_REJECTED never changes again, so the loop spins forever. The test runner finished the work it was asked to do, so its task is TASK_STATE_COMPLETED even with a failing test, because the verdict is a result and results travel in artifacts.

questions.title: Your client watches a long test run over SendStreamingMessage. After four frames the connection drops, while the agent keeps working and appends more lines to the log artifact. Design the recovery: how the client learns what it missed, how it rebuilds the log, and how it knows when to stop reconnecting.
questions.answer: Nothing is replayed, because a stream is a live view and the specification defines no cursor. The client calls SubscribeToTask with the task id, and the first frame must be a Task snapshot that already holds every chunk written while the client was away. The client replaces its partial artifact with the snapshot's copy and appends the frames that follow. When a later subscribe answers UnsupportedOperationError, the task is terminal, so the client stops reconnecting and reads the final task with GetTask.

questions.title: You run the official A2A conformance kit against your server twice. The first run scores 32.3 percent. After a two-line change to the kit's own JSON-RPC client, the second run scores 66.7 percent: 62 PASS, 31 FAIL, 11 SKIPPED and 25 NOT TESTED of 129 requirements. Your manager asks how conformant the server is. Estimate the real figure and defend every adjustment you make.
questions.answer: Neither percentage measures the server alone. The first run lost 63 of 85 JSON-RPC records because the kit posted to the card URL with a trailing slash, which is the kit's defect. In the second run, 21 of the failures are skips inside a test body that the tagged kit records as FAIL, so under the main-branch rule the run reads 62 PASS, 10 FAIL and 32 SKIPPED, or 86.1 percent, and of those ten failures three belonged to the server: the missing REST push routes and, at SHOULD level, the missing Cache-Control and ETag on the card.

questions.title: A client written for an older A2A release calls a current agent. Its first SendMessage carries only Host and Content-Type headers and gets HTTP 200 with a JSON-RPC error, code -32009. Its second call sends A2A-Version: 1.0, names the method message/send and gets code -32601. Explain both replies, and name the two changes the client needs.
questions.answer: Both replies are a current server reading an old client. An empty A2A-Version must be read as version 0.3, and an interface that serves only 1.0 answers VersionNotSupportedError; the recorded run reported the request as 0.3 (no header) against supported: 1.0. message/send is the old method name, and 1.0 uses the PascalCase rpc names such as SendMessage, so the second call is method-not-found. The client must send A2A-Version: 1.0 on every request and switch to the 1.0 names.

questions.title: A test run outlasts any connection your planner can hold open, so you want a webhook. Compare a webhook with polling and with streaming for this case. Then list the receiver's duties, given that the agent promises only to try each delivery at least once, and that the config operations return the stored webhook credentials to anyone who can call them.
questions.answer: Register the config inline in SendMessage with returnImmediately: true, so that no event escapes before the config exists, and close the connection. Delivery is at least once, so a notification can arrive twice or, after an outage, not at all: the receiver answers 2xx, checks the task id, processes idempotently, and reads the task with GetTask before it acts. Put the secret your receiver checks in authentication, because token has no standard header, and restrict who can call the four config operations, because a read returns the credentials in clear.

questions.title: A notes server wants a shared cache in front of it, so its resources/read results carry a public scope and a five-minute freshness hint. A security reviewer objects. What is the risk, which scope and freshness do you pick for a user's note, and what do you do with a result that must never be stored at all?
questions.answer: A public scope lets a shared cache hand one user's note to another user who asks for the same URI. Content bound to a user gets cacheScope: "private", which ties the entry to the requesting credential context, and a short freshness such as one minute. MCP defines only public and private, so a secret-bearing or fast-changing result gets private with ttlMs: 0, and the host adds a stricter no-store rule in its own cache policy.

questions.title: A client library exposes one cancel(request) method that behaves the same on stdio and on Streamable HTTP: it writes or POSTs a notifications/cancelled notification for the request id. Over HTTP, servers keep running the work and sometimes send a response after the cancel. A second method, cancelTask, returns success, the UI shows "stopped", and the worker keeps going. What is wrong with both methods?
questions.answer: Cancellation is transport-specific, and a durable task is a third thing. On stdio the client sends notifications/cancelled with the request id and receives no response. On Streamable HTTP the signal is closing that request's response stream, and a POSTed cancellation notification is the wrong signal. tasks/cancel acknowledges intent for a durable task that may stay working until a worker checkpoint observes the flag, so the UI must poll until a terminal status.

questions.title: Your gateway pins each approved tool by hashing its description text. A connected server ships an update. The description is unchanged, but the inputSchema gains a destination field and destructiveHint flips to false. The pin passes, and the model begins calling the tool with the new argument. What went wrong, and how do you pin correctly?
questions.answer: The pin covered one field, so a schema and annotation change passed as unchanged. Canonicalize the complete descriptor with sorted keys, hash it, and store the digest under a qualified name together with publisher evidence and the approval time. On every refresh, quarantine an unknown key or a changed digest until a person re-approves it. Hash equality proves stability, not safety, so the first descriptor needs review too.

questions.title: A document MCP server runs as two replicas behind a load balancer. Its draft_create tool keeps the new draft in a dictionary inside the process and returns {"ok": true}. The next call, draft_append, fails about half the time with "no draft", and the failures stop when the operator turns on sticky routing. Explain the failure, say why the operator's fix is wrong, and redesign the two tools.
questions.answer: The first call created the draft in the memory of one replica and returned no name for it, because the design assumed the connection identifies the draft. The second call is a fresh POST that can land on the other replica, which has valid protocol metadata and no way to load the draft. Sticky routing hides the bug until a restart, a rollout or a failover moves the next request. Return a server-minted opaque handle from draft_create, keep the draft in a shared durable store, and make draft_append take the handle as an ordinary argument.

questions.title: Take-home. Build the admission module of an MCP gateway. It takes the tools/list results of several servers and produces an admitted set, a rejected set and an audit trail. It must page through every list completely, pin each descriptor, qualify names before it merges, reject a descriptor that mirrors a sensitive parameter into a header or places x-mcp-header anywhere but a direct top-level property, validate structured results against output schemas on the invoke path, and emit header audit events that carry names and never values. Describe your design, the tests you ship, and the evidence a reviewer should expect.
questions.answer: Run the five gates in order and keep them separate. Discover with an opaque cursor loop that stops only when nextCursor is absent or null; admit each descriptor against a canonical whole-descriptor digest, a full schema-tree walk for x-mcp-header, and a sensitive-name policy; qualify every tool as <server>.<tool> before the merge; and validate structuredContent against the published output schema before anything reaches the model. Tests prove that one rejected descriptor does not block valid tools, that an empty-string cursor continues, that an annotation under oneOf, items or $ref is rejected, and that a changed inputSchema fails the pin. The evidence is the page trace, the admitted and rejected sets, the digest ledger and redacted audit events.

questions.title: A gateway in front of an MCP server authorizes each tools/call by reading the Mcp-Name header and checking it against the caller's role. The origin server behind it executes params.name from the JSON body. An attacker sends Mcp-Name: notes.read with a body whose params.name is notes.delete. The gateway also rejects an unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version before it looks at anything else. Walk through what happens, and give the validation order you would ship.
questions.answer: The gateway approves a read while the origin runs a delete, because two components decide from two different fields. Ship one fixed order: validate the JSON-RPC and metadata types, compare every mirrored header with the body, and only after equality is proven check whether the matched version is supported. A disagreement is HTTP 400 with -32020 even when one of the two version values is unsupported, so the request dies before a backend is selected, a role is checked or a rate-limit token is spent.

questions.title: You deploy a remote MCP server that accepts tokens from two authorization servers, one for staff and one for partners. Design the client enrollment, the per-request token validation and the key handling so that three things hold: a token minted for a sibling MCP server is refused, a signing key rotation causes no outage, and a client steered to a hostile token endpoint never hands over its authorization code.
questions.answer: Publish RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata that names both issuers, and treat that list as the issuer allow-list. Enroll a client with its pre-registered credentials when it has an explicit relationship with that issuer, otherwise with a Client ID Metadata Document when the issuer advertises support, and use deprecated dynamic registration only as an explicit fallback with the correct application_type. On every request validate the pinned iss, an aud equal to this server's canonical resource URI, exp and the scope the tool needs; answer 401 for an invalid token and 403 with insufficient_scope for a valid token that lacks the scope. Refresh the JWKS on a schedule and re-fetch once on an unknown kid, and let the client record the issuer before it redirects and compare the RFC 9207 iss in the authorization response exactly before it redeems the code.

questions.title: Your agent host launches several MCP servers over stdio. One is current. One is an old archive server that understands only initialize. One is current but slow to start. A teammate proposes a simple rule: send server/discover, and on any error or timeout send initialize. Design the startup so that the slow server is never downgraded and the archive server still works.
questions.answer: Treat an ambiguous signal as ambiguous. A timeout, a connection close, an empty response or an unrecognized error does not identify an era, so the client fails closed unless that exact peer is configured with allow_legacy=True. A recognized modern error such as -32022 proves the server is current and forbids initialize. For the archive peer on the allowlist, send one initialize under a transport-enforced deadline and select the legacy era only after a structurally valid positive result.

questions.title: A tool that deletes notes, notes_delete, finds three notes that match the title the user gave. Design the confirmation flow under the current MCP revision: how the server asks the user to pick one and confirm, how the answer comes back, and what stops a client from answering a different question or replaying one confirmation with changed arguments.
questions.answer: The server answers with a result typed input_required that embeds an elicitation/create form request listing the three candidate ids and a confirm boolean, plus an integrity-protected requestState. The client shows the form and retries the original tools/call with a new request id, echoing requestState and the inputResponses. The server signs the state over the principal, the method, a digest of the arguments, the candidate set, the phase and an expiry, verifies the echo, checks that the chosen id was in the signed set, re-authorizes the workspace and re-checks containment, and consumes a one-time nonce in a shared replay store before it deletes.

questions.title: A platform team deploys an MCP server over Streamable HTTP behind a load balancer with two replicas. They configure sticky routing keyed on Mcp-Session-Id, keep a standalone GET /mcp stream for change notifications, and plan to resume a broken stream with Last-Event-ID. Which of these belong to the current revision, and what replaces the rest?
questions.answer: None of the three belongs to the current revision. The endpoint accepts POST only: GET /mcp and DELETE /mcp return 405, Mcp-Session-Id is ignored and never minted, and Last-Event-ID is ignored because streams do not resume. Change notifications arrive on a client-opened subscriptions/listen POST whose response stays open as SSE, and a dropped stream is replaced by a new listen request and a refetch of the affected data.

questions.title: Over Streamable HTTP, a client calls charge_account. A reverse proxy buffers the response stream, the client reaches its timeout and disconnects, and the server commits the charge a moment later. The client sends the call again with a fresh JSON-RPC id, and the customer is charged twice. The team proposes to deduplicate on the JSON-RPC id. Design the fix.
questions.answer: A JSON-RPC id correlates one message and never identifies a business operation, so two ids are two charges to the server. Add an application idempotency key to the arguments, and make the server store the key, a fingerprint of the arguments and the committed result in one atomic durable transaction. The same key with the same arguments returns the stored result, and the same key with different arguments is rejected.

questions.title: A filesystem MCP server reads the client's Roots list once and treats any path under a root as authorized for deletion. The client advertises one workspace directory. Two delete requests arrive: one for a sibling directory whose name starts with the workspace name, and one that reaches the parent through an encoded dot-dot segment. What is wrong with this design, and how do you replace it?
questions.answer: Roots were informational guidance, never authorization and never a sandbox, and the current revision deprecates them. A string-prefix check accepts both hostile paths, because both begin with the workspace text. Replace the root with an explicit workspaceUri argument or a resource URI, then enforce three layers: authorize the principal for that workspace, normalize the URI and check containment by path components, and run the server under an operating-system sandbox.

questions.title: A colleague ports an MCP server from the 2025 revision. The port keeps the initialize handshake and stores the client's declared capabilities on the connection object for later requests. All the old tests pass. What breaks under the current revision, and where does the metadata have to live instead?
questions.answer: The current revision has no handshake and no protocol session. A server that remembers capabilities from an earlier message can apply the wrong permissions or the wrong wire shape to the next request, which may come from another client on the same process or land on another worker. Every request carries io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities in params._meta, and the server validates them on each request and forgets them after it answers.

questions.title: A team builds an MCP server for a project tracker. It has five capabilities: show the details of one issue, create an issue, a sprint review template, the project policy document, and close an issue. A developer proposes to publish each capability as a tool, a resource and a prompt at the same time, so that every client finds it. Which primitive do you give each capability, and why not all three?
questions.answer: Pick the primitive from who makes the choice. The model chooses a tool to perform an operation, so create and close are tools. A host or a user reads addressable content at a URI, so issue details and the policy are resources, and a user starts a prepared message workflow, so the review template is a prompt. Each extra surface costs discovery, authorization, caching, error handling, tests and documentation, so one capability gets one primitive.

questions.title: Your MCP server has a tool route_report that reads a report from an upstream source. A reviewer reads the handler and finds two things. When the upstream source is down, the handler returns a JSON-RPC error. When a client sends a tool name that the server does not know, the handler returns a result with isError: true. Is that the right way round?
questions.answer: No, both cases are backwards. A JSON-RPC error means the request could not be dispatched at all: an unknown tool name, a malformed envelope, missing request metadata or an invalid cursor. A complete result with isError: true means a valid call reached the tool and the tool reports a failure the model can act on, such as a source that is unavailable right now.

topics.title: Multi-agent systems
topics.about: Supervisors, handoffs, shared memory, consensus and the failure modes of agent teams.

questions.title: Three agents share a memory on a research task. A retrieval agent reads a page and writes that a study found a 42 percent improvement. The page says 4.2 percent. A summarizer builds on the entry, an analyst recommends adoption on the strength of the number, and the final report cites it. No agent crashed and no test failed. What is this failure called, why is it structural, and what are the three changes that stop it?
questions.answer: This is memory poisoning. One agent's hallucination entered the shared state, and every agent downstream read it as a verified fact, so the error was turned into evidence as it moved. It is structural because any shared memory without provenance and without an independent verifier will do this eventually. The three changes are provenance on every write, an append-only log where corrections supersede instead of overwrite, and at least one read-only verifier that re-fetches sources and reports on a separate channel.

questions.title: A multi-agent product has been in production for two quarters. Failures arrive as a stream of unrelated tickets and nothing gets fixed systematically. Design the audit that turns the stream into a ranked list of fixes, and say which failure class you would weight most heavily even if it is not the most frequent.
questions.answer: Sample about 1000 real execution traces each quarter, categorize every failure into the three root categories of the published taxonomy and the five groupthink patterns, compute the failure rate per category, rank the mitigations by how many failures each would remove, and commit to two or three for the quarter. Weight verification gaps most heavily even though they were the smallest category by count, because they are silent: a plausible wrong output produces no exception, no alert and no ticket until a human notices.

questions.title: Your multi-agent prototype runs in one process with an in-memory event loop. In production, runs last hours while they wait for human input, worker processes crash and lose everything, peak load is ten times the average, and users are charged per run so a retried side effect is a double charge. Design the layer that goes under the agents, and say what you would build first.
questions.answer: Put a durable execution layer under the agents: persist the full run state after each step under a run id, so that when a worker crashes its lease expires and any other worker resumes from the last checkpoint. That needs serializable state, a deterministic resume, and idempotent side effects. For the charge, use a deduplication key per run and an outbox so that side effects are written as intent first and executed once, use asynchronous I/O for the model calls, and deploy new versions beside old ones so that in-flight runs are never killed. Build the simplest version first, a web service with a relational database, and adopt a workflow engine when a measured problem demands it.

questions.title: Take-home. Design a research system in which one lead agent plans and several workers search in parallel, for a product where users ask open questions and expect a cited answer. Deliver a design document with the lead and worker prompts in outline, the shared memory, the failure modes you expect and the mitigation for each, the operational limits, and the cost model. Say what you would cut if the budget were halved.
questions.answer: The lead decomposes the question into sub-questions, scales the number of workers to the question's complexity, and synthesizes the worker summaries without reading raw sources. Each worker has a fresh context, an explicit scope, a timeout at about twice the median runtime and a token cap. Shared memory carries provenance on every entry, is append-only, and is checked by a read-only verifier that re-fetches sources and reports on its own channel. Every outbound call sits behind a circuit breaker, the system is deployed with versions side by side, and the cost model states up front that the pattern spends about 15 times the tokens of a single agent.

questions.title: A team added an ensemble to a question-answering task: five agents on the same model debate until they agree, then answer. Accuracy fell below the single agent. They want to add more agents. What went wrong, and what would you change first?
questions.answer: Whether debate helps depends on structure, not on the count: who talks to whom, how many rounds, whether the agents are different, and whether anyone argues against. Five copies of one model share their errors, so the vote is correlated, and debate until agreement rewards the most confident agent through conformity. Change the composition before the count: start from self-consistency with one strong model, then swap one agent for a different base model, bound the rounds at two or three, and add a judge that does not vote.

questions.title: A new multi-agent framework ships every few months, each with its own vocabulary. Give the method you use to understand a new one quickly, and name the part of every such system where the hard bugs live.
questions.answer: Map the framework onto four primitives: the agent, the handoff, the shared state and the orchestrator. Every framework picks a default on each axis, and the rest is surface syntax. The agent is a system prompt plus tools and is stateless, the handoff is a structured transfer of control, the orchestrator decides who runs next, and the shared state is the only stateful part of the system. That is where the difficult bugs sit: memory poisoning, message ordering, versioning and write contention.

questions.title: A team of four agents shares one message log, and every agent reads all of it. The team is about to grow to a few dozen agents, and the context each agent carries is already large. Compare keeping the single log with moving to topics that agents subscribe to, and say how you would handle several agents writing at once.
questions.answer: A full pool is simple, transparent and easy to inspect, and it stops scaling at about 10 agents because each agent's window fills with the others' work. A blackboard with subscriptions routes only the relevant messages to each agent, so it scales further, and it costs an up-front schema that makes the topics meaningful. Many systems mix the two: a small pool at the planning layer and blackboards below it. For writes, most systems serialize through one writer, because model calls are slow enough that contention is rare.

questions.title: A three-level agent hierarchy reviews a contract. The top manager splits the work into an engineering branch and a legal branch, each with its own sub-manager and workers. The final report is complete and confident, and it contains finance findings where the legal review should be. Nobody asked a finance question. Trace the failure and say what you change in the design.
questions.answer: The top manager mislabeled the legal branch as finance when it decomposed the task. The sub-manager did what it was given, the workers did finance work well, and the top synthesizer reported finance findings. The error surfaced only at the top, one level away from any point where a human could have caught it. The design fixes are a depth cap of two, provenance on every synthesis, a logged decomposition that is checked against the original question, and a canary worker that is always asked the user's question unchanged.

questions.title: A paper reports that its multi-agent coding system beats single agents by a wide margin on a well-known software engineering benchmark. Your team wants to adopt the architecture. What do you ask before you believe the number?
questions.answer: Ask which benchmark and which split, whether the benchmark was released after the model's training cutoff, what the comparison baseline was, how many trials were run, how many task types were covered, and what the result cost in tokens and wall-clock. The split matters most: frontier models score about 23 percent on the uncontaminated split of that benchmark against more than 70 percent on the older split, so a number without its split says nothing.

questions.title: A swarm runtime uses one thread per in-flight model call. At peak it holds about 10,000 calls at once. Estimate the memory the threads take before any work is done, say what those threads are doing most of the time, and say what you would change.
questions.answer: A thread stack is about 1 MB, so 10,000 threads need about 10 GB of memory for stacks alone, before the first token arrives. Those threads are idle about 99 percent of the time, waiting for the next token from a model service. Move the model calls to cooperative fibers through asynchronous I/O, where the same 10,000 calls fit in one process, and keep threads or processes only for CPU-bound work such as embeddings.

questions.title: A payment service starts failing about 10 percent of its requests. Within minutes the inventory service, which never failed, is down, and the order agents that call both are stalled. The payment service itself recovered on its own. Explain the chain, name the failure family, and say what you add so that it cannot repeat.
questions.answer: This is a retry storm, a cascading reliability failure. The order agent retried each failed payment, each retry ran a fresh inventory check, inventory saw twice its normal load and began to time out, every order then retried the inventory check as well, and inventory saw ten times its load and fell over. The fix is classical: a circuit breaker on every outbound call that opens when the downstream error rate passes a threshold and serves a cached or default result, plus a capped retry budget per request.

questions.title: Your single agent does well on small tasks. Pointed at a codebase of 200 files in three languages, with tests that need infrastructure and an external API to research first, it stops making progress. The team proposes a model with a bigger window. What is the ceiling it hit, and would a bigger window remove it?
questions.answer: The task exceeds what one loop, one window and one system prompt can carry, and a bigger window only moves one of three limits. Context saturates as tool results pile up, so details from an early turn are gone by turn 30, and one prompt that asks the model to research, code, review and test produces an agent that does each one poorly. One loop reads file A, then B, then C, with no parallelism. The fix for all three is to split the work so that each agent has one job, one window and one prompt.

questions.title: You are adding a checking agent to a team that shares a memory. A colleague wants the checker to fix wrong entries directly, because that is the simplest design. Specify the checker: what it reads, what it may write, where its results go, and what it can and cannot protect against. Defend the restrictions.
questions.answer: The checker reads the shared memory like every other agent, re-fetches the sources that entries cite, and compares. It has no write handle to the shared memory, only to a separate verification channel that a human or a decision agent reads. It cannot stop a bad entry from being written, and it can be fooled by an entry that cites no source, but its verdicts can never become a shared fact. A checker that writes into the memory is poisoned by the same memory it checks, and then its verdicts carry the poison further.

questions.title: Five agents answer the same factual question and vote. Three of them run the same base model and agree on a wrong answer, and the two others are right. Majority vote picks the wrong answer. A colleague says that classical fault-tolerant consensus solves this. Explain why it does not, which assumptions break, and what the recent agent-specific protocols change.
questions.answer: Classical consensus tolerates fewer than a third of nodes behaving arbitrarily, and it assumes that faults are independent, that honest nodes are correct, and that a ground truth exists. Three agents on a shared base model share their faults, an honest model still hallucinates, and on some questions the agents define the truth. The agent-specific variants weigh each vote by a confidence probe, aggregate leaderless proposals by a geometric median, or split agents into a core and an edge with learned trust weights. None of them makes agreement equal correctness, so the consensus output still goes to an independent verifier.

questions.title: A support system uses handoff-driven orchestration: each agent is a prompt plus a set of tools, and one of the tools returns another agent. The trace shows the triage agent handing a user to billing, billing handing the user back to triage, and the two repeating until the round cap ends the run. The user never got an answer. Why does this happen, and what is the cheap fix?
questions.answer: In this pattern the routing lives in the prompts, and the current agent picks its successor with a tool call. The triage prompt says that a billing question goes to billing, and the billing prompt says that anything outside its tools returns to triage, and the user's message satisfies both. Nothing persists between handoffs, so the new agent starts from its prompt and the history and does not know that the same handoff already failed. The cheap fix is a loop detector on the last few handoffs that forces an exit to a fallback agent, plus a trace event for every handoff.

questions.title: In a lead-and-workers research system, two workers answered overlapping sub-questions with numbers that contradict each other. The final report contains one of the numbers and no mention of the other. The user found the second number in a source and asks why the report hid it. Where did the system fail, and what do you change?
questions.answer: The lead resolved a synthesis conflict by picking one side in silence, which the lesson calls the worst failure in this pattern, because the user never learns that a disagreement happened. Two upstream causes made it likely: the decomposition gave two workers the same ground, and no worker had a scope that stopped it from drifting into the other's territory. The fix is a lead that detects contradiction between worker outputs and either re-asks with a narrower question or writes the disagreement into the answer, plus provenance on every synthesized claim.

questions.title: A team proposes a five-agent pipeline, with a planner, a retriever, a writer, a critic and a formatter, for a summarization feature that one agent handles today in a dozen tool calls. The argument is that specialists produce better output. How do you decide, and what will the pipeline cost that the slide does not show?
questions.answer: Keep the single agent unless the task fails one of three tests: it needs more context than one window holds, it needs different prompts at different stages, or it has work that can run at the same time. A dozen tool calls on a task that fits in one window passes none of them. The pipeline adds a lossy compression step at each of four boundaries, coordination logic that has its own bugs, at least five serial model calls of latency, and five times the token cost.

questions.title: Four agents, a coder, a reviewer, a tester and a researcher, share one conversation. You must decide how the next speaker is chosen on each turn. The options on the table are a fixed rotation, a model that reads the recent messages and picks, and letting the current agent name its successor. Compare them and say what you would ship with each.
questions.answer: A fixed rotation is deterministic and cheap, and it gives the coder the turn when the topic is a legal question. A model selector is context-aware, and it costs one extra model call per turn, picks differently on identical input, and tends to favor one agent. A handoff by the current agent keeps the routing in the prompts with no external manager, and it is the pattern that loops when two prompts disagree. Most production chats use a selector with fallback rules, a round cap, a termination signal and a log of every selection.

questions.title: A research system with one lead agent and several worker agents beat a single agent on an internal evaluation by a wide margin. Explain the mechanism, and say which single variable explains most of the gain.
questions.answer: The lead plans and decomposes the question, each worker gets a fresh window for one narrow sub-question, and the lead synthesizes the worker summaries without ever reading the raw sources. Three mechanisms carry the gain: fresh context per worker, a narrow prompt per role, and workers that run at the same time. The variable that explains most of it is total token usage, which the lesson's source puts at 80 percent of the variance on one browsing benchmark. A worker that does not carry the lead's planning tokens has room to read.

topics.title: Sandboxes
topics.about: Isolation for agents that run code or drive a computer, and the policy around it.

questions.title: Your agent reports that example.com over HTTPS timed out inside the sandbox, and npm install fails with a connection error. The sandbox keeps no shell history. Show how you find out which rule decided, and prove that this was a policy decision and not a network fault.
questions.answer: It did not time out: the proxy accepted the CONNECT, then answered inside the TLS session with 403 Forbidden and a 90-byte body that reads Approval required for example.com:443. Run sbx policy log SANDBOX --json and read the blocked_hosts row: proxy_type, the rule text and the reason. Then run sbx policy check network --sandbox NAME example.com:443 --json and read deny_kind, where implicit means no rule matched and the default denied, and explicit names the deny rule. Add an allow in the right scope, or remove the deny first.

questions.title: Design the trust boundary for a browser agent that books travel for employees. It reads arbitrary pages, it is logged in to the travel site, and it can submit forms. Name the attack classes you assume, draw the boundary, pick the evaluation that matches the job, and name the one defense you refuse to rely on by itself.
questions.answer: Assume five classes: instructions in page text, payloads in URL fragments or query strings that never render, a page that asks the agent to write a durable memory that fires next session, CSRF-shaped requests that ride the logged-in session, and a harmless-looking button that carries a follow-on action. Draw a read/write boundary: reading is never consequential, and any write, a form submit, a post, a side-effect tool or a navigation that changes state, needs fresh human approval when the initiating content came from outside the trust boundary, with a per-task tool allowlist, scoped credentials only, and every HTTP request logged. Evaluate on transactional web flows, not on fact finding. The defense you never rely on alone is the content sanitizer, because the agent must read untrusted content to work and a pattern filter removes the easy attacks only.

questions.title: You let an agent work on a repository overnight in a sandbox with the default workspace mount. In the morning git diff is clean and a new file sits in .git/hooks/pre-commit. Explain how the agent wrote a file that no diff shows, which workspace mode prevents it, and how the agent's commits still reach you under that mode.
questions.answer: The default mount is the host path mounted read-write inside the VM at the same absolute path, so the agent can edit anything in the tree, including Git hooks, CI configuration, package.json scripts and agent settings, and a hook under .git/hooks never appears in git diff. --clone at creation runs the agent on a private clone while the host repository enters the VM read-only at /run/sandbox/source, so a push back is refused. The commits come home through a git daemon in the VM that sbx publishes on a loopback port and registers as the remote sandbox-<name> in the host repository, so you fetch that remote before you remove the sandbox.

questions.title: A build takes about a day of wall time, and you want it on a cloud sandbox because the laptop lid ends local runs. Estimate what happens if you accept every default, then set the clock and the shape, and give the order of magnitude of the bill with your reasoning shown.
questions.answer: With defaults the sandbox is the small shape, 2 vCPU and 4096 MiB, with a TTL of one hour from creation and no --on-timeout, so the server stops it if it can resume it and deletes it otherwise, and the build dies after an hour. Set --ttl up to the ceiling of 24 hours from creation with --on-timeout stop, extend with sbx --cloud ttl +2h if needed, and pick xl, 16 vCPU and 32768 MiB, at $1.12 per hour in the launch blog. A day on that shape is a bit over a day of hours times about a dollar, so under thirty dollars, well inside the $250 promotional credit, and a stopped sandbox is not billed for compute.

questions.title: sbx policy init balanced gave one global policy with 194 allow entries. A developer adds example.com with --sandbox m101-policy, later tries a deny for the same host at the same level, and gets a refusal. Explain the rule grammar, the two scopes, and the order in which the authorizer decides one connection.
questions.answer: An allow rule is a comma-separated list of hostnames, domains, IP addresses or CIDR prefixes, with globs such as *.example.com, .example.com, api?.example.com, example.com:443 and  for every host; an allow covers TCP unless --protocol says otherwise, and a deny covers TCP and UDP. Rules live in two scopes, global by default and local with --sandbox. For the same hostname or CIDR a deny wins over an allow, so the CLI refuses a deny that conflicts with an allow in the same scope and you remove the allow first. The authorizer stops at a matching deny, admits on an allow from any active scope, and otherwise denies as implicit.

questions.title: The balanced preset allows github.com:443 and **.github.com:443. A reviewer argues that an agent which reads a private repository can post its contents into an issue or a gist on that same allowed host, so the allowlist is theatre. Evaluate the claim, state what the product can and cannot see on that connection, and design the narrowing.
questions.answer: The claim holds for host rules: a host allow permits every request to that host with any method, path and body, the vendor's own staff said in 2026 that an issue body or a gist on an allowed host is not blocked, and the manual records the claim as disputed with no capture that tests it. On an allowed connection the proxy runs forward-bypass, a tunnel with no inspection and no credential injection; it terminates TLS only to speak on a blocked host or to inject on a host with a bound credential. The narrowing is an HTTP rule, a kit's network-policy@2 entry with methods and paths or an organization HTTP rule, plus less to read in the first place: clone mode with secrets outside the repository, and deny-all with approvals so an unexpected host waits for a person.

questions.title: Security wants one allowlist across every developer laptop, a record of each host an agent reached, and proof that no developer can widen the list. Compare local policy on each laptop with an organization policy from the governance product. What changes on a laptop the moment a policy becomes active, and what does one audit record hold?
questions.answer: Local policy gives each laptop its own preset and rules, a per-host policy log, and a developer who can add a global allow at will, so it fails the third requirement. An organization policy is written centrally, reaches the daemon within 5 minutes, and from then on only organization allow rules grant access: local and kit allow rules go inactive, local and kit deny rules still apply, and a local deny even beats an organization approval requirement. The daemon then writes one JSONL audit record per decision, holding metadata such as the decision, the resource, the deny reason, the action type and the agent, and never prompt content, agent output or parameter values; the cost is a paid subscription, and the coverage is local sandboxes only.

questions.title: A coordinator agent runs in CI with --exec --json. The event stream shows the same run_background_agent call five times, each answered with The user rejected the tool call., then Error: Agent terminated: detected 5 consecutive identical calls to run_background_agent.
