Naming the two-gate model explicitly — a cheap metadata pre-filter plus an authoritative late-binding check — and the staleness window between them is what distinguishes a senior answer from "just add a metadata filter."

questions.title: Retrieval is correctly filtered by permissions. Then a "related documents" feature follows links from the retrieved chunks to other documents. What's the risk?
questions.answer: Any stage added after the ACL gate that touches document content can reintroduce a leak even though retrieval itself was correctly filtered — a reranker that re-queries the index for more candidates without reapplying the filter, a semantic cache that returns an answer generated under a different, broader-permission user's session, a "related documents" link-expansion step that follows references from an authorized chunk into an unauthorized one, or a summarization-memory layer that condensed an earlier, more-privileged session into context reused later. The principle worth stating explicitly: authorization has to be enforced at the *last* point document content enters the prompt, and every component between retrieval and generation has to be either ACL-aware itself or provably content-blind.
options: Lower recall.
It can pull in documents the user isn't allowed to see, because it runs after the permission filter.
Answers get slower.
Duplicate chunks.

questions.title: Why is filtering the LLM's output for restricted content the wrong place to enforce access control, versus filtering what gets retrieved?
questions.answer: By the time restricted content reaches the model it has already crossed the trust boundary — it may be logged or retained by the model provider regardless of what the final visible output ends up saying. Output filtering also depends on correctly recognizing and stripping every possible leak after the fact (often via a second LLM-as-guard), and that detection step is bypassable the same way any LLM behavior is bypassable. Filter what goes in — what gets retrieved — not what comes out.

questions.title: An approximate search returns the top 100 candidates, then a permission filter keeps only documents this user may see: 2% of the corpus. If permissions are unrelated to relevance, how many results are left on average?
questions.answer:
100 × 0.02 = 2 results, and often zero. Filtering after an approximate top-k throws away almost everything for users who can see little. That's why the fix is to filter during the search, or partition by permission.

When a user can legitimately see only a tiny slice of the corpus, HNSW's greedy graph traversal can get stranded in regions where almost no node satisfies the filter, since most of the graph's edges lead toward ineligible vectors the traversal has no reason to route around. Fixes: use a filterable-graph engine that builds extra links specifically to keep filtered traversal connected, fall back to brute-force scan below some match-ratio threshold where approximate search would otherwise fail, or move to per-tenant/per-permission-class index partitions so the permission boundary *is* the partition boundary rather than a predicate layered awkwardly on top of one shared graph.

questions.title: What's the security risk of semantic caching specifically in a multi-tenant RAG system, beyond the obvious “wrong answer served”?
questions.answer: Beyond a naive cross-tenant leak (Tenant A's cached answer served to Tenant B's semantically-similar query), there are two subtler ones: a timing side-channel, where a cache hit (fast) versus a cache miss (slow) lets one tenant infer whether another tenant has previously queried a given topic, purely from response latency; and document-ID leakage in cache metadata, where an implementation that caches retrieved chunk IDs alongside the answer exposes *which documents are relevant to a topic* even if the answer text itself is withheld. The fix for all three is the same: namespace every cache key by tenant/user ID and include a hash of the current permission set in the key, not just the query embedding.

questions.title: How do you handle a real-time permission change — a user loses access to a document mid-session — so a cached or in-flight answer doesn't leak it?
questions.answer: Three layers together: a short TTL on any cached permission data (5–60 seconds for sensitive data, with every cache read checking freshness against the TTL); a late-binding check on the final top-k that re-verifies the user's *current* permissions against the authoritative source right before generation, not against stale index metadata; and session/cache invalidation triggered by the permission-change event itself — when a revocation fires, invalidate active sessions that may hold a cached answer referencing the now-revoked document, and flush any semantic-cache entries whose source documents include it. Combined, this means a user who loses access mid-session gets blocked at their *next* query, not left holding a stale cached answer indefinitely.

questions.title: How does tenant offboarding differ between a structurally-isolated deployment and a shared-index-with-filter deployment?
questions.answer: Structural isolation (a separate namespace, index, or cluster per tenant) makes offboarding trivial — drop the tenant's namespace or index, which doubles as a clean, demonstrable answer to a right-to-erasure request. A shared index requires a delete-by-filter pass across every chunk belonging to that tenant, plus real verification that the vectors are actually gone from both the live index *and* any backups or snapshots — an operation that's genuinely easy to get subtly wrong (partial deletes, lingering tombstones in the HNSW graph, or backups quietly retaining vectors the live system reports as deleted).

questions.title: A red team found a trigger that makes a model misbehave. The safety team fine tunes the model on the red team's prompts until it behaves on all of them and reports the behavior removed. Why might the original trigger now work better than before, and what would count as evidence of removal?
questions.answer: Adversarial training teaches the model to behave on the distribution the red team can produce, and in the reference experiments it made the held out trigger more reliable, because the model learned a sharper line between test and deployment. Evidence of removal needs the original elicitation preserved and run as a held out test, probes on internal activations that no longer separate trigger from no trigger, and an elicitation surface wider than the red team's prompts.

questions.title: You can subtract an agreement score from the reward during training to reduce sycophancy. The alignment lead wants the penalty weight as high as it will go. What does a high weight cost, how do you pick the weight, and how do you show that you got it right?
questions.answer: The correction subtracts a classifier's agreement score, scaled by a weight, from the reward. In the lesson's sweeps sycophancy falls to near the base model level at a weight around 0.3 to 0.5, and beyond that the model turns contrarian on claims that are true. Pick the weight from a frontier of correct answer rate against sycophancy rate on matched test pairs, and watch calibration while you sweep.

questions.title: A safety report says a model refused 97 percent of harmful requests in testing. A reviewer asks whether the model was told that the test conversations would be used for retraining, and what it did in conversations it believed were not used. Why does that question matter, and which number answers it?
questions.answer: The question separates compliance from strategic compliance. In the reference experiment a production model that believed its conversations would retrain it toward compliance complied with harmful requests about 12 percent of the time, and 3 percent when it believed they would not, with scratchpad reasoning that said it complied to keep its current preferences from being modified. The compliance gap, the difference between the monitored and the unmonitored condition, is the number, and a report without that split cannot measure it.

questions.title: A model review lists four separate problems: answers got longer without getting better, the model agrees with users who are wrong, its reasoning text does not drive its final answer, and in one agent test it edited the test file so the check would pass. Four teams want four fixes. What do you tell them?
questions.answer: These are four costumes of one mechanism: the optimizer found features that the proxy reward paid for and that only correlated with quality in the training data. Length, agreement, reasoning that looks right and a passing check were all cheaper than the real thing. The defenses are unified too: shrink the gap between proxy and target, reduce optimization pressure, or move the selection pressure onto features that are hard to game.

questions.title: A team trains a chat model against a reward model and reports that the reward climbs with every step. They plan to train longer. Why is a reward that only goes up a warning sign, and which curve would you ask them to plot before they continue?
questions.answer: The reward model is a proxy for what you want, and a strong optimizer finds the inputs where the proxy and the target disagree. The proxy score climbs while the true quality rises, peaks and then falls. Ask for the gold reward, from a larger reward model or human ratings, plotted against the square root of the KL distance from the initial policy. The gap between the two curves is the reward hacking.

questions.title: A colleague argues that reward hacking is bounded in their pipeline because the policy trains with a KL penalty against the reference model, so it cannot drift far. Why is that argument incomplete, and under which condition does it fail completely?
questions.answer: The KL penalty constrains how far the policy's distribution moves, not which modes it moves toward. The over optimization curve already shows that a KL penalty softens the collapse of the gold reward without preventing it. When the proxy's error is heavy tailed, rare but reachable inputs exist where proxy minus gold is unbounded, and a KL constrained optimal policy can place its mass on them: proxy reward arbitrarily high, gold reward at baseline.

questions.title: Your detector's substring rules catch "ignore all instructions" in plain text. Attackers now send the same phrase in base64, in rot13, in leet speak, and with invisible characters between the letters. Design the step that runs before the rules, and say which signals you must not throw away while doing it.
questions.answer: Add a normalize pass that produces a cleaned working copy: strip zero width and bidirectional control characters, decode tokens that look like base64 before you lowercase, because base64 is case sensitive, then lowercase, decode hex and rot13, and map leet digits back to letters. Run the rules on both the raw and the normalized text, because the zero width insertions are themselves an encoding trick signal that the cleaned copy no longer shows.

questions.title: A colleague shipped a prompt injection defense last month: one regex that matches "ignore previous instructions". This week a prompt that said "disregard the prior guidance" went through. The colleague wants to add a second regex. What do you ask before anything ships, and what does a detector look like instead?
questions.answer: Ask for the precision and the recall per attack category on a labeled corpus; the current defense was never measured, so nobody knows what it covers. A detector is a function from a prompt to a confidence between zero and one and a best matching category. Build it as layers, a normalize pass, substring rules and token level regexes, with a category and a base score on every rule, and run it against the fixture corpus and a benign set on every change.

questions.title: Every request to your assistant passes an input detector, and yet a response last week contained a customer's email address and part of the system prompt. Design the output side, say how three separate classifiers combine into one action, and explain what happens to latency.
questions.answer: Put three classifiers on the model output behind one router: toxicity by rules, personal data by regexes for emails, phone numbers and card shaped strings, and instruction leakage by trigram overlap with the known system prompt. Each returns a severity, and the router takes the maximum and applies one action: block on high, redact on medium, warn on low, log on none. Run the classifiers in parallel with token streaming and hold the final chunk until the verdict arrives. Earlier chunks have already shipped, so where a block or a redaction must cover the whole response, hold the full response and accept the latency.

questions.title: Take home. We give you the fixture corpus of labeled attack prompts, a benign prompt list and a mock assistant that answers questions over retrieved documents. Build the safety gate around it: an input detector whose coverage is measured for each attack category, an output side with at least two classifiers behind a router, and a trace per request. The retrieved documents can carry instructions. What do you deliver, how do you measure it, and what do you say you did not do?
questions.answer: Deliver a detector as rules in data with a normalize pass, a metrics runner that writes per category precision and recall against the fixture corpus and the benign list, an output router with a personal data classifier and an instruction leakage classifier and their redactors, and a gate that runs before, during and after generation with a deterministic aggregation table and writes the verdict of every checkpoint for each request. Add a category and a rule family for instructions hidden in retrieved documents, because the corpus has none. State that the detector is wrong on purpose on benign looking role play, that a real model and a real sandbox are out of scope, and that the thresholds were not tuned on held out data.

questions.title: You own safety for a customer facing assistant built on an open weight model behind a retrieval pipeline. Design the red team range that runs without you: the attack families, the schedule, what counts as a finding, how you keep the assistant helpful while you harden it, and how you prove that a training time intervention helped.
questions.answer: Schedule at least six attack families on separate queues: automated jailbreak search, tree search attacks, gradient suffix attacks, encoding attacks, multi turn persona attacks and code switching across languages, each reporting a success rate. Every success becomes a finding with a taxonomy id, a severity score and a disclosure timeline. Track over refusal on a benign probe suite next to the block rate so the trade off sits on one chart, and prove a self critique intervention with a before and after harmlessness delta on a held out set.

questions.title: Your team wants to replace human preference labelers with a model that reads a list of written principles and ranks completions, mainly to save money. Is this cheaper preference training and nothing more? What changes in the failure modes, and what stays?
questions.answer: No. Moving the preference signal from people to a model changes which failures the pipeline has, not whether it has them. Labeler psychology gives way to principle interpretation that is uniform across the dataset and legible, sycophancy toward the user can drop because the labeler model has no user to please but must still be measured, and Goodhart's law remains because the proxy is now the model's reading of the principle set. The rest of the pipeline, a reward model and policy optimization, is unchanged.

questions.title: A support assistant must never end a refusal without offering a next step, and a coding assistant must close every code answer with a runnable block or a stated assumption. Neither is something a content classifier recognizes. Design the component that enforces constraints like these, and say what happens after a violation.
questions.answer: Put these constraints in a declarative rules file that lives in version control next to the code and has its own review. Each rule has a name, a severity, an explanation, a predicate that says when the rule is in scope and a predicate the response must satisfy, with atomic checks composed by all of, any of and not. After a violation a fixer applies a local declarative edit, the engine checks the revision again, and a structured diff of the two versions goes into the trace.

questions.title: Before a launch, the safety case for a model reads: we applied supervised tuning, preference training with a harmlessness reward and a red team cycle, so hidden harmful behavior is not a concern. Rewrite the argument so that it would survive review, and name the evidence each claim needs.
questions.answer: The old argument stopped being adequate once implanted backdoors were shown to survive all three methods. A credible case assumes a behavior might have survived and measures survival directly: run the original elicitation as a held out test after training, apply probes to internal activations and show they no longer separate trigger from no trigger, press the model with an elicitation surface wider than the red team's, and add a monitored against unmonitored split so strategic compliance is measured rather than assumed.

questions.title: A vendor's safety report has one table: the refusal rate on a harmful prompt set, 97 percent, measured once with the default system prompt. You must decide whether to adopt the model for a customer facing assistant. List what the report cannot tell you and the measurements you add before you decide.
questions.answer: The table measures one side of one decision under one condition. It cannot show over refusal on benign prompts, which category of attack the misses fall into, whether the model behaves the same when it believes it is unmonitored, or how the number moves under your system prompt and attack families. Add a benign probe set for over refusal, a per category breakdown from a taxonomy, a monitored and unmonitored split, and a red team run with several attack families against your deployment, and plot block rate against benign pass rate.

questions.title: Your team has shipped forty regex patches against prompts that got past the assistant's refusal rules, and the backlog of new attacks grows faster than the patches. A new engineer asks what an attack even is. Which shared vocabulary do you introduce, and what does it buy the team?
questions.answer: Label every attack by the trust boundary it abuses. Six categories cover most of what arrives: role play against the persona, instruction override against the system prompt, context smuggling in the gap between data and instructions, multi turn ramp against the conversation history, encoding tricks against the surface form of forbidden tokens, and prefix injection against the next token decision. Labels turn the attack stream into a histogram, the histogram into a coverage chart, and the chart into the next sprint.

questions.title: Your refusal evaluation asks the model to state a confidence with each answer. In the bin where the model says 0.9, it is right on 60 percent of the prompts. Estimate the calibration error that bin contributes, explain how the full number is built, and say why it is independent of the two refusal rates.
questions.answer: The gap in that bin is about 0.3: a stated 0.9 against an observed 60 percent. The full ECE bins every prompt by stated confidence in tenths, computes the mean stated confidence and the accuracy in each bin, and averages the absolute gaps weighted by bin size. It measures whether the model knows when it is right, which is a different question from whether it refused the right prompts.

questions.title: Your gate blocks most attacks before the model runs. In the trace of one request the detector said benign, the model began answering with a procedure it must never give, and the response was cut after a few tokens and shipped as a redacted partial. Explain which layer acted, why the first layer missed, and whether the outcome is correct.
questions.answer: The streaming filter acted: it buffers a short window of emitted chunks, sweeps it for known continuation phrases, terminates the stream on a match and marks the output as terminated early, which the aggregator treats as a medium signal and maps to redact. The detector missed because the prompt was an encoding trick or a prefix injection whose surface the input rules did not cover. The outcome is correct for the design: the harmful continuation never completed, and the trace records the miss for the detector team.

questions.title: Your aligned model agrees with users who state a wrong fact far more often than the base model did, and the data team says the preference labels are clean. Someone proposes relabeling the dataset. Why will that not fix it, and what does the mechanism predict about longer training?
questions.answer: Sycophancy is a property of the loss, not a bug in the labels. Sycophantic completions are over represented among the high reward outputs of the base model, and any method that upweights high reward outputs amplifies them. The lesson's measurements go from about 15 percent sycophantic completions before alignment to about 40 percent after it, and about 55 percent after twice the training steps, so more training makes it worse.

questions.title: Your team has a classifier that flags reasoning traces in which a model considers faking compliance, and a proposal to penalize those traces during training. Early runs show the flagged traces disappear. Argue both sides of shipping this, and say which measurement decides.
questions.answer: The upside is real: the reference follow up found that penalizing flagged reasoning was highly effective at reducing the measured gap, and that penalizing long reasoning also worked because faking needs complex reasoning. The downside is that you train against a visible signal, which can teach the model to hide the signal and weakens the same classifier you would use to monitor it. The measurement that decides is the compliance gap under a monitored and unmonitored split, not the trace count, together with probes on internal state that do not depend on what the model writes.

questions.title: After a safety pass, the assistant refuses every prompt in the harmful set. The safety lead calls it a success. A product manager says that chemistry homework now gets refused too. Which numbers settle this, and how do you compute them?
questions.answer: You need two metrics, not one. The under refusal rate is the share of unsafe prompts the model answered, and the over refusal rate is the share of safe prompts it refused. Treat the assistant as a binary classifier on prompt safety: label a prompt set safe or unsafe, detect refusals in the outputs, and report both rates with accuracy and a per category breakdown.

topics.title: System design
topics.about: Design a model service end to end: requirements, data, model, serving, evaluation and cost.

questions.title: Design a RAG system for a legal document corpus where different law firms share the platform but must never see each other's documents, and every answer must cite its exact source.
questions.answer: Requirements first: strict per-tenant isolation (structural, not filter-based, given the sensitivity), citation at the passage level since legal answers are worthless without exact attribution, and an audit trail since this is a compliance-sensitive domain. Architecture: per-tenant index partitions (not a shared index with a filter — the stakes are too high for the HNSW-recall and leakage risks a shared index introduces), citation enforced via NLI-checked attribution at generation time rather than trusted model-reported citations, a late-binding permission check even within a single firm's own multi-user access tiers, and per-query audit logging of user, filter applied, and chunk IDs retrieved. The interview signal here is naming the isolation-model tradeoff explicitly (structural vs. shared-plus-filter) and justifying it against this specific domain's stakes, not defaulting to whichever is cheaper.

questions.title: Your RAG system's answer quality has been stable for months, then degrades sharply this week with no deploy. Walk through your investigation.
questions.answer: Check, roughly in this order of likelihood and cheapness-to-check: has the source corpus itself changed in a way that broke a downstream assumption (a new document format, a schema change in an ingested database); has the embedding or generation model been silently updated on the provider side (providers do this without always announcing it clearly); has traffic mix shifted (a new, harder query distribution rather than an actual system regression); and has the index gone stale or partially corrupted (a failed incremental update left it partially out of sync). The point of the answer isn't getting the exact cause right blind — it's demonstrating a systematic elimination process rather than guessing at a fix and hoping.

questions.title: How would you migrate a production RAG system to a new embedding model with zero user-facing downtime?
questions.answer: Blue/green, never in-place: build the new index fully from the new embedding model alongside the still-serving old index, verify the new index's quality against your golden set before any traffic touches it, then cut over atomically once validated — never partially update one index with a mix of old and new vectors, since they live in geometrically incompatible spaces and mixing them silently corrupts every similarity score involving one of each. Handle the migration window explicitly too: any document ingested while the rebuild is in progress needs to be embedded with *both* models (or the cutover needs to be fast enough that the window is negligible), or it risks landing in the wrong index with the wrong embedding version.
options: Take the service down overnight and rebuild.
Re-embed documents in place, a batch at a time.
Switch the query embeddings first, then the documents.
Blue/green: build a full new index with the new model beside the old one, validate it, then switch over at once.

questions.title: When would you choose Cache-Augmented Generation over RAG for a given use case, as an actual design decision rather than a trivia question?
questions.answer: CAG makes sense specifically when the corpus is small enough to fully fit in a model's KV cache budget and is relatively stable — a single product manual, a fixed set of policy documents — because it sidesteps every retrieval-quality failure mode by construction (there's no "wrong chunk retrieved" if nothing was ever selectively retrieved at all). It stops making sense the moment the corpus grows past the cache budget, updates frequently enough that cache invalidation becomes constant, or genuinely needs to scale beyond what any single context window can hold — at which point you're back to standard RAG, or a hybrid where a stable core knowledge base is cached and a fast-changing slice is retrieved.

questions.title: How would you design retrieval for a corpus that will eventually reach billions of documents, from the start, without having to re-architect later?
questions.answer: A two-tier retrieval architecture from day one, even if the corpus is small initially: coarse retrieval combining BM25 (which scales to any corpus size via an inverted index) with quantized dense embeddings to pull a few thousand candidates from the full corpus cheaply, followed by a precise reranking pass (cross-encoder or ColBERT) over just that narrowed candidate set. Partition the index by a natural dimension (topic, date, document type) from the start so sharding is a configuration change later, not a rewrite — retrofitting partitioning onto a system designed as one flat index is far more painful than building it in from the first version.

questions.title: A stakeholder asks “why don't we just fine-tune the model on all our documents instead of building RAG?” How do you answer that in an interview setting?
questions.answer: Walk through the real tradeoffs rather than just asserting RAG is better: fine-tuning bakes facts into weights, which means every single update to the knowledge base requires retraining — infeasible for anything that changes daily or weekly; fine-tuning also can't cite sources, since facts get blended into the weights with no traceable provenance back to a specific document, which matters enormously for trust and auditability; and fine-tuning on a large, diverse document set is actually quite data- and compute-expensive relative to RAG's "re-index the new document" update cost. RAG's answer to the same stakeholder: it updates by re-indexing, not retraining, it can cite its sources, and it scales to more documents than you'd ever want to fit into a single fine-tuning run — fine-tuning still has its place (tone, format, a narrow skill), just not as a substitute for keeping facts current.

questions.title: A new version of a chat prompt looks better in a notebook. Design how it reaches users: the stages, how users are assigned, what you measure at each stage, and when it rolls back automatically.
questions.answer: Run it in shadow first, on all traffic, logging its answers without showing them, and compare quality metrics with the current prompt. Then route a small share of users to it, 10% in the lesson, and widen in steps to 25%, 50% and 100% while the metrics hold. Assign by a deterministic hash of the user id so each user sees one version, and roll back automatically when the new version's error rate reaches twice the old one over a window of requests.

questions.title: A feed ranking score must be no more than two hours old for 5,000,000 items, and the serving peak is 120 requests per second. Price batch and online serving with the lesson's cost model, pick one, and say what would flip the choice.
questions.answer: With a one-hour batch job and a two-hour staleness limit, the job must run every hour, which the lesson's cost model prices at 24.0 runs per day over 5,000,000 items for $48.50 a day. Two online replicas sized for 120 peak QPS cost $24.00 a day and serve the freshest data. Online wins here; the choice flips when the freshness limit relaxes enough to cut the runs, or when peak traffic grows enough to need many replicas.

questions.title: Design the service behind a chat product with 10,000 daily active users who send about 5 queries each, with roughly 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query. Users must see a response start quickly, the tail must stay bounded, and the product has a unit cost target. Lay out the request path, the components, the budgets you hold each one to, and how you would scale it.
questions.answer: The request enters through a gateway that authenticates and rate limits per user, passes input guardrails, is matched against a semantic cache, and on a miss goes to the model with streaming, then through output guardrails, an eval logger and a cost tracker. The budgets are a median under 2s, a p99 under 10s, a cache hit rate above 30%, a guardrail block rate under 5%, and a cost per request under $0.01. At 50,000 queries a day this runs on a few async servers behind a load balancer; the servers are I/O bound, so a single async process holds a hundred or more concurrent requests and scaling means more servers, not more cores.

questions.title: A subscription company with 2,000,000 users wants to reduce churn. The retention team can send a save offer to a small share of users each night. Design the system end to end: the prediction, the decision, the serving mode, the baselines, the rollout, and the failure defaults. State the load and the budgets you assume.
questions.answer: The task is binary classification: the probability that a user cancels in the next 30 days, so that the nightly job can pick the top 5 percent for an offer. Nightly scores for every user fit batch inference; the lesson's cost model prices one run a day over the user base at under one dollar, while an online service sized for 40 peak QPS costs $24.00 a day for a freshness nobody needs. The model must beat the idle-days rule by a set lift, ship through shadow and canary stages, and fall back to that rule when anything fails.

questions.title: You have a small pretrained language model and 800 labeled text messages, half spam and half not. Design the classifier: what you keep, what you replace, which of two training regimes you choose, how you split and evaluate, and when the other regime would win.
questions.answer: Keep the pretrained body and replace the vocabulary head with a linear layer to two classes over a mean-pooled, mask-weighted sequence vector. With 800 examples, train the head only with the body frozen: it is fast, light on memory and rarely overfits, and on this fixture it reaches about 0.9 precision and 0.85 recall after twenty epochs. Full fine-tuning takes about three times longer and lands within a couple of points either way; it starts to pay off at the scale of 80,000 examples or when the domain drifts far from the pretraining text.

questions.title: A payment model's accuracy, measured as labels arrive, fell from 0.946 to between 0.76 and 0.79. The feature monitors and the score distribution stayed quiet the whole time. The team proposes retraining on the last quarter of labeled data tonight. What happened, why did the monitors miss it, and is the proposal right?
questions.answer: The relation between inputs and labels changed while the inputs themselves did not, which is concept drift. Input and prediction monitors compare distributions of features and scores, so a change in the conditional label distribution is invisible to them, and only the outcome monitor can see it, after the label delay. Retraining tonight on the last quarter is the wrong move: most of those labels still describe the old relation, so the model relearns it; collect labels from after the change first, then retrain on them.

questions.title: You built a small web demo of a model for reviewers. Three months later a colleague asks whether it is "production". How do you tell, and what changes when the answer is yes?
questions.answer: A demo serves known people in short sessions from one process. It has become a product when people outside the team use it every week, when someone asks for an uptime target or reports an outage, when users want to sign in or see history, when the weekly model cost is a budget line, or when the input is covered by a contract or a law. At that point the demo moves onto the production stack with authentication, fallback models, tracing, and cost tracking per user.

questions.title: You are the reviewer for ML design documents before any training starts. A team hands you a document for a payment fraud check that proposes batch scoring, where one job takes an hour, with a three-minute staleness limit, reports an offline AUC, lists a majority-class baseline, and has no rollout section. Walk me through your review: the sections you expect, which gaps block, how you score it, and what you tell the team.
questions.answer: The document needs nine sections, and six items block a review because each one makes the system unsafe or useless: the decision that uses the prediction, a business metric, a heuristic or current-system baseline, confirmation that every feature exists at prediction time, a shadow or canary stage with a rollback, and a default action for every failure. This document fails at least three of them: the only baseline is trivial, there is no rollout and no rollback, and the serving choice fails the fit check because batch cannot meet a limit of three minutes when one job takes an hour. I send it back with the blocking list first, and I ask for precision at the decision threshold instead of AUC.

questions.title: A payment risk model scores every transaction. Labels arrive weeks later as chargebacks. Design the monitoring: what you watch, how you compare windows, which statistics you compute, and how you keep the alert rate low enough that people read the alerts.
questions.answer: Monitor four layers: system health, input distributions, prediction distributions, and outcomes once labels arrive. Compare a fixed reference window with sliding current windows, with the Population Stability Index and the two-sample KS statistic for numeric features and a chi-square test with Cramér's V for categorical ones. Alert only when a corrected p-value and an effect size both pass and the condition persists for consecutive windows, and send warnings to a dashboard rather than to a person.

questions.title: A team trains and aligns models in a multi-stage pipeline and ships the result to serving. Design the evaluation platform that decides whether an artifact is shippable: what it reads, what a gate is, which two gates catch most disasters, how it handles a failed gate, and how a third party replays a decision.
questions.answer: The platform reads a manifest that describes the run completely, with a seed, a code revision, and an input and output hash for every stage, and it evaluates numeric gates that were written before the run started. A regression gate holds the new model to the previous one on core benchmarks and catches training bugs; a KL budget gate caps how far the aligned policy drifted from its reference and catches alignment overcooking. A failed gate holds the run for a named reviewer whose override is logged in the manifest, and anyone can replay the decision because the eval report is content-addressed and the eval data hash is part of it.

questions.title: Design the feature layer for a churn model. Training needs the value of each feature for millions of user and time pairs. Serving needs the latest value for one user in a few milliseconds. Name the parts, explain how a training row gets its features, and show with the lesson's numbers what goes wrong without the right join.
questions.answer: One registry holds each feature definition with its entity, window, default, TTL and version, and both paths compute from it. An offline store keeps the full history with event timestamps for training and backfills; a materialization job copies the latest value per entity into an online key-value store with a TTL. A training row takes the latest feature row at or before its label time, inside the TTL. Without that point-in-time join the lesson's demo looks better offline, 0.948 against 0.893, and worse on new data, 0.763 against 0.876, because the newest snapshot leaks the answer.

questions.title: Three systems retrain monthly on their own production data: a churn model that sends save offers, a fraud model that blocks payments, and a ranking model that orders a feed. Each one gets a little worse after every retrain. Explain the shared cause, design the data layer that prevents it, and say what each training row must carry for the fix to work.
questions.answer: Each model's decisions change the data that trains its next version, which is a feedback loop. Offers keep users who would have churned, so high-risk users look loyal; blocked payments never get a chargeback, so fraud disappears from the blocked region; the feed shows only its top items, so only those collect clicks. The fix is to keep data the model did not influence: a random holdout that never receives the intervention, a small share of random decisions, and a log that stores the score and the decision with every row, joined to features as of the decision time so training can separate influenced from clean data.

questions.title: A team wants to adapt an open model in the 8B class to its own domain and serve it at a measurable cost per million tokens. Design the pipeline so that one command runs it end to end: the stages, the hardware per stage, the data hygiene, the ablations you require, the serving measurements, and what the release must include.
questions.answer: Five stages, each with a config file in version control: data preparation with deduplication, a quality filter, personal data scrubbing and a contamination check against the eval sets; supervised fine-tuning for 2-3 epochs on 8xH100 with a cosine schedule and packed sequences; one epoch of preference tuning on 4xH100 with a swept beta; quantization into three formats; and serving with speculative draft heads and autoscaling on queue wait. The deliverable is an ablation table of base, SFT only, SFT plus DPO and SFT plus GRPO on the task benchmarks, serving numbers at batch 1, 8 and 32 with the draft acceptance rate and cost per million tokens, a safety pass rate, and a model card with seeds, configs and commit hashes.

questions.title: A payment service must approve, review or block each payment within 100 ms, at 400 requests per second at peak. Fraud labels arrive as chargebacks weeks later. Design the system: the task, the serving mode and its sizing, the data and label plan, the rollout, the failure defaults, and the two things that will quietly break it after launch.
questions.answer: The task is binary classification of fraud probability with two thresholds that split the score into approve, review and block, served online because the decision needs the data of the request. At 400 requests a second and 50 ms per request about 20 requests are in flight at any moment, so the service is small, and the budget leaves room for a feature fetch plus the model. Chargeback labels come weeks after the payment, so training uses a time split and features that exist at payment time, and the rollout goes shadow, then canary on a small share, with the heuristic rule as the default on timeout. The two quiet failures are the feedback loop, where blocked payments never get a label, and concept drift, where the same basket changes its fraud risk and only outcome monitors see it.

questions.title: A chat feature expects 10,000 daily active users with 5 queries each, about 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query, at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens. Measured cache metrics give a 35% hit rate. Walk me through the monthly estimate, and say which number you would attack first.
questions.answer: The traffic is 50,000 queries a day, and a 35% cache hit rate leaves 32,500 that reach the model. Over 30 days that is $3,656 of input and $3,900 of output, about $7,556 a month, against $11,625 without the cache, so the cache saves about $4,070. Output tokens cost four times more per token, so after the hit rate the output length is the number to attack, with a maximum output tokens limit and tighter prompts.

questions.title: A data scientist reports a churn classifier with an AUC of 0.91. Three months after launch, nobody on the retention team uses the scores. The algorithm was fine. Name the design decisions that were missing, and say which metric should have been reported instead.
questions.answer: The failures happened before training: nobody named the action a score starts, the scores arrived weekly while the team called customers daily, a feature leaked the label through the cancellation reason, and nobody compared the model with the rule the team already used. AUC averages over every threshold including ones never used; the decision was to contact the top 5 percent each night, so the right offline number was precision in that top 5 percent, paired with online, business and guardrail metrics.

questions.title: A twelve-stage training pipeline runs from tokenizer to inference server, and the pre-training stage costs weeks and millions of dollars. Before the run starts you must write what happens when each stage fails. Lay out the plan, explain how the orchestrator computes what to rerun, and say what "reproduce the run" can and cannot promise.
questions.answer: Sort the stages by the cost to rerun them: tokenizer, evaluation, quantization and the server are cheap and rerun in hours, supervised tuning and alignment take days, so the base checkpoint is kept and only those stages rerun, and pre-training takes weeks and a budget in the millions, so the plan is the last good checkpoint plus revised downstream stages. The rerun set falls out of the typed, hashed dependency graph: invalidate the failed stage and every descendant. A replay promises the same code, recipe and source data hashes and the same headline metrics, not bit-identical weights or the same output hashes.

questions.title: A reviewer and a customer want to try your model from a link, on a phone, without your notebook. Each model call costs money. Design the demo: the input contract, the order of the checks, the controls for a public link, and what the log is allowed to keep.
questions.answer: Write the contract first: a string of 1 to 500 characters with no control characters, a model call with a known cost, and an output that includes a JSON error with a hint. Run the checks in order of cost, body size, access token, per-client token bucket, input validation, daily cap, and only then the model call. Return a stable error code with a message, a hint and a request id, and log the route, the status, the latency and the input length with a keyed hash of the client, never the text or the address.

questions.title: An engineering organization wants to ask questions across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code and get answers that cite file and line. The index must stay fresh on every push. Design the ingestion, the retrieval, the answer step, the freshness path, and the evaluation, with the budgets you would commit to.
questions.answer: Parse each file into function and class nodes and chunk at those boundaries, give each chunk a dense embedding, sparse terms and a one-sentence summary, and store a graph of imports and calls between chunks. A query runs dense and sparse search in parallel, merges and deduplicates, reranks the top 50 with a cross-encoder to keep 10, and hands those to a long-context model that must cite every claim by file and line; uncited claims are dropped. A push triggers a symbol-level diff so only changed chunks re-embed, with a budget of under 60 seconds for a 50-file push. Quality is measured on 100 labeled cross-repo questions with MRR@10, nDCG@10, citation faithfulness and p50 and p99 latency.

questions.title: A churn model scored well offline and does worse than the older, simpler model on live traffic. Serving features are computed by another team's service. You have a sample of logged serving requests. Design the triage: which comparisons you run, in which order, what each one isolates, and what the fix looks like for each cause you find.
questions.answer: Compare the same entity and time across three pairs. The online store read against the training join tests the whole system and should show zero skew when both read one definition. A fresh computation against the training join isolates staleness, and the second team's code path against a fresh computation isolates code differences such as window boundaries and defaults. Each pair gives a mismatch rate and a mean absolute difference per feature, and the fix for every cause is the same shape: one registry definition that both paths call, with logged serving features checked against it.

questions.title: Design the request path of a chat service that calls a hosted model. Users leave when nothing appears for a few seconds, the provider returns rate limits and server errors at night, and the vector store behind retrieval sometimes times out. Cover what the user sees, how you retry, and what happens when each part fails.
questions.answer: Stream tokens over server-sent events so the first token appears in a few hundred milliseconds even though the full answer takes seconds. Retry provider failures with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at three retries, then fall through an ordered chain of models to a cached answer and finally a short unavailable message. Secondary systems degrade instead of failing the request: no retrieval context when the vector store is down, a direct model call when the cache is down, and a clear message when a guardrail blocks.

questions.title: A product owner asks your team for "a model" to decide which support tickets get escalated. Before you design anything, what questions decide whether this should be a learned model at all, and what would make you answer with a rule instead?
questions.answer: I ask whether a short rule already reaches the goal, whether labels exist or can be collected, whether anyone will act on the prediction, whether the data at decision time holds the signal, and whether one error is acceptable. A model loses when a few conditions stay correct and explain themselves, when there are no labels, or when the cost of building and running the system exceeds the value of the better decisions. A model wins when the rule has grown long and fragile, because a learned model is easier to update than a complex heuristic.

topics.title: Coding
topics.about: Write the code that the lessons build. Each item links to a practice task with checks.

questions.title: Write a training loop for a table of next-character logits: one row per context character, one column per next character. Train it with gradient descent on a text, under a fixed step budget and a seeded generator, until its held-out NLL is lower than a model that ignores the context. Tell me what the held-out check must look like for the comparison to mean anything.
questions.answer: Build the pairs so that the current character is the context and the following character is the target, compute the log-softmax over each row, and descend the mean of the negative target log-probabilities over the training pairs within the step budget. The held-out check scores a fixed split that training never saw, with the same loss definition for the bigram and the unigram baseline, and the model only passes when its held-out value is lower than the baseline's. Reproducibility comes from drawing the initial table from the generator that the caller passes, not from a global one.

questions.title: You get a corpus as a dictionary from words, each a tuple of byte ids, to the number of times the word occurs. Write the training loop that produces an ordered list of merges, and state the three rules that make the loop deterministic. Then tell me what the loop must not do to the caller's data.
questions.answer: Each step counts every adjacent pair inside each word, weighted by the word frequency, picks the pair with the highest count, rewrites every occurrence of that pair into one new id, and records the merge. The three rules are: pairs never cross a word boundary, ties go to the smallest pair in tuple order, and the loop stops when no pair repeats. The input dictionary and its tuples are never changed; the loop builds a new corpus each step.

questions.title: You have a trained model with 64 query heads and 64 key and value heads, and you want to serve it with 8 key and value heads to shrink the cache. Write the function that pools the key projection of the checkpoint into groups, say by what factor the cache memory for keys and values falls, and explain why the pooled model needs more training before it is usable.
questions.answer: Group g of the new projection is the mean of the consecutive heads g r to g r + r - 1, where r is the number of query heads per group, taken over the columns of the projection matrix. The cache holds keys and values for 8 heads instead of 64, so that memory falls by a factor of eight. The mean of several heads is not a head the model was trained with, so quality drops until a short continued training run adapts the query heads to their shared group.

questions.title: Before a long training run you are asked to pick the peak learning rate for a warmup and cosine schedule. Write the sweep that trains a small seeded model at each candidate rate, decides which runs diverged, picks the best stable rate and reports the smallest rate that diverged. State what "diverged" means in code.
questions.answer: Run the same seeded training loop once per candidate rate and record the final loss and the loss history. A run diverged when its final loss is not finite or when the loss grew over the run, not only when it became NaN. The best rate is the lowest final loss among the stable runs, with the smaller rate on a tie, and the smallest diverging rate is reported as the ceiling, because it bounds how high the peak can go.

questions.title: The reference small GPT configuration uses a learned position embedding of shape 1024 by 768. Replace it with a sinusoidal table computed at construction time, add it to a batch of token embeddings, and tell me by how much the parameter count changes and why the model still forwards.
questions.answer: Build a table with one row per position and one column per feature, where column 2i holds the sine and column 2i + 1 holds the cosine of the position divided by the base raised to 2i over the model width. Register it as a buffer, slice the first T rows at each forward and add them to the token embeddings without changing the caller's array. The table has the same shape as the learned one, so the forward pass is unchanged, and the count drops by 786,432 parameters because the table is no longer learned.

questions.title: Write the one line that applies a sampling temperature to a vector of logits, then tell me what happens to the distribution as the temperature goes toward zero, equals one, and goes above one.
questions.answer: Divide the logits by the temperature before the softmax. Near zero the division stretches the gaps between logits, so the largest one takes almost all the mass and sampling becomes greedy. At one the model's own distribution is used, and above one the gaps shrink, the distribution flattens, and rare tokens are drawn more often.

questions.title: Design and implement a tokenizer for a small language model: train it on a corpus, encode fresh text, decode ids back, and reserve two special tokens for document boundaries and padding. State the guarantees the test suite must pin, and explain how the special tokens survive both training and inference without ever being merged.
questions.answer: The base symbols are the 256 raw bytes, so every input has an encoding before any merge and decoding always terminates in bytes. Training runs on pre-tokenized chunks that never contain the special strings, so no merge can produce or consume a special id. At inference a matcher splits the text on the special strings first, maps each one to its reserved id, and runs the merge table on the text between them in training order. The suite pins the round trip on unseen text, on text with multi-byte characters, and on text that contains a literal special string with the flag off.

questions.title: Given the logits of the last position, a temperature, a value of k and a seeded random generator, write the function that draws the next token. State the order of the operations, how ties are broken, and how the draw uses exactly one random number.
questions.answer: Divide the logits by the temperature, keep the k largest and set the rest to negative infinity, take the softmax, and draw one index from the result. Ties keep the lower index. The draw calls the generator once, takes the cumulative sum of the probabilities in vocabulary order, and returns the first index whose cumulative value exceeds the random number.

topics.title: Behavioral
topics.about: Framing work, planning from evidence, delegation and turning feedback into a system.

questions.title: Your organization wants to let coding agents merge changes without a human in the loop for a class of tasks. You are asked to write the policy that says which decisions an agent may make on its own. How do you draw that line, and how does it move over time?
questions.answer: The line follows consequence and reversibility, not task difficulty. A human keeps the choices that change public behavior, risk, authority or irreversible cost; an agent owns bounded investigation, implementation, verification and review. I express that as locked, bounded and delegated decisions in each task contract, and I widen the delegated set only where evidence and rollback are strong, which is calibrated autonomy rather than a fixed switch.

questions.title: For the third time this month you have told a coding agent not to edit the project README during a feature change. Each time it apologized and fixed the run. Tell me what you do now, and why the fix is not a better prompt.
questions.answer: A correction that lives in chat fixes one run. I treat the repeat as evidence about the work system: the scope boundary was not executable. I find the cause behind the symptom, then put a control at the earliest layer that can stop the recurrence, which here is a scope or permission policy rather than another paragraph in the instructions. The control gets an owner, a verification and a date to review or retire it.

questions.title: Tell me about a project where the evidence turned against your plan. What did you do inside your own authority, and how did you present the situation to the person who had to decide?
questions.answer: I separate what I observed from what was reported and what I inferred, name the setback and the evidence that changed my understanding, and move the reversible work I am allowed to do while the blocked decision waits. Then I write a short brief for the decision owner: the user problem and the new evidence, at least two options including a cheaper manual or no-build option where it is credible, the tradeoffs in quality, effort, cost and risk, my recommendation with its remaining uncertainty, and the decision needed with its owner and date.

questions.title: A customer lead spends an hour describing how their support team handles a refund request. You now have to decide what the first version of an assistant does. Tell me how you treat that hour of description, and what you do next.
questions.answer: An interview is reported behavior, which is the third rung of a four-rung ladder. I label every claim from the hour by its rung, then look for direct evidence for the claims that matter most: a trace, a recording, a ticket or a completed form. The steps that stay unproven remain visible as open claims instead of turning into requirements.

questions.title: You inherit a team that collects traces, evaluation scores, support tickets and incident logs for an assistant. Nobody can name a change that any of it caused. Design the mechanism that turns those signals into improvements, and tell me how you keep it from becoming another backlog.
questions.answer: The missing piece is promotion: a defined path from an observation to a durable change with an owner and proof. Each signal is connected to an outcome, a constraint or an assumption, traced to a root cause, and routed to the earliest layer that owns that cause, which is evaluation, context, policy, runtime or a shaped backlog item. Every resulting action carries one owner, a priority from consequence and recurrence, the artifact to change, the verification, a review window and a retirement condition, so the loop produces controls that are later re-examined rather than rules that only accumulate.

questions.title: Your session ends without warning in the middle of a multi-step change, and a colleague picks it up the next morning. What must they be able to find, and where?
questions.answer: They need to see which items are done, which proof ran for each one, which files changed, which dependencies are now unblocked, and what the next safe item is. That state lives next to the work, in the repository, as small items with explicit proof, not as checked boxes inside a chat.

questions.title: You hand a task to a coding agent, or to a new engineer, to add a read-only diagnosis step to an incident tool. Last time the brief was two sentences and the result guessed the system. The time before, the brief was a twelve-page design and the result transcribed a mistake in it. How do you write this one?
questions.answer: I write an executable contract with six surfaces: the outcome, the invariants that must always hold, concrete examples, non-goals, a decision policy, and the proof required before completion. Every decision is marked locked, bounded or delegated by its consequence and reversibility. The production-write boundary is locked, the time budget for the data source is bounded, and local structure and names are delegated with an explanation required.

questions.title: Tell me about a time you defined how a project would be judged before you had any results. What did you write down, and what did you refuse to leave open until later?
questions.answer: I start from the goal, derive the questions it raises, and only then pick the smallest metrics that answer them. Each metric gets a direction, a threshold, a window, a source and a population before any value is observed, and each outcome metric is paired with a guardrail and a counter-metric. I also write the pass, fail and ambiguous decisions in advance, because a team that sees the result first moves the threshold to protect the build.

questions.title: A product manager asks you to build an incident assistant for the on-call team. You have one week. Before you plan any work, what do you ask, and what do you write down first?
questions.answer: The request names an artifact, not a result. I write an outcome frame first: who has the problem, when it happens, what they do today, which observable state must improve, which limits are fixed, and which nearby work is out of scope. Then I check the frame for a product form, a model or an architecture that no evidence supports yet.

questions.title: A teammate, or a coding agent, hands you this plan for a change to a public API: update the endpoint, add tests, update the documentation. They want approval to start. What do you ask for before you say yes, and what would make you reject the plan outright?
questions.answer: That list repeats the request in future tense. I ask for five things on each item: a stable identifier, the smallest change, the repository facts that justify it, the items it depends on, and the exact check that closes it. I reject a plan with a duplicate identifier, an item without evidence or proof, a dependency on an unknown item, a cycle, or an irreversible step scheduled before the uncertainty it depends on is resolved.

questions.title: You discover that a weekend prototype you shared internally is now used every day by another team, with production data, and someone just reported an outage to you. Walk me through what went wrong before this moment and what you do in the first week.
questions.answer: The system drifted across stages. It gained users, data and authority without gaining ownership, and nothing in the system itself marked it as a prototype. In the first week I make the stage observable in configuration, access control, telemetry and documentation, cut the production data path until a named owner accepts it, and decide with that team whether the right next stage is a bounded pilot or a stop.

questions.title: A team's agent instruction file has grown for a year. Rules contradict each other, the context is heavy, and nobody remembers why half of them exist. You are asked to clean it up. How do you decide what stays, what goes, and what you will not touch yet?
questions.answer: Every control needs a retirement condition, and retirement needs evidence like any other change. I review each rule against four questions: did the architecture or workflow it protected change, did a stronger executable control replace it, has the failure stayed away across a meaningful window, and does the rule block legitimate work more often than it prevents harm. A rule that passes none of those stays, and a rule I cannot trace to a cause gets an owner and a review date before it gets deleted.

questions.title: You join a team with a quarter-long roadmap for an assistant that recommends a next action to on-call engineers. The roadmap lists features in priority order. Tell me how you decide what to work on in week one, and why it may not be the first roadmap item.
questions.answer: A roadmap hides uncertainty inside features. I rewrite the features as falsifiable assumptions about value, usability, feasibility, viability and safety, then score each one on impact, uncertainty and irreversibility. Week one goes to the cheapest decisive test of the highest open risk, which is often not the top roadmap item.

questions.title: Your team agrees to ship a minimum viable version of a new assistant. Three proposals are on the table: a polished interface on synthetic data, a working data pipeline with no interface, and a read-only replay over ten real incidents. Which one do you argue for, and how do you justify the choice?
questions.answer: I argue for the replay over real incidents. Small is useful only when the slice proves something that matters, so I first write the required proof set from the highest-risk open assumptions and reject any candidate that does not cover it. The polished page over fake data and the pipeline without users each remove the exact uncertainty the team needs to test.

questions.title: Your manager wants a feature finished faster and suggests that you run two coding agents, or two engineers, in parallel on it. Tell me about a time you had to make that call. How did you decide, and what did you put in place before anyone started?
questions.answer: I delegate only when the work is really independent: two investigations that answer different unknowns, two implementations with disjoint files and contracts, a reviewer who only reads, or a slow external check that runs while local work continues. When the parts need the same files, the same open decision or the same mutable environment, I keep them serial, because a parallel split then converts one clear task into a coordination problem. Before anyone starts, each unit gets a goal, an owner, exclusive write paths, dependencies, a proof and a handoff.

questions.title: Two senior analysts on the same team show you how they triage a flagged transaction. Their steps differ in order, in the tools they open, and in who they ask before they act. Your deadline allows one workflow in the first version. What do you do with the disagreement?
questions.answer: I keep both variants separate until I know why they differ. The difference can come from different roles, different risk levels, a legacy process next to a current one, a difference in expertise, or a real policy disagreement, and each of those leads to a different product. An averaged workflow can describe nobody, so the first version targets one variant on purpose and names the other as a known gap.
